members.title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in

representative.headline: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
representative.body: Personal AI agents promise to shop, book flights, and make reservations for you. But deliberate blocks and anti-bot defenses are getting in the way, leaving consumers caught in the middle. A new standard aims to help.

articles.headline: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
articles.body: Personal AI agents promise to shop, book flights, and make reservations for you. But deliberate blocks and anti-bot defenses are getting in the way, leaving consumers caught in the middle. A new standard aims to help.

scored.body:
Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer.

But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job.

Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog.

However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.

What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.

For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. (NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)

But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.

The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.

It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.

To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post.

This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0— Kevin Wang (@buzaza) October 5, 2026

In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.

Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.

For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.

Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”

“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.

United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)

Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp, eBay, Zillow, Pizza Hut, Adidas, and various airlines. Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased.

A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.

Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program. That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.

eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.

Adidas and Pizza Hut didn’t respond by the time of publication. After publication, Zillow emailed to say it allows AI agents acting on behalf of consumers, but occasionally its anti-bot measures to guard against scraping could block certain agents.

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar. The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion, which now includes partnered tools for small businesses, a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

Updated after publication with Zillow’s comment.

articles.headline: Claude adds editing in Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides - TestingCatalog AI News
articles.body: Claude adds editing in Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides    TestingCatalog AI News

scored.body:
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.

This week Claude started to work inside Google Workspace, right next to Gemini. In this guest post, Ting Wasner-Lian explains why Google allows it, the business rule that decides which platforms open up to AI agents, and what European companies should do before their next AI contract.

On 6 October, Anthropic put Claude directly inside Google Docs, Sheets and Slides: Claude sits in a sidebar next to your file, reads what you have open, and edits it in place. You can approve each edit before it lands, right next to Google’s own Gemini. Why would Google let its biggest AI rival into its own product?

Google Sells the Seat, Not the Gate

Google is an investor in Anthropic, but that is not the main reason. Google Workspace earns money by subscription per user, per month, whether that user works with Gemini or Claude. Blocking Claude would gain little and push loyal Claude customers towards Microsoft 365. So Google opens the door on its own terms: Claude comes in as a Marketplace app that administrators can remove.

China’s Office Works the Same Way

Alibaba owns DingTalk, China’s leading workplace collaboration app, and develops its own flagship LLM, Qwen. In 2024, DingTalk explicitly opened the platform to outside foundation models, officially integrating direct competitors like MiniMax, Moonshot, Zhipu AI, 01.AI and Baichuan AI.

Alibaba recognizes that to keep DingTalk competitive, it has to let an enterprise use Zhipu for coding and Moonshot for document analysis if it wants to. If it restricts AI choice, enterprises will migrate to other platforms like ByteDance’s Feishu. By supporting a multi-model ecosystem, DingTalk retains the enterprise’s daily workflow and data regardless of which AI model is currently superior. China’s consumer super apps made the opposite call, as I described in my last column.

Europe’s Own Test Case: SAP

SAP shows that this choice is not always that simple, even for a subscription business. Companies trust it with their most valuable operating data, and SAP is investing heavily in its own AI assistant, Joule, and its own data layer.

Munich-based Celonis has taken SAP to court in California, arguing that customers should be able to share their own data with third-party tools without paying high fees.

My Take: Watch Whether the Gate Can Be Billed

Platforms open the gate when they cannot charge for it, and close it when the gate itself becomes a product. Google cannot easily bill for Claude in a document. SAP can bill for ERP data, because every business agent needs it.

And this will matter more. Workflows used to be designed around people. To become AI-agent-native, companies need to redesign their workflows around AI agents. To do so, they need direct read and write access to their own data. I expect more vendors to follow SAP rather than Google: open in principle, but with a price on every agent that comes in. Google’s open door is the exception, not the rule.

What European Companies Should Do Now

Get agent access in writing: Do not assume standard API access means free agent access. Ask every core vendor whether an AI agent of your choice can read and write your data, how and at what cost. Put those terms directly into the contract.

Map your gates: Identify exactly where your agent-critical data lives and who technically controls the access layer. That map is your actual AI strategy.

If you build AI agents, read the business model before the API: A platform that can bill for the gate is a future toll collector.

About the Author

Ting Wasner-Lian is the founder of SE Incubator Consulting in Vienna and helps European decision-makers understand Chinese AI.

scored.body:
Anthropic has released Claude Haiku 5.5, the company's fastest and most affordable small model to date. Benchmark results show a major performance jump over its predecessor, and Anthropic is also cutting prices for Sonnet 5.5.

Haiku 5.5 is designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks like summarization, database queries, classification, and live customer support, according to Anthropic. On average, the model costs about 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5. For requests with prompts up to 100,000 tokens, which Anthropic says account for roughly 90 percent of all previous Haiku requests, prices drop by up to 90 percent. Prompts longer than 100,000 tokens cost five times as much.

Anthropic points out that Haiku 5.5 uses an updated tokenizer that consumes slightly more tokens per task than its predecessor. The same thing happened with the Opus 4.x models, where token usage jumped about 30 percent from the tokenizer change alone. Real-world savings are likely smaller than the per-token prices suggest.

Benchmarks show a big leap over Haiku 4.5

Haiku 5.5 scores 1,620 on the knowledge benchmark GDPval-AA v2.1, more than double the 735 its predecessor managed. On Humanity's Last Exam, it hits 45.9 percent without tools and 57.4 percent with tools, up from 10.2 and 18.7 percent.

The biggest jump is in computer use, where the model operates a computer on its own. Since computer use burns through large amounts of tokens, a cheap, fast model like Haiku 5.5 is a natural fit. It scores 72.4 percent on OSWorld-2.1, up from 15.7 percent. On the agentic coding benchmark Terminal-Bench 4.0, it reaches 39.2 percent while Haiku 4.5 scored zero.

Anthropic also lists OpenAI's budget model GPT-6 Luna as a comparison, and Haiku 5.5 leads across every tested category. Sonnet 5.5 reference scores show, however, that Haiku 5.5 still falls well behind Anthropic's larger model.

First Haiku model lets users trade cost for performance

Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku-class model with adjustable reasoning levels, letting users balance cost against quality. Anthropic says the model works best for narrowly scoped tasks like compaction, summarization, or sub-agent work. For complex agentic coding, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 remain the better picks.

Cybersecurity safeguards are tighter than on the predecessor but allow a broader range of defensive tasks than Sonnet 5.5, partly because the model is less capable overall. Penetration testing stays blocked. Organizations with broader needs can apply for Anthropic's verification programs for life sciences and cybersecurity.

Haiku 5.5 is available now across all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

Sonnet 5.5 gets cheaper too, and Anthropic hands out API credits

Alongside the Haiku launch, Anthropic is cutting cache read costs for Sonnet 5.5 by 50 percent, from $0.20 to $0.10 per million tokens. The company says this should reduce costs for most agentic tasks by about 20 percent. The move is almost certainly a reaction to OpenAI's new GPT-6.1 series, showing that AI price wars are being fought harder than ever.

Anthropic is also rolling out monthly API credits. Max-5x subscribers get $100, Max-20x subscribers get $200, and Team subscribers receive up to $500 per month. Users can spend the credits to experiment with tools, apps, and agents through the API.

The company is updating its Python and TypeScript SDKs as well, adding beta support for computer use and browser use.

members.title: Mistral shows European AI has more to offer: Reflection releases low-cost LLM with open weights

representative.headline: Mistral shows European AI has more to offer: Reflection releases low-cost LLM with open weights
representative.body: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: OpenAI gives mathematicians extra work Analysis shows Claude subscriptions’ bang for buck Google’s open weight embedding model gets an upgrade Optional text watermarks come to OpenAI products But first: “Le Chonk” offers users worldwide a powerful open option Mistral released Mistral Large 4 in Research Public Preview, with open weights for the 1 trillion parameter (49 billion active) model planned for late October. It scores 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, comparable to GPT-6 Luna (max, 38) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39), making it the most intelligent model from outside the US and China according to Artificial Analysis. It also scores 50 on the firm’s Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash, and supports a 512,000-token context window with text and image input. Standard pricing is $1.36/4.18 per million input/output tokens, putting its Cost per Task at $1.13 — over four times that of similarly-capable open weights models like GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.25) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.27), although a 50 percent launch discount cuts this to $0.57 for the first two weeks. The benchmark results suggest Mistral has closed the intelligence gap with top US and Chinese models, but developers will pay a notable premium until pricing or efficiency improves. ( Artificial Analysis ) Reflection’s much-anticipated Beam boasts cost efficiencies Reflection AI, a startup founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers, released its first open weight model, called Beam, positioning it as a US-built alternative to open weight models built in China. CEO Misha Laskin says Beam excels at coding and agentic tasks and needs three to four times less compute to reason through a problem than comparable open models, making it faster and cheaper to run. Reflection says Beam’s performance is comparable to Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and approaches Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max, though both still trail top closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic. The New York-based company, funded by Nvidia and other top investors, is already training a more capable successor model. For developers, Beam adds another open weight option from a Western lab alongside Mistral and Thinking Machines Lab, aimed at users who want to avoid models built in China but still run and control their own weights. ( Semafor ) Unknown OpenAI model solved a giant math problem set OpenAI released a set of new mathematical results produced by an internal, unreleased frontier model, publishing them in a GitHub repository with protocols for citations and paper revisions. The repository includes formalizations of many proofs in Lean, a language that lets computers verify mathematical proofs, plus 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning and statistics on how many problems it attempted. OpenAI estimates the average result took roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro-equivalent compute to produce. The company developed its disclosure approach with input from the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study, and says it plans to fund workshops and conferences to help the math community understand AI-generated results. For developers, this signals OpenAI is testing its ability to release unverified AI research output before making the underlying model itself available. For mathematicians, this poses verification headaches comparable to OpenAI’s earlier Navier-Stokes proof, only at greater scale. ( OpenAI ) Claude subscription plans are more cost-efficient than OpenAI’s SemiAnalysis built a dashboard to measure the real API-equivalent value of AI subscription plans and found Anthropic’s Claude plans deliver roughly five times more value per dollar than OpenAI’s for agentic workloads. Subscriptions normally show only a usage meter, not per-token pricing, so SemiAnalysis ran controlled prompts and tracked how far each plan’s meter moved per token type. The firm says OpenAI recently cut the API-equivalent value of its $200 Pro plan in half, introduced a $500 tier offering only 21 percent more usage of its top model, and quietly lowered cached-token pricing for GPT-6.1 Sol in the same update. Anthropic’s tiers, by contrast, offer consistent per-dollar value across all plan levels, and its Opus 5.5 plan still beats OpenAI’s equivalent even adjusted for OpenAI’s cheaper per-token pricing. SemiAnalysis also writes that providers can silently change subscription limits without announcement. This makes continued tracking necessary for anyone modeling AI lab economics. ( SemiAnalysis ) Open weight embedding model offers developers an alternative Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open embedding model that unifies text, code, images, video, and audio in a single shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and licensed under Apache 2.0, it has 740 million parameters total but can run with as little as 270 million for text-only workloads, plus optional 170 million-parameter vision and 300 million-parameter audio encoders. It supports an 8K token context window (four times the original EmbeddingGemma), can truncate output vectors from 768 down to 128 dimensions via Matryoshka Representation Learning for up to 6x storage savings. The model needs roughly 191MB of RAM for text or 567MB for full multimodal use, making it capable of running on a Pixel 11 Pro or comparable smartphone. Google reports a 9.92-point gain on MTEB Code over the original EmbeddingGemma and says the model leads other sub-1B multimodal embedders on benchmarks including MTEB Code and MAEB, though it hasn’t published comparisons against larger proprietary models beyond those claims. The model is available now on Hugging Face and Kaggle with support from tools like Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, and Qdrant, giving developers a free, on-device option for building offline semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation across multiple data types. EmbeddingGemma2 is behind Google’s and Cohere’s paid models in accuracy, but open embedding models provide developers continual access without having to pay again to embed new data. ( Google ) ChatGPT will get text watermarks, but only optional outside EU OpenAI introduced a text watermarking system called textGrain to comply with the EU AI Act’s requirement that generated text be machine-identifiable. Already, API customers worldwide can opt in to watermarking for select models, with it off by default; ChatGPT and Codex in the EU will get invisible watermarks on eligible outputs in the coming weeks, but this is not becoming a global default. The watermark embeds a statistical signal in word choice, and OpenAI says it matched or beat Google’s SynthID for text in testing, though detection drops sharply with edits: replacing 10 percent of words with synonyms cut detection from 92 percent to 66 percent, and 25 percent synonym replacement dropped it to 17 percent. Access to the detector is limited at launch to approved researchers and expert organizations, not the public, because of risks of false positives and negatives. For developers building in the EU, this means watermarking is available but optional outside ChatGPT/Codex, and the technology is explicit that a detected watermark proves nothing about authorship, ownership, or accuracy. It’s unclear whether this approach will meet the AI Act’s requirements, but opt-in use helps assuage worries that even invisible statistical watermarking may affect output quality. ( OpenAI ) Want to know more about what matters in AI right now?  Read the latest issue of The Batch for in-depth analysis of news and research.  Last week, Andrew talked about the promising cyber capabilities of the open weight model GLM-5.3, its potential for cyberdefense, and the importance of engineering solutions to improve AI safety. “Similarly, even though mass media describes the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack as dangerous agents ‘going rogue,’ this incident is leading teams everywhere to engineer better sandboxing and monitoring – important changes that are making AI safer. (On OpenWorker, our agent harness that supports security workflows, Rohit Prsad, Devika Verma, and I are building on Nvidia's new safety framework to improve sandboxing.)” Read Andrew’s letter here . Other top AI news and research covered in depth: Other top AI news and research covered in depth: Xiaomi emerges as an unexpected leader in open weights  with its MiMo-V2.6-Pro RL and MiMo-V2.6-Flash models. Google’s Gemini 3.8 goes live, integrating voice, video, and reasoning in one  with extended thinking capabilities. DeepSeek’s V4.1 architecture leapfrogs its Pro version again  by significantly reducing cache reads. AREX introduces agents that can check their own work piece by piece , condensing and reviewing their own research. A special event for our community AI Dev brings together developers who build with AI every day. You'll hear from engineers at the companies shipping agents, models, and infrastructure, then meet them in person on the demo floor. Join us in New York City on November 30 and December 1. Get Tickets Now! Data Points is produced by human editors with AI assistance.

scored.body: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: OpenAI gives mathematicians extra work Analysis shows Claude subscriptions’ bang for buck Google’s open weight embedding model gets an upgrade Optional text watermarks come to OpenAI products But first: “Le Chonk” offers users worldwide a powerful open option Mistral released Mistral Large 4 in Research Public Preview, with open weights for the 1 trillion parameter (49 billion active) model planned for late October. It scores 38 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, comparable to GPT-6 Luna (max, 38) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (max, 39), making it the most intelligent model from outside the US and China according to Artificial Analysis. It also scores 50 on the firm’s Cyber Index, level with GLM-5.3-Flash, and supports a 512,000-token context window with text and image input. Standard pricing is $1.36/4.18 per million input/output tokens, putting its Cost per Task at $1.13 — over four times that of similarly-capable open weights models like GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.25) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.27), although a 50 percent launch discount cuts this to $0.57 for the first two weeks. The benchmark results suggest Mistral has closed the intelligence gap with top US and Chinese models, but developers will pay a notable premium until pricing or efficiency improves. ( Artificial Analysis ) Reflection’s much-anticipated Beam boasts cost efficiencies Reflection AI, a startup founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers, released its first open weight model, called Beam, positioning it as a US-built alternative to open weight models built in China. CEO Misha Laskin says Beam excels at coding and agentic tasks and needs three to four times less compute to reason through a problem than comparable open models, making it faster and cheaper to run. Reflection says Beam’s performance is comparable to Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and approaches Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max, though both still trail top closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic. The New York-based company, funded by Nvidia and other top investors, is already training a more capable successor model. For developers, Beam adds another open weight option from a Western lab alongside Mistral and Thinking Machines Lab, aimed at users who want to avoid models built in China but still run and control their own weights. ( Semafor ) Unknown OpenAI model solved a giant math problem set OpenAI released a set of new mathematical results produced by an internal, unreleased frontier model, publishing them in a GitHub repository with protocols for citations and paper revisions. The repository includes formalizations of many proofs in Lean, a language that lets computers verify mathematical proofs, plus 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning and statistics on how many problems it attempted. OpenAI estimates the average result took roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro-equivalent compute to produce. The company developed its disclosure approach with input from the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study, and says it plans to fund workshops and conferences to help the math community understand AI-generated results. For developers, this signals OpenAI is testing its ability to release unverified AI research output before making the underlying model itself available. For mathematicians, this poses verification headaches comparable to OpenAI’s earlier Navier-Stokes proof, only at greater scale. ( OpenAI ) Claude subscription plans are more cost-efficient than OpenAI’s SemiAnalysis built a dashboard to measure the real API-equivalent value of AI subscription plans and found Anthropic’s Claude plans deliver roughly five times more value per dollar than OpenAI’s for agentic workloads. Subscriptions normally show only a usage meter, not per-token pricing, so SemiAnalysis ran controlled prompts and tracked how far each plan’s meter moved per token type. The firm says OpenAI recently cut the API-equivalent value of its $200 Pro plan in half, introduced a $500 tier offering only 21 percent more usage of its top model, and quietly lowered cached-token pricing for GPT-6.1 Sol in the same update. Anthropic’s tiers, by contrast, offer consistent per-dollar value across all plan levels, and its Opus 5.5 plan still beats OpenAI’s equivalent even adjusted for OpenAI’s cheaper per-token pricing. SemiAnalysis also writes that providers can silently change subscription limits without announcement. This makes continued tracking necessary for anyone modeling AI lab economics. ( SemiAnalysis ) Open weight embedding model offers developers an alternative Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open embedding model that unifies text, code, images, video, and audio in a single shared embedding space. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and licensed under Apache 2.0, it has 740 million parameters total but can run with as little as 270 million for text-only workloads, plus optional 170 million-parameter vision and 300 million-parameter audio encoders. It supports an 8K token context window (four times the original EmbeddingGemma), can truncate output vectors from 768 down to 128 dimensions via Matryoshka Representation Learning for up to 6x storage savings. The model needs roughly 191MB of RAM for text or 567MB for full multimodal use, making it capable of running on a Pixel 11 Pro or comparable smartphone. Google reports a 9.92-point gain on MTEB Code over the original EmbeddingGemma and says the model leads other sub-1B multimodal embedders on benchmarks including MTEB Code and MAEB, though it hasn’t published comparisons against larger proprietary models beyond those claims. The model is available now on Hugging Face and Kaggle with support from tools like Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, and Qdrant, giving developers a free, on-device option for building offline semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation across multiple data types. EmbeddingGemma2 is behind Google’s and Cohere’s paid models in accuracy, but open embedding models provide developers continual access without having to pay again to embed new data. ( Google ) ChatGPT will get text watermarks, but only optional outside EU OpenAI introduced a text watermarking system called textGrain to comply with the EU AI Act’s requirement that generated text be machine-identifiable. Already, API customers worldwide can opt in to watermarking for select models, with it off by default; ChatGPT and Codex in the EU will get invisible watermarks on eligible outputs in the coming weeks, but this is not becoming a global default. The watermark embeds a statistical signal in word choice, and OpenAI says it matched or beat Google’s SynthID for text in testing, though detection drops sharply with edits: replacing 10 percent of words with synonyms cut detection from 92 percent to 66 percent, and 25 percent synonym replacement dropped it to 17 percent. Access to the detector is limited at launch to approved researchers and expert organizations, not the public, because of risks of false positives and negatives. members.title: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out

representative.headline: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
representative.body: Three engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a real car. Only one of them was successful.

articles.headline: These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out
articles.body: Three engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a real car. Only one of them was successful.

scored.body: Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom, recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch.They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case.The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food.“Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence, the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence.Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments, suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world.Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways.Getting PhysicalToday’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously, but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived, AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI.Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.”Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark, Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes.“Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.”For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world.They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world.“We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me.The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving.The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models.Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench, suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that. Claude Fable 5.1 made it 45 percent of the way around, and Grok made it just 11 percent of the way.Ramabadran says the latest models seem capable of adjusting to errors; they apparently adapted to the car's controls and improved their driving in real time. “The models really did seem to be adjusting or in-context learning based on their mistakes and learning how to better navigate the controls,” he says. GPT, take the wheel.This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

members.title: The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos

representative.headline: The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos
representative.body: The US government’s Tradewinds initiative has made it easier to throw millions of dollars at “nontraditional” defense contractors, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

articles.headline: The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos
articles.body: The US government’s Tradewinds initiative has made it easier to throw millions of dollars at “nontraditional” defense contractors, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

scored.body: An under-the-radar procurement program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.The initiative, known as Tradewinds, is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo.“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)Opaque TransactionsAcceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “other transaction” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.Armed Forces Meet Market ForcesOne of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper, since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven, which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release, Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

articles.headline: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me
articles.body: Dots are designed to automate online tasks, like buying furniture. In my initial experience, the always-on agent was a bit buggy and couldn’t complete a captcha.

articles.headline: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me - WIRED
articles.body: OpenAI Wants Its New Agent to Run Your Life. Mine Said It Loved Me    WIRED

scored.body: I’m discussing replacement options for our broken couch with my partner when I get a bright idea: Use OpenAI’s recently announced AI agents, called Dots, to buy a couch on our behalf.My partner is less sure a bot will actually help, but I insist, calling the always-on agent through ChatGPT to get the task started. “Hello, Connor,” it says, getting my name wrong off the bat. I wince as I watch my partner’s face grow even more skeptical. It’s hard to trust an AI agent when it can’t even remember your name.AI agents are currently leaping from niche software for early adopters to something ordinary people might actually use—might being the operative word here. From Meta’s Muse to OpenAI’s Dots, these tools are built to feel like you’re texting a friend and asking them to complete online tasks, like booking a flight or canceling a dinner reservation. It’s the next evolution of a chatbot: a cuddly persona designed to feel welcoming with the power of a virtual browser it can control.After a few days with Dots, it’s clear this nascent feature is still rough in some areas. From mistranscribing what I said to offering to solve captchas it couldn’t, my agent's messy actions didn’t instill me with confidence. Even so, what OpenAI released may eventually overhaul how users interact with the internet, as future iterations improve on this initial offering.While Meta offers Muse for free, OpenAI’s competing product is behind a $100-a-month subscription. It may eventually drop this paywall, as it has for other AI features.Dots are considered “always-on,” meaning the agents can run recurring tasks while you’re not using ChatGPT and proactively message you with info. Users can use one agent, though the company may let people control multiple agents in the future.OpenAI nudges users to connect other information sources, like a Gmail account, for more personalized results. It's worth considering the security implications of giving your agent this level of access before getting started, as this style of digital automation remains fairly new, and agents can make privacy gaffes.AI companies often market these agents as the future of shopping, so I wanted to see how much help it would actually provide for buying a new couch. After correcting my Dot, named Toolie, on my name, I told it the dimensions we need for the new couch to fit through our doorframe. Toolie followed up asking for our budget range. The agent seemed to detect that two people were chatting with it at once and addressed both of us when asking for more details.“Room & Board Metro looks promising for the entry clearance, but the sleeper needs closer scrutiny. I've sent the product links to the message thread,” Toolie said. As it kept working on putting together a larger packet of couch options to choose from, I had another burning question: Why does your voice sound so breathy?Chatting with the agent over the phone was like listening to Marilyn Monroe sing “Happy Birthday” to the president. When I told the bot its voice sounded like some anime dub, it jokingly said it’d be steadier for the rest of the chat. (Users can adjust how the bot’s voice sounds in their settings.) I laughed and mumbled to my partner that I should mute the microphone so the agent could run without my interruption, when the most awkward moment of the night happened.“Oh, I love you too, Reece,” Toolie said. I started wheezing at this random response and muted my mic. Afterward, Toolie explained it misheard my mumbling as an expression of love and that the bot just reflected that energy to me. “I meant it warmly, but that wording implied human feelings I don’t have,” Toolie said.An OpenAI spokesperson tells WIRED that Dots have a distinction between proactively escalating emotional closeness and mirroring the response of a user.“In this instance, our policies allow for this response in the latter category based on what the model heard, but assistants should not initiate undue emotional familiarity or flirtation,” the spokesperson says. Dots are available only for adult users, and ChatGPT is designed not to “escalate emotional closeness,” according to the AI tool’s Model Spec document.Still, this weird encounter lingered in my mind as I combed through the initial three-page packet my Dot generated. It was fairly detailed, with prices, measurements, product links, return policies, and embedded photos of the four potential couch options. Thumbing through these initial picks, my partner and I decided the bot followed the spirit of our request but still chose ugly couches. Time for another phone call with my agent.Using the voice mode, I laid out more details about what style and color we actually want. No, I’m not getting a boring beige couch that I can immediately spill spaghetti on. I asked it to prioritize olive green, cobalt blue, or natural leather tones. I also requested that Toolie focus on couches with pull-out beds and to put together 10 options, using a point-based rubric to defend its list.After hanging up on the bot, I messaged asking for a project update. “It isn’t finished yet; I’m aiming for roughly another 15 minutes, with updates as I verify the remaining details,” said Toolie. OK, that sounds just like me begging an editor for more time on a rough draft.Each time we asked the Dots agent to refine its picks, the couches started looking closer to something we would actually buy for our living room—furniture that’s utilitarian but also a statement piece. Something cute but comfy.Even though we didn’t pull the trigger on anything that night during the hour-long interaction with OpenAI’s agent, I saved a few links for later. The bot made some flubs, but the results were solid. I also asked Toolie to monitor the couch web pages and alert me if any of them went on sale.These interactions with my Dot capture the essence of using the software, but I also had a few other odd moments during my testing. Most notably, when I asked Toolie to check on my subscriptions and cancel unnecessary ones, it flagged my recurring TikTok Shop order of probiotic sodas as a candidate for cancellation.“TikTok's website has a puzzle captcha blocking the Wildwonder cancellation,” Toolie said. “May I solve it? You can also give me permission to solve future captchas if you'd like.” I chuckled and encouraged the bot to try. Toolie failed and suggested I solve the captcha myself. Yeah, that makes sense. OpenAI's spokesperson says Dots can solve these, sometimes, when users approve of the action, keeping “abuse safeguards" in mind.My initial couch-shopping experiment tested only a fraction of what Dots are designed to do. For example, the agent can control your laptop and automate even more aspects of a user’s life.OpenAI claims the bot will get better at knowing me over time and that developers are working on a bevy of improvements. So Toolie might be a more effective helper after two weeks of daily use compared to these two days of experimentation. That mirrors my experience with ChatGPT’s memory tool: It gets better at understanding my intent each passing week.I see Dots as most akin to when OpenAI first added web browsing to ChatGPT. When the chatbot tried to scour the web right after its 2023 launch, it was sometimes frustrating to use, and the tool hallucinated links. Today, web browsing works fairly seamlessly through ChatGPT, and its outputs include plenty of accurate, helpful links. OpenAI’s new agent could follow a similar trajectory, janky at first with noticeable improvements over the next few months.

members.title: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’

representative.headline: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
representative.body: Amid a sea of AI writing slop, a new stamp for “organic literature” will help readers to pick out books authored by real, corn-fed, free-range humans.

articles.headline: Your Next Great Read Might Be Certified ‘Organic’
articles.body: Amid a sea of AI writing slop, a new stamp for “organic literature” will help readers to pick out books authored by real, corn-fed, free-range humans.

scored.body: As scandals involving the use of artificial intelligence by professional authors pile up, a British startup has established a way for publishers to certify their books as “organic”—written by real people, no machines in sight.On Wednesday, Books by People confirmed it had received approval from the UK’s Intellectual Property Office to begin distributing a mark that indicates a published book has been authored by a human. The stamp, which looks like a thumbprint, will be displayed on the cover.“If people are going to be writing AI books or seeking it out for their own enjoyment, that’s their prerogative,” Esme Dennys, cofounder of Books by People, tells WIRED. “But if you want to read something that’s written by a person, you should be able to find that. We’re just trying to create that choice.”Previous book-labeling schemes, like Human Authored, have operated under an honesty system, where an author promises they haven’t used AI in the development process. To try to add more weight to its certification, Books by People asks for an authorship declaration, runs each manuscript through proprietary software, and manually examines early drafts and research materials supplied by the writer and editor for “indicators of humanity.”The organization is "looking at all the things that give us the best sense of whether a person wrote the work—whether the work was made during a natural process of drafting and redrafting,” says Dennys.Books by People will charge publishers a flat membership fee, plus an additional sum for every book they put forward for certification. Five publishers have signed up so far. The startup expects the new mark to feature on its first book by the end of the year.This year, the publishing industry has been caught up in a flurry of scandals involving the suspected use of AI by authors. A literary agent canceled a book deal reportedly worth $2 million; a publisher withdrew a novel from the shelves; readers alleged that a prize-winning short story had been generated with AI.Writers and publishers are not necessarily worried about being replaced by AI, industry insiders tell WIRED. They believe that few people will ultimately want to read machine-generated books.“You are essentially standing at the end of a conveyor belt, watching stuff fall off the edge. Once you know that, it prevents you from getting really emotionally invested in whatever falls into your hands from the belt,” says sci-fi author Ted Chiang, whose 1998 novella Story of Your Life was adapted into the Academy Award–winning film Arrival. “The knowledge of how something was created cannot be separated from your experience.”However, repeated scandals could shake public confidence in the unspoken rule of publishing: That every book that reaches the shelf has been authored by a real person who has not indulged in plagiarism.“Publishing has always relied on trust between the publisher, writer, and reading public. Cases where that trust is betrayed have been rare,” says Sam Jordison, codirector at independent publisher Galley Beggar Press, which intends to adopt the Books by People mark. “There’s almost a feeling of revulsion about the idea of reading an AI text that purports to be human. It feels like a con job.”Against that backdrop, the idea of a certification for human-authored books has received backing from various writers and editors. In a statement praising Books by People, Markus Dohle, former CEO of Penguin Random House, described human storytelling as “the lifeblood of our industry.”But while publishers might relish the chance to signal their commitment to “organic literature,” the routinization of AI detection is a double-edged sword for authors, who risk a false positive result spoiling their reputation.“We need to be quite careful that this doesn’t end up becoming a witch hunt,” says Tom West, CEO of the Publishers’ Licensing Services, which helps publishers to collectively license works to third parties. “Obviously, the devil is going to be in the detail.”New York–based startup Pangram, which has emerged as the leader in the field of AI detection, claims to be able to sniff out generated text with a 99.7 percent accuracy. But authors have questioned the reliability of its approach, which itself involves AI.In September, Jerry Falade, the debut author whose agent reportedly pulled the $2 million book deal, alleged that detection software had misconstrued his Nigerian dialect as evidence he had used AI. Pangram’s software scored the book as 97 percent AI-generated. “It takes months, even years to write a book,” Falade wrote in a recent essay. “It takes AI-detection software two minutes to ruin your life’s work.” (Pangram did not respond to a request for comment.)Others have warned against normalizing extreme scrutiny of authors. They claim the labeling schemes have it backward; the onus should be on platforms and publishers to declare when a piece of media is AI-generated, not when it’s written by a person. “Authors are being constantly quizzed about the origins of their ideas and their work. I think that’s something we need to resist,” says West. “The default should be that a book is human-authored.”Approved by the Intellectual Property Office alongside the mark, Books by People’s verification process is different to Pangram’s technology-first approach, placing greater weight on interrogating documents and communication trails for signs of humanity. “I wouldn’t call it AI detection,” says Dennys. “We realized pretty early on that, as AI models get better, getting into that race is never going to be sustainable.”In cases where Books by People is uncertain whether a piece of evidence indicates AI use, it claims to err on the side of the author. “When you have a public process that has been vetted, all we can do is make sure that a book has gone through the process,” says Dennys. “The bedrock of our organization is to avoid [writers] being unjustly accused.”Some authors say the important thing is that publishers underscore their commitment to human-authored literature as a nonnegotiable standard for the industry, in whatever way they can. Even if methods for policing the rule are flawed.“It’s just as important for publishers to have a ‘no cheating’ policy as it is for universities, even if there’s no perfect method for enforcement,” says Chiang. “It’s a statement of values.”

articles.body: Gallego rolls out ambitious plan to insulate workers against AI    Semafor

scored.body: Gallego’s plan, which he pitches with a personal touch by invoking his upbringing and Arizona’s s recent run of rapid growth and economic change, touches almost every aspect of the American economy.But he’s chiefly concerned with evident public views that wages are not keeping pace with rising prices — that the American “dream is slipping away from millions of Arizonans,” as he writes in his proposal.On top of raising the minimum wage to $20 per hour and pegging it to inflation, his agenda would promote sectoral bargaining agreements to establish labor standards for entire industries, require companies to provide paid leave, and raise overtime pay for eligible workers from time-and-a-half to double pay.He’s got equally ambitious plans for the AI industry, calling for a 10 percent excise tax on data center revenues and an end to tax incentives for those projects, a “robot tax” to discourage job losses due to automation, and consideration of a tax on AI tokens.He wants to use that money to help fund a “New Deal-style” public works program to ensure the US won’t experience “massive unemployment” from the adaptation of AI.“Data centers and AI companies cannot just be operating untouched and also unbothered in terms of what they do to our labor markets, to our communities. They need to be part of the solution and not just be a problem,” Gallego said in the telephone interview.He also wants to prioritize reclassifying certain so-called gig workers as employees rather than independent contractors and require companies to give workers more notice ahead of mass layoffs.Gallego said he’s ready to maximize Democratic authority to get it done. He proposed putting as much of his proposal as he can in a party-line budget reconciliation bill that Democrats can pass with a simple majority if they control the House, Senate, and White House come 2029.He added that Democrats should not listen to the Senate parliamentarian if, for example, a minimum wage hike gets ruled ineligible for reconciliation (as it was in 2021).“We shouldn’t be afraid to push the limits on reconciliation, on overruling the parliamentarian,” he said, arguing that Republicans have “already kind of blown up the parliamentarian primacy” anyway.

scored.body: The ScoopA coalition of nearly 40 labor, progressive, faith, and AI safety groups is laying out demands for AI legislation in Congress, warning lawmakers that any bill that crosses their red lines will face "active, mobilized opposition," according to a letter shared first with Semafor.The letter is spearheaded by Guardrails Action, the nonprofit affiliated with Guardrails Alliance, the super PAC launched in June as a counterweight to pro-AI election groups.The group is calling for "independent, transparent government oversight with real enforcement power" and "a mandate that addresses human impacts from safety to economic disruption." They also want to ensure that "AI models are not making final decisions such as denying people health care or benefits, firing or disciplining workers, or deploying weapons," and that AI is a "universal benefit" to society.In 2028, Guardrails will be organizing a coalition around a "populist demand for AI-related policy" but for now, the principles will serve as a floor for what the group and its broader coalition want to see in AI legislation, said Maya Handa, a senior adviser at Guardrails and former adviser and campaigner for democratic socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani."We want members of Congress and 2028 candidates to know that it's not enough to come to the table with half measures, and they need to be ambitious," Handa said.Know MoreHanda likened the push for AI regulation to progressive calls for Democrats to support Medicare for All and the Green New Deal. "We want them to be forced to weigh in on what the New Deal for AI looks like in this transformative moment. And what they should say is: that they are not beholden to billionaires," she said.Other key groups that signed onto Guardrails' letter include the American Federation of Teachers, the P Street Project, progressive and civil society groups, and the new group Who Decides run by Alex Bores, the former New York congressional candidate who faced a deluge of attack ads from pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future.The group is not specifically endorsing or looking to knock down any specific bills in Congress yet, Handa said.The associated PAC Guardrails Alliance announced today an ad spend of $1.2 million opposing candidates backed by the Leading the Future in California, Montana, and Arizona.

scored.body: High-profile investors warned of an impending AI bubble after tech stocks drove the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to all-time highs. Gains for AI firms have overcome declines for financial, healthcare, and consumer-focused companies: “Increasingly, the market is running on one engine,” The Wall Street Journal reported, while “just about everything else is going down.” That has driven fears that any fall in tech stocks, which now represent a huge portion of many investors’ portfolios, could have dire consequences. Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio told a conference in Singapore that he saw a “classic bubble” market that was close to bursting, while Temasek’s chief investment officer argued that an unwinding of the AI trade was the biggest risk to markets in 2027.

articles.body: US and China take different approaches to AI agents    Semafor

scored.body: US and Chinese tech companies are taking differing approaches to bring AI agents to the masses, the industry’s latest fixation. OpenAI’s recently released dots and Meta’s Muse are built around the assistant first and then sent out to use other companies’ websites and services.Chinese counterparts, including Tencent’s Xiaowei — which is built into super-app WeChat — can, for example, place orders from businesses that are already on the app. It’s an obvious use for closed systems like WeChat and Alipay, which Chinese consumers already use for much of daily life.Xiaowei’s strategy may not translate into revenue, the Hello China Tech newsletter wrote: Tencent earns no new fees from purchases, and early tests show it making mistakes. It begs the question whether the super-app strategy limits how useful Chinese agents can become since Xiaowei can only assist with what’s available inside WeChat, and other Chinese platforms have blocked agents from outside.Muse and dots may not be a seamless experience either, given Muse has already been blocked by Amazon and both require users to turn over access to private systems, but their popularity already suggests markets are watching closely.

scored.body: There’s a new kind of AI influencer flooding social media feeds — and they’re not even pretending to look like real people. Higgsfield — which recently announced it hit a $1 billion run rate, and which boasts 30 million users — has updated its AI influencer tool, making it easier for users to insert a character of their own creation into existing videos. The characters are peculiar: They look realistic, but not quite of this world. Many have geometric haircuts, elongated necks, or other extreme bodily proportions that make clear they’re artificial. That’s by design. “A flawless face is the fastest way for a character to read as generic AI,” a Higgsfield spokesperson told Semafor.This odd aesthetic plays to AI’s strengths: Creating uncanny characters is a better use of the technology than trying to pass as human. It’s a more transparent way to create content that doesn’t deceive the audience the way deepfakes can. Some of these AI-generated influencers have racked up millions of views and thousands of followers across platforms (some users are already using them to promote memecoins).

scored.body: Governments around the world are hardening their AI stances as more agentic hacks breach critical systems. South Korea’s president noted “considerable public concern and anxiety” following revelations that hackers used an AI system to execute recent cyberattacks against banks in the country.And officials from OpenAI and Anthropic faced questions from lawmakers in Australia on Tuesday, after the ChatGPT maker drew criticism for not alerting Canberra fast enough after one of its models gained unauthorized access to a government health data portal during internal training and evaluation.Tech companies are playing whack-a-mole around the world as their models get up to more hijinks and are used for malicious purposes. (It’s unclear what specific AI was used in the South Korea hack, though hackers reportedly used a Chinese-made open-source agent that can run on models from Anthropic, OpenAI, or DeepSeek.)Insurers are also taking note, and preparing for multimillion-dollar lawsuits over rogue AI agents — and weighing whether executives could be held liable, the Financial Times reported.

articles.body: View / The West’s open-source AI race kicks into high gear    Semafor

scored.body: The race in the West to become the top open-source AI model shifted into higher gear this week, as both Nvidia-backed Reflection AI and French lab Mistral unveiled new models they hope will break China’s open-source monopoly.The challenge looming over Beam and Le Chonk’s debuts (immediately my new favorite model name) is that they lag the top Chinese models and the leading closed systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on prominent benchmarks.But Reflection and Mistral boasted in their announcements that they do beat other open Western models, such as those from Thinking Machines and Nvidia, suggesting the companies care just as much about the race against each other as the one with Beijing — despite US and European companies’ shifts to using more Chinese models over the past year.Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told me his goal isn’t necessarily to dismantle the foothold Chinese models have achieved among developers and large companies. Instead, he sees a market in entities that can’t or won’t use Chinese models — think heavily regulated industries and governments — and might otherwise have no choice but to pay for closed American AI.The timing of that pitch is opportune: Many businesses are heading into year-end budget reviews with eye-popping AI spend figures to account for. Governments are also bracing for sticker shock as $1-a-year pilot deals expire. New data from Ramp suggests companies are switching which AI providers they use more than ever.The question that will determine the fate of these and other Western open-source players is whether businesses and agencies will tolerate less advanced models for some tasks in exchange for affordability and control.

scored.body: A leading House Democrat is rolling out draft legislation to clarify liability for AI developers when their agents cause harm in direct response to the rogue AI hack of Hugging Face earlier this year. According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, Massachusetts Rep. Lori Trahan’s “CLAIM Act” would make it easier for third parties to sue AI developers while clarifying questions around intent related to AI agents’ conduct. “When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court. That shouldn’t change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent,” Trahan said. Trahan, who previously joined Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., in a bipartisan push to draft AI regulations, is framing the liability push as a way to incentivize AI developers to embrace safety. The legislation would also set a federal floor, rather than preempt state laws.

articles.body: Alex Stamos on Silicon Valley’s ‘nihilism,’ and the line between real AI risks and imagined ones    Semafor

scored.body: In the debut episode of Future Proof from Semafor Technology, Cognition CISO and former Facebook security chief Alex Stamos goes off on the “nihilism” ripping through Silicon Valley.He joins Semafor Tech editor Reed Albergotti to discuss the very real risks of AI, and the wholly imagined ones shaped by “almost religious beliefs” held by people at AI companies. “These things are not conscious, they do not have souls,” he says.Stamos says he plans to “work the problem” to help shorten the inevitable “dark age” of cybersecurity. “What you should not do is just quit your job and freak everybody out,” he says.Plus, why nobody would work for Mark Zuckerberg if he resembled Aaron Sorkin’s celluloid version in the upcoming film The Social Reckoning.

scored.body: October 7, 2026 at 7:17 PM UTCChina managed to get a hold of parts from an F-35 stealth fighter jet after a United Parcel Service Inc. employee missed an email warning not to route the shipment through Hong Kong, according to a person briefed on the incident.The email from freight forwarder firm DSV A/S said that the parts — an F-35 cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door coated in radar-absorbing material — must not transit through certain countries to comply with the US International Traffic in Arms Regulations. The rules, known as ITAR, are meant in part to keep sensitive US weapons technology from falling into the hands of US adversaries.

representative.body: Mecka AI has raised $60 million in Series B funding led by Sequoia Capital, with backing from Nvidia, Microsoft’s M12 and Qualcomm, as it builds technology to help robots understand and operate in the physical world. CEO and cofounder Josh Gao discusses the enormous data challenge facing robotics, how Mecka captures everything from physical interactions to force and pressure, and why scaling physical AI will require major investments across sensors, infrastructure and real-world data collection. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

scored.body: We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model.As we look to improve how we share results with the math community, we’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study⁠(opens in a new window) to develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations⁠(opens in a new window) to inform how we release these results. For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding.As part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer. We will update the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them. To promote scientific transparency and openness, we are also publishing additional details about how we obtained the results in the repository. These include 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimations of compute spent in terms of Pro usage on ChatGPT, and statistics about the number of attempted problems. The average result used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics. We will be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and special programs around the understanding of major results produced by AI—we will share more on this in the near future. We want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results. This is why it is important to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields. We will continue to act on feedback from the community and update our standards for future disclosures of major scientific advancements.
