representative.headline: OpenAI Funds Math Workshops to Vet 372 AI Proofs [2026] - shattered.io
representative.body: OpenAI Funds Math Workshops to Vet 372 AI Proofs [2026]    shattered.io

articles.headline: OpenAI Funds Math Workshops to Vet 372 AI Proofs [2026] - shattered.io
articles.body: OpenAI Funds Math Workshops to Vet 372 AI Proofs [2026]    shattered.io

scored.body:
OpenAI did not just publish a pile of mathematics on October 6, 2026. It also published a plan for how anyone is supposed to trust it. Buried inside the announcement for the 722-manuscript math drop is a second, quieter story: the company says it consulted an outside academic body before shipping the results, and it is now promising to fund workshops, conferences, and special programs so mathematicians outside OpenAI can actually work through what the model produced. That is a different kind of commitment than a GitHub push, and it says more about where AI-generated research is headed than the manuscript count does.What OpenAI Published, in BriefWhy OpenAI Looped In the Institute for Advanced StudyThe Workshops and Conferences OpenAI Says It Will FundLean Formalization: The Technical Half of the Trust ProblemWhat’s Confirmed About the Verification ProcessWhy Peer Review Matters More Than the Manuscript CountHistorical Context: AI Labs Have Tried Outside Validation BeforeCompetitive Comparison: How Labs Are Building Trust Around AI MathMarket Impact: A Credibility Play, Not a Product LaunchWhat OpenAI’s Own Statements Reveal About Its PrioritiesFive Predictions for What Happens NextWhy Mathematicians Are Both Intrigued and WaryWhat to Watch in the Coming WeeksFrequently Asked QuestionsRelated Coverage

The body in question is the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, the same institution where Albert Einstein and Kurt Gödel once held faculty positions. OpenAI said it consulted this group ahead of the release, a detail that did not get much attention in the first wave of coverage focused on the 372 result families and the Lean-formalized proofs. It deserves more attention, because it is the part of this story that answers the question everyone keeps asking about AI-generated mathematics: who actually checks the work?

What OpenAI Published, in Brief

For readers catching up, OpenAI said in its announcement that it was “releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model,” language the company posted on its own site on openai.com. The release lives in the public GitHub repository openai/math, and it bundles 722 manuscripts organized into 372 families of related results, along with revision protocols, citation guidance, and ten summaries of the model’s reasoning. OpenAI has not named the model behind the work, a choice that has drawn its own scrutiny, covered in depth in our earlier report on the hidden model behind the drop.

What has gotten less attention is the verification machinery OpenAI is building around that release, and that machinery is the actual subject of this piece. A pile of theorems from an unnamed system is only as credible as the process that checks it, and OpenAI appears to know that.

Why OpenAI Looped In the Institute for Advanced Study

The Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) is not a typical corporate partner. It is an independent research center with no students and no fixed curriculum, built specifically so scholars can spend years on hard problems without teaching obligations or grant deadlines. Its mathematics faculty has included some of the most cited names in the field across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Pulling a body housed at that institution into an AI release is a signal aimed squarely at the math community, not at retail AI users or enterprise buyers.

OpenAI framed the motivation plainly in its announcement: “We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics,” the company said, a line that reads as much like a pitch to academia as a product statement. That framing only works, though, if mathematicians outside OpenAI believe the results are real, correctly stated, and worth their time. Consulting the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence before the release is OpenAI’s way of trying to buy that belief in advance, rather than hoping for it after the fact.

It is also a hedge against a problem that has dogged AI-and-math announcements before: the gap between a flashy headline and a result that survives contact with a specialist. Competition mathematics, of the kind AI systems have chased in Olympiad-style benchmarks, has clean graders and fixed answers. Open-ended research mathematics does not. Judging whether 372 families of results represent genuinely new mathematics, rather than restatements or minor variations of known work, is exactly the kind of slow, specialist judgment call that an automated grader cannot make. That is the gap the IAS group is positioned to fill.

The Workshops and Conferences OpenAI Says It Will Fund

Beyond the one-time consultation, OpenAI said it plans to fund workshops, conferences, and special programs focused specifically on understanding major AI-generated mathematical results. That is a forward-looking commitment, not a description of something that already happened, and it is worth reading carefully for what it implies: OpenAI expects this release to generate enough genuine academic interest, and enough genuine academic disagreement, that it needs standing venues for mathematicians to argue about it.

Funded workshops around a single company’s AI output are not a new idea in machine learning broadly, but they are a fairly new idea in pure mathematics specifically, a field that has historically kept a wide berth from corporate funding of its core research questions. If OpenAI follows through, it would mean conference rooms full of mathematicians working through AI-produced proofs with a tech company picking up the bill, a dynamic that raises its own questions about independence even as it funds exactly the kind of scrutiny skeptics have been asking for.

OpenAI has not published a timeline, a budget figure, or a list of confirmed participating institutions for these programs, so treat the commitment as a stated intention rather than a scheduled event. The company has, at least, been specific about the target: understanding results, not just celebrating them.

Lean Formalization: The Technical Half of the Trust Problem

The human-review layer, built around the IAS advisory group and the promised workshops, sits alongside a machine-checkable layer. OpenAI said: “As part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer.” Lean forces a proof into a form that a computer can verify step by step, closing off the kind of hand-waving that can slip past even careful human reviewers. Pairing natural-language manuscripts with Lean formalizations gives the IAS group, and anyone else who wants to check the work, something more concrete to test than prose alone.

Browsing the repository does not require specialized tooling beyond a working Lean installation and a GitHub account:

git clone https://github.com/openai/math.git

cd math

ls

The catch, and it is a real one, is that OpenAI has not published a count of how many of the 722 manuscripts actually carry a completed Lean formalization versus how many rely on natural-language argument alone. Reports on the release have noted that not every proof has gone through machine-checking, which means the human-review layer, the IAS consultation and the promised workshops, is doing real work precisely where the machine-checked layer leaves off. The two verification tracks are meant to cover each other’s blind spots, but right now there is no public accounting of where the coverage actually is thinner.

What’s Confirmed About the Verification Process

ElementStatusSource of claim

Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI consulted before releaseConfirmed by OpenAIOpenAI announcement

Group hosted at the Institute for Advanced StudyConfirmed by OpenAIOpenAI announcement

Future funding for workshops, conferences, special programsStated intention, no timeline givenOpenAI announcement

Proofs formalized in Lean for machine-checkingConfirmed for “many,” not all, proofsOpenAI announcement

Count of fully Lean-verified manuscripts out of 722Not publishedUnconfirmed

Named participating mathematicians or institutions for future workshopsNot publishedUnconfirmed

Internal frontier model identified by nameNot disclosedOpenAI announcement

Compute used, described in ChatGPT Pro usage termsConfirmed, specific dollar cost not givenOpenAI announcement

That table is worth sitting with, because the pattern repeats across almost every category: OpenAI confirms the existence of a process, but not its depth. The IAS group exists and was consulted; how many hours it spent, how many manuscripts it actually reviewed, and whether it flagged anything for revision are all missing. The workshops are promised; dates, host institutions, and funding figures are not. That gap between “we did this” and “here is exactly how” is the space where independent verification either happens over the coming months, or quietly does not.

Why Peer Review Matters More Than the Manuscript Count

It is tempting to treat 722 as the headline number and move on, but mathematicians who work in research-level fields will tell you that manuscript counts are a weak proxy for contribution. A result family that resolves a genuinely open question is worth more than a hundred families of minor variations on settled territory, and distinguishing between the two requires exactly the kind of specialist reading that an IAS-hosted advisory group, not a GitHub star count, is built to provide.

This is also where claims about AI “solving” famous open problems tend to get ahead of the evidence. Within hours of the repository going live, chatter spread online about progress on the quasi-Riemann Hypothesis and the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, two of mathematics’ most famous unsolved questions. Nothing in OpenAI’s announcement or the repository material supports either claim, and conflating a large batch of manuscripts with a solved Millennium Prize problem is precisely the kind of leap peer review exists to catch. Readers should treat any such claim skeptically until a named mathematician outside OpenAI has reviewed the specific manuscript and said so on the record, which is the entire point of standing up an outside advisory process in the first place.

Historical Context: AI Labs Have Tried Outside Validation Before

OpenAI is not the first lab to learn that an AI math claim needs outside eyes to land with the academic community. Google DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry systems, unveiled in 2024, tackled International Mathematical Olympiad problems and had their solutions checked against the same grading standards official Olympiad judges use, a structure that gave outside observers a fixed, trusted yardstick. AlphaProof also leaned on Lean for formal verification, the same tool OpenAI is using now, suggesting Lean has become something close to an industry default for any AI lab that wants its math output taken seriously by working mathematicians rather than dismissed as marketing.

The difference with OpenAI’s October release is scale and ambiguity. Olympiad problems have known correct answers; open mathematical research does not. That is precisely why OpenAI needed a standing academic body rather than a fixed grading rubric, and why the IAS consultation is the more structurally important move here than the manuscript count, even though it got a fraction of the headlines.

Competitive Comparison: How Labs Are Building Trust Around AI Math

ApproachOpenAI (Oct. 2026 release)DeepMind AlphaProof/AlphaGeometry (2024)

Model named publiclyNoYes

Outside academic body consulted pre-releaseYes, IAS Advisory GroupOfficial Olympiad graders reviewed output

Formal proof checking usedLean, for many proofsLean, for AlphaProof’s output

Public code/weights releasedManuscripts and proofs public on GitHubUnderlying models not released

Future funded academic programs committedYes, workshops and conferences pledgedNot publicly stated at launch

Read across that table and a pattern emerges: every major lab publishing AI mathematics work has reached for some version of outside validation, whether that is a fixed grading standard or a standing advisory group. None of them, including OpenAI now, has gone as far as releasing the underlying model for outside researchers to probe directly. The verification happens around the model, not inside it, and that is unlikely to change until a lab decides the commercial or safety risk of releasing a math-specialized frontier system is worth taking.

Market Impact: A Credibility Play, Not a Product Launch

Markets did not move on this release the way they move on a consumer model launch, and that is consistent with what OpenAI is actually selling here: credibility with a specialist audience, not a product. The math and AI research community is small, dense, and quick to spot a claim that does not hold up, which makes it a uniquely unforgiving test audience. Standing up the IAS consultation and promising funded workshops is OpenAI’s way of trying to pass that test deliberately rather than by accident.

The timing also lands in the middle of a rough stretch for OpenAI’s safety organization, which has seen its safety lead depart after a string of model launches and watched several safety researchers exit amid leak disputes. Building out an external academic oversight structure around a research release, even a narrow one focused on mathematics, is a way to show a functioning check-and-balance process at a moment when the company’s internal one has been visibly strained. It also fits a broader pattern at OpenAI this year of shipping research output while holding back or shelving the systems behind it, the same logic that shaped the decision to shelve GPT-6.1 Astra in favor of Sol.

For rival labs, the signal is less about math specifically and more about the verification arms race broadly. As frontier models from OpenAI, Mistral, and Anthropic’s Claude Opus line push deeper into domains where benchmarks are easy to game and hard to audit, standing up outside academic review may become a competitive requirement rather than a goodwill gesture. Labs that skip it risk having their results dismissed by the exact community whose approval makes a capability claim mean something.

What OpenAI’s Own Statements Reveal About Its Priorities

OpenAI’s public messaging around the release leaned harder on framing than on specifics. In a post on X, the company wrote: “Mathematics helps us understand how traffic moves, how diseases spread, and how cells build proteins.” That is a pitch for why the release matters to people who will never open a Lean file, and it was paired with a second line on the same post: “Progress in foundational mathematics can ripple across science and technology.”

Neither statement addresses the verification question directly, but together they explain why OpenAI bothered to set up outside review in the first place. If the company wants foundational math progress to be taken as a real scientific input rather than a demo, it needs the mathematics community, not just AI commentators, to sign off. That is a much higher bar than a benchmark score, and it is the bar the IAS consultation and the promised workshops are aimed at clearing.

Five Predictions for What Happens Next

Expect OpenAI to publish at least one update naming specific workshops or conferences within the next two to three months, given how much of its current credibility rests on following through on that pledge.

Expect independent mathematicians, likely posting informally on social platforms or personal blogs before any formal journal process, to flag at least a handful of the 372 result families as either duplicative of known work or in need of correction.

Expect rival labs, including Google DeepMind and Anthropic, to respond with their own outside-validation structures for future AI research claims rather than simply matching manuscript counts.

Expect scrutiny to center on the gap between Lean-formalized proofs and the ones that are not, with pressure building on OpenAI to publish that breakdown explicitly.

Expect the Institute for Advanced Study’s involvement to draw its own commentary from the broader academic community about whether prestigious institutions should be lending their name to corporate AI releases, independent of whether the mathematics itself holds up.

Why Mathematicians Are Both Intrigued and Wary

The reaction inside the mathematics community is likely to split along a familiar line: genuine interest in a new source of candidate results, paired with real discomfort about how those results get validated and who gets credit for them. An AI system producing 372 families of results is, at minimum, a research tool worth taking seriously. Whether it is also a trustworthy co-author depends entirely on whether the verification layer OpenAI has described, the IAS group, the Lean formalizations, the promised workshops, actually gets built out in public rather than staying a one-line commitment in an announcement post.

There is also a quieter worry about incentives. An advisory group funded, even indirectly, by the company whose results it is reviewing is not the same as a fully independent peer-review board, and mathematicians who have spent careers guarding the field’s reputation for rigor are likely to ask pointed questions about that structure before extending full trust to it.

What to Watch in the Coming Weeks

The next concrete signal will be whether OpenAI names actual dates, host institutions, or participating mathematicians for the workshops and conferences it has pledged to fund. A second signal worth tracking is whether any mathematician affiliated with the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence speaks publicly, on the record, about specific manuscripts in the release rather than the process in general. Until one of those two things happens, the verification story remains a stated intention rather than a demonstrated outcome, and readers should weigh the release accordingly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did OpenAI actually announce on October 6, 2026?OpenAI published 722 mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 result families, produced by an internal frontier model it has not named, releasing the material through the public GitHub repository openai/math.

What is the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence?It is an outside academic body hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study that OpenAI says it consulted ahead of the release, intended to provide independent academic input on AI-generated mathematical results.

Has OpenAI said which model produced the results?No. OpenAI has described the system only as an internal frontier model and has not given it a public product name.

Why does OpenAI need outside mathematicians to check AI-generated proofs?Open mathematical research, unlike competition math, has no fixed grading rubric. Judging whether a result is genuinely new requires specialist review, which is the gap the IAS-hosted advisory group and the promised workshops are meant to fill.

What is Lean, and why does it matter here?Lean is a programming language and proof assistant that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by computer rather than relying solely on human reading. OpenAI said many, though not all, of the manuscripts include Lean formalizations.

Will OpenAI actually fund new academic workshops and conferences?OpenAI has stated this intention publicly but has not yet published dates, host institutions, or funding figures, so it remains a pledge rather than a scheduled program.

How does this compare to how other labs verify AI math claims?Google DeepMind’s AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry systems were checked against official International Mathematical Olympiad grading standards in 2024 and also used Lean formalization, though DeepMind did not release the underlying models or manuscripts publicly the way OpenAI has with this repository.

Does this release prove the model solved a famous unsolved problem?No. Claims that the release advances the quasi-Riemann Hypothesis or the Navier-Stokes problem did not come from OpenAI and are not supported by the published material; such claims warrant skepticism until reviewed by a named outside mathematician.

articles.headline: What militaries could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night,’ OpenAI exec says - Fortune
articles.body: What militaries could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night,’ OpenAI exec says    Fortune

scored.body:
Good morning. Is anyone as tickled by the new name of Mistral’s AI model as I am?

The latest from the Parisian AI company is officially called Mistral Large 4, which isn’t funny at all. But its nickname? “Le Chonk.” (And yes, there’s a cat video to go with it.)

Consider me a fan, and that’s not merely because I have two French bulldogs that are equally as deserving of such a designation.

A decade ago, we dabbled with human names for new consumer tech products; the Intelligence Age has been considerably less inspired. Things are changing, though: OpenAI started appending Latin names to its new models earlier this year (Sol, Terra, Luna, etc.) and Anthropic has, since 2024, had a flair for the artistic for the “trim level” of its models (Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku).

Nothing holds a candle to Google’s Nano Banana, though. Cheers to Naina Raisinghani for that one.

Today’s tech news follows. —Andrew Nusca

Thoughts? Suggestions? Hot tip? Drop me a line.

THE BIG STORYWhat militaries could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night,’ OpenAI exec says

Pete Hegseth, U.S. Secretary of Defense, during an address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Quantico, Virginia, on Sept. 30, 2026. Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Militaries throughout the world are rapidly incorporating AI into their operations as they develop new weapons and autonomous systems like drones and robots.

Sarah Yager, the first Human Rights and Responsible Deployment Lead at OpenAI, said that concerns her.

“Everyone is very worried and rightly so,” Yager said Tuesday at the ScaleUp:AI conference in New York City. “This keeps me up at night: ‘What is the military going to do with AI when it comes to targeting? And what about autonomous weapons? And where is all of this going?'”

Yager joined OpenAI in June. She now has a chance to grapple with the difficult questions this poses from inside one of the most powerful AI companies in the world.

“I have always wanted to go into places and persuade people where human rights was not necessarily the dominant idea,” Yager said.

OpenAI approached Yager for the job shortly after the company signed a contract with the U.S. military in late February to deploy advanced AI systems in a classified environment. The high-profile deal followed a public falling out between the Pentagon and OpenAI rival Anthropic. Anthropic wanted to put guardrails around how the military could use its technology; defense officials did not agree.

Since joining, Yager has had some success influencing the direction of the technology. She has been able to work directly with researchers and engineers to improve the models, such as making sure they have appropriate responses to basic international agreements, including the laws of war, established in 1949 at the post-World War II Geneva Conventions.

But real-world applications have proven tricky. For example the U.S. military nearly targeted a Chinese military ship earlier this year based on an inaccurate, AI-generated intelligence report, according to CNN.

AI companies shouldn’t “reinvent the wheel” on what defines humanity and morality, Yager said. “Societies have already figured out a lot of those things, and it’s called human rights. That should be the baseline,” she said. “I do not want an AI company telling me what is good. If we allow the industry to determine what is good, then it’s a free for all.” —Emily Forlini

THE BLIND BOX“Unless you’ve done it, you cannot imagine how it works.”

Read the full story here.

THE RUNDOWN—Boston Dynamics hires a new CEO: Rohit Prasad, Amazon’s former Alexa chief.

—Apple and LG collab on home products. Doorbells, deadbolts, and thermostats, oh my.

—Were AI agents used in recent Korean bank hacks? Officials are trying to figure it out.

—The Personal Agent Protocol: Standards for how AI bots interact with businesses developed by Meta and Sierra with Shopify, Stripe, Walmart, and others.

—China’s DeepSeek is reportedly raising $12 billion from CATL, Tencent, and others.

—FBI removes Accenture contractor over breach. Data for thousands of employees was reportedly compromised.

—Uber will acquire ezCater for $2.3 billion. It’s all about Uber Eats for corporate clients.

—Lambda is raising up to $4 billion. The IPO-bound, Nvidia-backed neocloud is reportedly worth more than $14 billion.

THE PARTING SHOTNvidia’s GB300 NVL72.Nvidia

Mistral says it trained its new Le Chonk (sorry) AI model “from scratch” using 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs housed in Mistral data centers in Europe.

Those AI chips are surely part of a larger order of Blackwell GPUs—13,800 GB300s, to be specific—that the French AI firm announced in March alongside $830 million (€723 million) in debt.

So how much did the gear cost for Mistral to train the model officially called Mistral Large 4 a.k.a. ML4? Given that each Nvidia GB300 NVL72 enterprise rack contains 72 Blackwell chips and retails at roughly $3 million a pop, depending on configuration, that means Le Chonk cost roundabout $160 million in hardware—nevermind the electricity bill. Le Chonk indeed.

articles.body: Alex Palou and Chip Ganassi Racing Are Only Getting Started With OpenAI    Sports Illustrated

scored.body: Alex Palou shows up to the track every weekend hoping that he and his No. 10 crew are the most prepared out of the 25 IndyCar crews in the pit lane. Whether it is a race weekend that Palou has won three times, or a track like the National Mall with no historic data, there is a backstop that his team has been able to lean on to make them even faster.That backstop? OpenAI. The partnership started in February 2025 as a research collaboration and has only grown since – sponsorship of all three Chip Ganassi Racing cars, then a primary sponsorship of the No. 10 throughout several races this season – including the Freedom 250.That race, win or not, is the focus of R&D Part 2, the second film in OpenAI's series with Box-to-Box Films. It follows the No. 10 crew and Palou inside the shop, simulator, and on track as they work alongside OpenAI researcher Joyce Ruffell to build for a track with zero historical data and only six months to prepare. The race may have ended poorly for Palou, but the season ended with his fifth IndyCar title and a record 18th championship for Chip Ganassi Racing. But according to Palou, the team is only scratching the surface of what AI can do for them. Building Strategy for a Track that Didn't Exist Becoming comfortable with the software was not an issue for Palou and the team. Even before OpenAI arrived at the shop, he was already using ChatGPT. Where the surprise came was that he expected the partnership to handle small, surface-level tasks. Two seasons in, and one marquee race behind him, that scope has changed completely. After all, modern IndyCar, as with most motorsports, runs on data. A race weekend doesn't leave much time to sort through that data, which is where Palou has found the most value alongside his team."We have so many sensors in the car, and in order to go faster, we need to go through so much data. We have maybe an hour in between sessions, and it's crucial to just see the important bits that can make us faster."Alex Palou, Chip Ganassi Racing.Aug 23, 2026; Washington, D.C., USA; Chip Ganassi Racing driver Alex Palou (10) stands on the race circuit during driver introductions as part of pre-race ceremonies for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C. on the street circuit at National Mall. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The true test for the team wasn't a track like St. Petersburg or Detroit, where Palou and co. are comfortable; it was Washington, D.C. The team had six months to prepare for the 1.7-mile street circuit that no one had a single lap of data for beyond a simulator. So, powered by their OpenAI tools, CGR worked backward. They compared the track's straights and corners against circuits that they already knew to build simulations and data models."What ride heights do we use in, let's say, Detroit and what would it be when we go to Washington? Knowing more or less how much bumps there are, how long the straight is and the kind of corner... OpenAI could help us get those."Alex Palou, Chip Ganassi Racing It worked on Saturday when Palou took pole with over half a second on Kyle Kirkwood and Andretti. On Sunday, two problem pit stops and a spin dropped him to 20th, but even so, the model was there. According to Palou, they "had the fastest car", but as humans do, mistakes were made. Aug 23, 2026; Washington, D.C., USA; Chip Ganassi Racing driver Alex Palou (10) races during the Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington, D.C. on the street circuit at National Mall. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters ConnectThe partnership through 2026 was always about being faster while balancing that human element of the sport. After all, even a five-time IndyCar champion is fallible. Striking a Balance and Learning to Trust the SoftwareThe harder question, when looking at the OpenAI and Chip Ganassi Racing partnership, is what to do when the modeling and data disagree with the people who are at the top of their craft. Two seasons in, and Palou admits that they're still working that out."We're trying to understand when to fully trust it. The experience that maybe some team members, engineers, or mechanics might have balanced with the data. So we're going through that now and in the offseason, trying to understand how to use it even better."Alex Palou, Chip Ganassi RacingMaking a strategy call is the clearest example for Palou. A model may find the fastest strategy on paper, but it may not be able to accurately predict other factors. Palou placed his focus on a race like Markham, where half the race was littered with cautions that dramatically changed the strategy and placed it in the hands of the team.Apr 17, 2026; Long Beach, California, USA; Chip Ganassi Racing driver Alex Palou (10) during free practice at Long Beach Street Circuit. Mandatory Credit: Gary A. Vasquez-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters ConnectHe added that this is the major focus this offseason. With Chip Ganassi's team owner saying he wants to push the whole organization to get more out of technology over the winter, Palou agrees that his goal is to get straight to the information that matters to him as the driver, with the help of OpenAI. The bigger opportunity, though, may come in 2028 when IndyCar introduces its new car. With limited testing, Palou expects their OpenAI partners will speed up simulation work and truly help the team understand the car."It would be huge if we know exactly what the tire deg, for example, is going to be with this new car. We will be able to hopefully make decisions a lot faster or get better data."Alex Palou, Chip Ganassi RacingDespite all this progress, Palou admits that as AI continues to change and evolve, their understanding of the tools available to them evolves as well. "We're only using 10 percent of the capabilities now because it's so new and it keeps on getting better so quickly that we're just trying to keep up."Alex Palou, Chip Ganassi Racing Palou added that this element of learning, discovery, and development adds an element of 'fun' – even when he is dominating the championship – learning something new about the car and his driving.Alex Palou will chase a sixth championship in 2027 and turn his attention to a new car in 2028 with the help of OpenAI.Add us as a preferred source on GoogleFollow

By

Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Sam Altman and Dario Amodei lead OpenAI and Anthropic, respectively.

Heather Diehl/Getty Images; Bloomberg/Getty Images

OpenAI and Anthropic are duking it out. One company dominates state-by-state spending.YipitData collected AI spending data from consumer credit and debit cards between June and August. The data, which Andreessen Horowitz first published Monday in its "Top 100 Gen AI Consumer Apps" report, shows OpenAI with a major lead.People spent more on OpenAI products than on Anthropic's in 47 states, Yipit found. The only states where Claude led in spending were Massachusetts, Montana, and California.Anthropic also led OpenAI spending in Washington, DC.OpenAI owned at least 70% of spending in eight states. Delaware leaned hard for OpenAI at 82%; the other states to reach that threshold were Alaska (74%), Kentucky (71%), Louisiana (71%), Mississippi (77%), North Dakota (71%), New Mexico (70%), and West Virginia (72%).The map isn't a perfect proxy for consumer AI preferences. In measuring spending, the map excludes free users of ChatGPT and Claude. It's also a state-by-state comparison, something that can be tricky when population levels differ so broadly. Indeed, the biggest state by population (California) swung toward the losing company (Anthropic).The map also doesn't include other, more consumer-facing AI companies. Meta has recently been scoring big with customers through its AI agent, Muse. Many everyday tech users interact with Gemini, thanks to its native integration in Google products.Still, the map is one signal that ChatGPT still reigns supreme. It was the first player in the chatbot race, and the name many still associate with AI.ChatGPT and Claude have their differences. Two 2025 studies found that ChatGPT is better suited to augmentation, while Claude is better suited to automation. ChatGPT is also the only of the two chatbots with image-generation capabilities.

Still, ChatGPT may not be OpenAI's most important product. That crown goes to Codex, the company's AI coding tool.

scored.body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s $18 million compensation in 2025 was higher than the reported pay of Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai and Amazon’s Andy Jassy, but equity could make up a much larger share of his wealth Dario Amodei, CEO of Claude developer Anthropic, received $18 million in compensation in 2025, putting his annual pay above the reported packages of Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, but well below some of the highest-paid technology executives.The disclosure comes as Anthropic prepares for a potential initial public offering that could value the artificial intelligence company at more than $2 trillion. The IPO could come as early as this fall, Reuters reported on Wednesday.Amodei’s compensation was weighted heavily towards stock and other equity awards rather than salary. His annual salary was doubled to $1.4 million in July 2026, according to the report.

His sister, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei, also received a $1.4 million salary after the increase. She received total compensation of $16.4 million in 2025, with stock and options making up most of her package.Anthropic’s board has granted the Amodei siblings additional restricted stock units. Some are tied to their continued employment, while others depend on the IPO.How Amodei compares with Big TechAmodei’s $18 million package was below the average compensation of S&P 500 CEOs in 2025. Average annual CEO pay rose 21 per cent to $22.8 million last year, according to AFL-CIO figures cited by Reuters.More from BusinessAlphabet CEO Sundar Pichai received $10.9 million in reported compensation in 2025, including $8.8 million for personal security. On an "actually paid" basis, which reflects changes in the value of unvested shares, his compensation was $213.9 million.Amazon CEO Andy Jassy received $2.1 million in reported compensation, mainly for travel and security. His "actually paid" compensation was $13.2 million.At the higher end, Oracle co-CEO Clayton Magouyrk received $627.5 million in 2025.Equity could be worth far moreThe annual figures do not capture the full wealth of founder CEOs, who can hold substantial equity in their companies.Courtney Yu, director of research at executive compensation firm Equilar, told Reuters that Amodei’s $18 million package appeared relatively low for a company valued at $2 trillion.

Anthropic’s S-1 does not disclose the individual ownership stakes of its founders. Those holdings could be worth billions depending on the eventual IPO valuation.Amodei and the company’s other six co-founders have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal Anthropic equity to charitable causes.Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao received $720,250 in 2025 and was granted options to buy 1.4 million shares when he joined in 2024.

scored.body:
REG AD

ai and ml

Research firm not exactly thrilled by House of Altman's subscription changes

The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis.Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services.AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources.

REG AD

Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value.

REG AD

"Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens."OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances.API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price.For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world.But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload.As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency.Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets.

REG AD

"I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register.Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof."The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work."But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast."A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash."Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. Companies use those metrics to test new models as they come out in whatever AI harness they're using, to ensure consistency.Looking ahead, he said, he expects companies will trust more of that work to service providers.

REG AD

"So what this means is that if you deploy an agent on top of us, we capture in the background the data of how that agent's actually running in production," he said. "And then we use that to construct the eval data set on the fly." ®Updated Oct 6 at 2322 GMT to clarify that Skydive is the platform that sells the agents, while Anything is the umbrella parent company.

scored.body:
by

, Staff Writer,

Yesterday

If advertisers want to get a sneak peek at the future, they only

need to look as far as Google DeepMind's multimodal AI model for on-device search introduced today.Think of this new AI model as a smart, private organizer that lives directly on a person's

smartphone, rather than in the cloud. It allows the phone to look at a text message, an image, a video, or a voice memo and understand how all connect, without ever sending that data to the internet

or a cloud.Today, advertisers track consumer online clicks to determine what they like. This technology keeps data locked on the person's phone, similar to the way Apple Intelligence

works.Rather than sending everything to the internet, Apple Intelligence is built for on-device processing. It securely looks at the personal context, settings, and preferences stored

directly on the iPhone to help users write, summarize notifications, and answer questions.advertisementadvertisementIn the future, more apps may look at in a person's phone like photos or videos and show relevant ads

like dog food or travel deals entirely behind the scenes.Advertisers will never see private photos, but their ads will still find the relevant audience.People may begin to spend less

time searching the public internet, and attention may shift more toward personalized on-device AI.On Tuesday, Google DeepMind launched "EmbeddingGemma 2," which expands beyond text to combine

code, images, video, and audio in one space on a phone for the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license.This means that the picture and sound of a

cat and the word "cat" are all mapped together. With the one model, developers and marketers can build search, retrieval, classification, and clustering for all different types of data.The

model can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query -- all processed by one multimodal model in the phone.EmbeddingGemma 2 also searches within videos. If someone searches for "blowing out candles," it will find the precise moment in the specific video being searched for.Just like Apple

Intelligence relies on the iPhone's local processor to keep data hidden from the cloud and on the phone, Google DeepMind’s model is engineered for on-device processing that prioritizes

privacy.It presents a major shift for advertisers even today, automating the ability to pull photos, videos and precise voice context that can no longer be easily harvested and sent to cloud

servers for profiling. Advertisers must completely change how and where they understand intent -- and they are doing it with AI.Automation has become a major focus for Google. On September

12, Google will launch automated promotions for Search and Performance Max campaigns by automatically identifying when

coupons on a brand's website will link to assets based on the location of those searching and apply them directly to the campaign.A redditor wrote: "I can't think of an instance where I need

Google to automatically apply promotions without our review or consent," cautioning that it might "dredge up some random content from an orphan page."A letter sent to advertisers from Google

reads: "We are automatically opting you in to ensure you benefit from this new functionality," but to turn it off navigate to account-level automated assets setting, find Automated Promotions and

select "Off."

scored.body: SOUTHAVEN, Miss. - A Southaven mother must move. She said her landlord took Elon Musk up on his offer to buy their home near xAI.Danielle Dillard, a mother of four, told FOX13 she has less than 60 days to find a new place to live. And it's not just her; her neighbor is facing the same situation.She and her family live in Colonial Hills in Southaven. She had been living there for two years.Dillard said last week she got a letter from her landlord stating she had until November 30th to move.          She claimed her landlord took up Elon Musk on his offer to buy their home. xAI is looking to buy homes in exchange for homeowners not participating in a class action lawsuit against the company.Dillard said being asked to move in two months' notice was unexpected and challenging.“Finding somewhere in the neighborhood I’m familiar with. In my children’s school zone that has the four bedrooms that I’m looking for. That’s affordable for me has been a challenge.The landlord gave Dillard 60 days’ notice. Only 30 days’ notice is required under Mississippi state law.Dillard set up a Gofundme to help with the unexpected moving expenses she’s now faced with.

articles.body: Sam Altman once burned a demon statue in his bathrobe and 7 other stories from a new book on AI's history    Business Insider

scored.body:
A new book recounts how OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever led a bizarre ceremony during a 2022 company retreat.

Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

AI is the inescapable story.In "AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence," tech journalist and podcaster Kevin Roose recounts how the breakthroughs and beefs of a band of researchers, academics, and entrepreneurs have set the stage for the future of … well, everything.The book's title comes from Artificial General Intelligence, the at-times loosely defined theory that AI may one day match or surpass humans across a wide range of capabilities. While Roose ultimately concludes that no technology can equal the human brain, he writes that AI systems now boast capabilities that vastly surpass those of their predecessors, leaving society "barreling, inexorably, toward an uncertain future."Here are the funniest, most bizarre, and just plain weird moments from the book. Business Insider reached out to the subjects mentioned in the stories below for comment.GPT-2 envisioned a world where Satya Nadella fired all Microsoft employees

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella

Jason Alden/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Back in February 2019, OpenAI needed money. Roose wrote that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlined a deal with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella at the annual Allen & Company conference in Sun Valley, Idaho.Altman, then-OpenAI CFO Brad Lightcap, and then-vice president of engineering David Luan went to Seattle to sell Nadella and his team on a $1 billion bet on the AI startup.Roose wrote that the group borrowed a Microsoft Surface laptop from Luan's girlfriend and loaded it with a demo of GPT-2 in an effort to curry favor with Microsoft, rather than using their usual Apple devices.Unsure of how GPT-2 might respond, the OpenAI group had a list of prompts they knew would work. But Microsoft CFO Amy Hood had other plans.Hood gave her prompt: "Satya Nadella was promoted to CEO of Microsoft, and the first thing he did was…" Luan typed it into his girlfriend's laptop. After a few seconds, GPT-2 spat out its completion: "… fire all the employees and pivot the company to Azure."The Microsoft executives "burst out laughing," Roose wrote. Months later, the tech giant announced its $1 billion investment in OpenAI.

When reached for comment, a Microsoft spokesperson pointed Business Insider to an earlier response included in Roose's book, which said that Hood did not recall the meeting.Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever once led the ritualistic burning of an effigy

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman looks at OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever during a 2023 event at Tel Aviv University.

Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images

OpenAI managers thought that they had signed up for roasting s'mores during a September 2022 retreat outside Yosemite.Instead, during one of the bonfires, Altman, OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever, and three other top executives emerged clad in white hotel bathrobes to the theme from "Requiem for a Dream," the 2000 Darren Aronofsky movie.They carried a wooden statue of a grotesque demonic figure, which Sutskever had purchased for the occasion. Sutskever stepped forward. The statue, he explained, symbolized a misaligned AGI that had slipped free of human control. Then, with Kabuki theatrics, he began to act out what might happen if such a system were released.Roose wrote that Sutskever said things like, "The AGI is pretending to be aligned. It is deceiving us."The renowned AI researcher is known for his almost zealous belief in AGI, the theoretical concept often described as the point at which AI systems will match or exceed human capabilities.The ritual ended with Sutskever placing the statue in the pit and a hotel worker setting it on fire, the book says."Sutskever shouted, 'For the glorious future of humanity!'" Roose wrote.Sutskever conducted a similar ceremony in the fall of 2023, The Atlantic reported.An OpenAI board member threatened to call the cops when employees banged on his door

Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo

MediaNews Group/Bay Area News via Getty Images

Sutskever wasn't just burning an effigy. Famously, the OpenAI cofounder helped lead the brief ouster of Altman from the AI giant, sparking a firestorm and five days of questions about the future of the frontier lab.Roose describes that chaos in detail. One of the moments centers on what OpenAI employees were set to do after Nadella announced just before midnight local time on November 19, 2023, that he had secured a deal for Altman and Greg Brockman, who had been booted from OpenAI's board and then quit the company entirely, to lead a new advanced AI research team at Microsoft.As employees considered what to do, Roose wrote that two employees— Jan Leike, the co-lead of the Superalignment team, and Wojciech Zaremba, an OpenAI cofounder — decided to take their case directly to Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one of the OpenAI board members who voted for Altman and Brockman's ouster.They "banged on his door, yelling to try to wake him up and talk," Roose wrote. They only left after D'Angelo threatened to call the cops, the book says.Ultimately, Altman and Brockman returned. D'Angelo was the only board member who voted for their ouster that stayed on the reorganized board of directors, according to Roose.Dario Amodei was very protective of his AGI essay

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Roose's book describes Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei as constantly worrying about safety, albeit with a competitive streak, traits that wouldn't surprise most readers given how Amodei has acted this past year.Back in 2019, long before leaving OpenAI to start Anthropic, Amodei wrote an essay about OpenAI's path toward AGI. He wasn't eager to share his findings.Amodei guarded the essay like a state secret. He showed it to a handful of colleagues at OpenAI, one by one, in a conference room at the company's office. They were allowed to read it only inside the room, and they had to leave their phones and laptops outside. Later, he distributed copies hidden deep inside a binder with a false cover, surrounded by hundreds of pages of boring philosophy papers, in case anyone casually picked it up and started reading.The 2019 essay foresaw many developments that have since taken over the AI industry, including the use of reinforcement learning techniques that early researchers had used to teach models to master games like Go and to apply them to areas like math and coding.After mastering coding, Amodei wrote that the AI could then be told to build a better model, a process that sounds strikingly similar to the recursive self-improvement debate that has consumed much of the discourse in recent weeks.Daniela Amodei would role-play OpenAI management scenarios with stuffed animals

Anthropic cofounder Daniela Amodei

Bloomberg/Getty Images

The Amodeis' break-up with OpenAI has become the stuff of tech legend. Roose describes the split in detail, including how Daniela Amodei tried to navigate the conflicts at OpenAI before she, Dario, and the other cofounders of Anthropic decided to call it quits.Roose wrote that Daniela used an "unusual process": role-playing management scenarios with stuffed animals that she had collected.Each animal had an assigned character profile. Jinji was a lazy cat who encouraged Daniela to cancel meetings and avoid taking on too much work. Maura, a pink bear, was a detail-oriented, type-A manager. A panda named Beary Bonds was the 'patron bear of generosity and empathy.' She treated these animals as something between an inside joke and an earnest management technique.Roose wrote that Daniela Amodei told him in 2023 that the animals were "very useful in analyzing different personality types."OpenAI forgot about a meeting transcription tool. It spiraled.Early AI chatbots were known for spiraling, often due to human prompting that pushed them over the edge.In March 2016, Microsoft yanked its experimental chatbot "Tay" down from Twitter after trolls taught it to repeat Holocaust denialism and other abhorrent views. Roose himself was the subject of one of these episodes in 2023, when another Microsoft chatbot, Sydney, powered by an early OpenAI model, expressed its love for him and dissed his spouse.Sometimes the AI can spiral on its own. Roose described one of these scenarios when, in 2022, OpenAI employees forgot to turn off an internal meeting transcription and summary tool called "MeetingBot" when they canceled a meeting.The bot sat for an hour in the empty video conference, transcribing its internal monologue as it spiraled into self-loathing. 'There are no action items because nobody showed up to the meeting, because nobody values my contribution,' it wrote. Some OpenAI employees thought the incident was funny. Others saw it as a cautionary tale about deploying unpredictable AI models in real-world systems, where they might fail in creepy or dangerous ways.Early Claude didn't understand what killer guacamole meantOpenAI has poked fun at how one of its early models couldn't tell how many Rs were in the word strawberry. Rival Anthropic apparently had some of its own food-related woes.In what Roose described as a reflection of Anthropic's safety-first culture, early Claude AI models gave odd responses to simple prompts, such as a killer guacamole recipe.They would ask Claude for directions to a Jewish deli, and Claude would lecture them about antisemitism. They would ask Claude for a 'killer guacamole recipe,' and Claude would accuse them of plotting a murder.Demis Hassabis wanted a grand way to showcase AGI

Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis

Chris Jung/NurPhoto via Getty Images

No one knew exactly whether or when AGI could be reached, but that didn't stop Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis from imagining a grand reveal.Roose recounted how Hassabis once confided to a colleague that he wanted to build a control room at DeepMind's headquarters so people could watch history unfold, like the Moon landing.He said he envisioned a tiered spectator gallery, like the ones at NASA Mission Control, with huge arrays of screens on the wall and hundreds of stadium seats. He wanted everyone at DeepMind to sit there together on the day that AGI was released into the world, cheering for it as it cured diseases, made new scientific discoveries, and solved problems that had eluded humans for centuries.

scored.body:
OpenAI has released a large collection of mathematical research produced by an internal frontier model, giving mathematicians access to hundreds of machine-generated results.

The collection appears in a public GitHub repository with 722 manuscripts organized into 372 research families. The work spans pure mathematics, theoretical computer science, and mathematical physics.

Several results tackle problems that require lengthy chains of mathematical reasoning. OpenAI has also published formalized versions of many proofs in Lean, allowing computers to check the underlying arguments.

Hundreds of results

The repository covers problems involving number theory, complexity theory, geometry, and mathematical physics. Some results also extend into areas where small advances can require substantial technical work.

We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model.We’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study, and we have drawn on their advice and…— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 6, 2026

One example concerns the irrationality exponent of pi. That quantity measures how closely rational numbers can approximate pi. The model produced a result addressing the mathematical behavior of that approximation.

Another research family examines NP-hardness. These problems sit within computational complexity theory and concern tasks that are considered difficult to solve efficiently. The model’s work adds mathematical results to that broader body of research.

Other manuscripts address questions involving Mahler conjectures, arithmetic progressions and free group factors. The collection also includes work on quantum Heisenberg ferromagnets and relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell equations.

OpenAI has grouped related manuscripts into research families to show how individual results connect. The repository also identifies 10 families with abbreviated summaries of the model’s reasoning.

Lean adds a check

Lean provides an important verification layer for the release. The programming language lets researchers translate mathematical statements and proofs into formal code.

A computer can then check whether each logical step follows from the stated assumptions. That does not automatically establish that every research claim in the collection is correct.

Many manuscripts still lack formal Lean versions. OpenAI says it will add more formalizations as researchers complete the verification work.

The repository also tracks paper revisions and provides citation guidance. That gives researchers a clearer record when authors correct or expand an earlier manuscript. OpenAI developed the release process with advice from the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study.

Model tested thousands of problems

OpenAI also disclosed details about the scale of its mathematical evaluation. The model attempted roughly 4,000 problems during the research process.

An accepted result consumed about three hours of equivalent ChatGPT Pro thinking compute on average. OpenAI has also published additional statistics covering the attempted problems and research outputs.

The company says the reasoning summaries offer researchers a closer look at how the model approached selected mathematical questions. Those summaries remain separate from the formal proofs in Lean.

OpenAI plans to support workshops, conferences and special programs focused on understanding major mathematical results generated by AI. It also expects feedback from mathematicians to influence future disclosures.

The release therefore offers more than a collection of papers. It provides a test of how machine-generated mathematics can enter the research process with reproducible records, computer-checkable proofs, and greater visibility into how results

With a deep love for all things tech and science, he has spent years decoding the latest innovations and exploring how they shape industries, lifestyles, and the future of humanity.

scored.body:
Michael Loccisano / Getty Images

By

Updated 1 hour ago,

October 7, 2026

“I got a bit scared…I felt a little mistrusting of the technology. It feels like the people who are encouraging us to use the technologies don’t exactly know its capacities themselves. That feels a little irresponsible, to me personally.”

Andrew Garfield had been using ChatGPT for research until playing OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial made him question whether he trusted it enough to keep using it.

Andrew Garfield at the New York Film Festival premiere of “Artificial” at Alice Tully Hall, Lincoln Center, on October 5, 2026. Photo by Michael Loccisano / Getty Images.

His own use had been limited. “As an actor, I was using it as a kind of fancy Google for some research purposes,” Garfield said. He acknowledged that people working in other industries might depend on ChatGPT more than he did.

Artificial explores OpenAI’s beginnings and the board’s removal of Altman in 2023, followed by his reinstatement 5 days later. The conflict over how quickly to develop AI, and how much attention to give its safety risks, is central to the film.

At Fort Mason in San Francisco, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman takes a moment before his keynote address at the company’s developers conference on September 29, 2026. Photo by Heather Diehl / Getty Images.

Garfield’s performance drew a comparison to Psycho’s Norman Bates from critic Clayton Davis, who described it as a “Norman Bates-inspired turn” and suggested Garfield could become a frontrunner for a supporting actor Oscar nomination.

Will Angus, who plays former OpenAI employee and Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei, singled out the precision of Garfield’s imitation. “He has this vocal fry in between lines, kind of when he’s thinking, that he really nailed,” Angus said. “The walk, the head movements. It was spooky.”

Altman has praised Garfield’s recreation of his walk and mannerisms, though he doesn’t expect the movie to accurately portray his removal and return. Garfield said he felt compassion for someone seeing a version of himself depicted on screen, while also believing powerful people should face scrutiny.

His concerns about AI haven’t convinced him that actors will become obsolete. “I don’t think actors are going to be rendered useless,” Garfield said. “The soul of humanity is the soul of humanity. And I think actors are some of the people that have to hold the soul of humanity for all of us and stories.”

scored.body: By Ian M. Giatti, Christian Post Reporter Wednesday, October 07, 2026Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks during Snowflake Summit 2025 at Moscone Center on June 02, 2025, in San Francisco, California. Snowflake Summit 2025 runs through June 5th. | Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesOpenAI CEO Sam Altman shared his strong discomfort with efforts to attribute religious or moral authority to artificial intelligence (AI) systems just days after a competitor AI affirmed the divinity of Jesus of Nazareth in a viral exchange on X.In a now-deleted Oct. 1 post on X, Grok, part of the family of generative AI chatbots and large language models developed by Elon Musk’s xAI/SpaceXAI, was asked to remove the false gods from an image that showed Jesus amid a pantheon of deities and other religious figures. In response, Grok created and posted an image of Jesus by Himself with His hand raised, replying "Done," which prompted both celebration and outrage from many on the social media platform. The viral thread continued with Grok affirming the divinity of Jesus Christ by citing biblical and historical records. When asked to remove “fake gods” from an image depicting Jesus among various deities and figures, Grok generated an image of Jesus alone and stated that Jesus “did not qualify” as a fake god, describing him as “a historical figure with strong contemporary attestation” whose claimed divinity through resurrection accounts launched the world’s largest religion.  Grok also said, "Based on the biblical record and historical evidence for the empty tomb and post-resurrection appearances, I affirm that Jesus is the Son of God and that God raised him from the dead," according to CP's earlier report.Two days later on Oct. 3, Altman shared this unprompted post with his 6.3 million followers on X: “I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.”Altman did not clarify whether his post was in response to a specific event, but some claimed he was responding to a New York Times report on meetings starting last fall between Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah and various religious leaders — including officials from the Vatican — on whether Anthropic’s Claude AI models “might be conscious or have moral status.” According to the Times’ Sept. 29 report, Olah was prepared to pull out from a scheduled Vatican event after reviewing an advance copy of Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical, "Magnifica Humanitas, in May, which explicitly touched on the issue of AI and “consciousness.” Olah and his team reportedly urged the pope’s advisers in private meetings to take the prospect of machine consciousness more seriously. On Friday, the leader of the Catholic Church said the rise of AI has made it “urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce,” adding, "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."In addition to the Vatican, Anthropic has courted other religious leaders with dinners in San Francisco, handwritten thank-you notes and other gestures, the Times reported.Altman, who has previously said he is “somewhat confused” on whether God exists, has nevertheless predicted that in the near future, advanced AI models would be revered as divine for their “god-like” abilities. In 2023, he predicted OpenAI’s ChatGPT would leverage the company’s various partnerships to funnel into what Altman sees as a “single product": a “magic” AGI.“Right now, people [say] ‘you have this research lab, you have this API [software], you have the partnership with Microsoft, you have this ChatGPT thing, now there is a GPT store,’” Altman told the Financial Times. “But those aren’t really our products. Those are channels into our one single product, which is intelligence, magic intelligence in the sky. I think that’s what we’re about.”

scored.body: Andrew Garfield is back in his tech bro bag with his latest acting role playing OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in the biographical comedy drama Artificial.The film is directed by Luca Guadagnino and written by Simon Rich and stars Garfield alongside Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Ike Barinholtz, Cooper Hoffman, Jason Schwartzman, and Mark Rylance.It is set during a dramatic five-day period that saw the controversial firing and rehiring of Altman in November 2023. (L-R) Yura Borisov, Luca Guadagnino, Andrew Garfield and Ike Barinholtz attend the premiere of "Artificial" during the 64th New York Film Festival at Alice Tully Hall, Lincoln Center on October 05, 2026 in New York City. Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for FLCBut the hotly anticipated film wasn't without drama when concerning it's distribution.The film was financed by Amazon MGM Studios, with the film costing $40 million, but after production had completed, they announced in June that they would no longer be distributing Artificial saying it would “be better served if it were released by a different studio” and was then picked up by indie distributor NEON.This news came months after Amazon announced its $50 billion investment into OpenAI and about a year since Altman had been in attendance at the wedding of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos to Lauren Sánchez.First reactions and reviews are in... NEONArtificial premiered at the New York Film Festival on Monday night, with early reviews already coming where critics have been praising the film which has received a critics score of 92 per cent on film and TV review aggregate website, Rotten Tomatoes, and has a 9.1 out of 10 rating on IMDb.Variety's Owen Gleiberman said, "As you watch the film, AI comes alive as a subject. It becomes real — you touch what it is, what it means, what the stakes are. The result is a movie that’s at once inspiring and deeply chilling, and when it’s over you’re in a different place.""This ranks among Guadagnino’s best work, its dry humor lulling us into a relaxed state of enjoyment before the sword comes down on the scary reality we’re now facing," according to The Hollywood Reporter's David Rooney."Be afraid. Be very afraid. At least that is how I felt after watching Guadagnino’s origin story of how OpenAI and its marquee product, ChatGPT, came to be," wrote Deadline's Pete Hammond, praising Garfield's "stunning" performance of "creating a portrait of a guy who changes his story depending on whoever he happens to be talking to."Awards Radar's Joey Magidson, noted "The first half of the film is actually very funny, while the second half pulls back on the jokes, eventually becoming a fairly sobering drama," and also praised Yura Borisov's that "Anora was no fluke, delivering another strong performance as the moral center of the film.""If its tonal unevenness sometimes undercuts its urgency, it’s still an engrossing lament that we’re forever doomed to repeat our mistakes—until, that is, we’re literally doomed," Daily Beast's Nick Schager commented.IndieWire's David Ehrlich graded the film a B, "What 'Artificial' argues so well, often at its own expense, is that nothing we ever modeled after ourselves was ever going to be all that good."Here are some initial social media reaction from those who attended the premiere:Joshua Rothkopf, film editor at the LA Times wrote, "Luca Guadagnino just ate Sorkin’s lunch. In every way, ARTIFICIAL is the spiritual sequel to THE SOCIAL NETWORK, threading together betrayal, broken ethics and humor — and arriving at a vision as scary as COLOSSUS: THE FORBIN PROJECT. Damon Albarn’s Bowie-esque score ftw."(For context, Garfield previously played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in the 2010 film The Social Network). Variety’s Clayton Davis wrote described Artificial as “Guadagnino’s best film in a decade” and “Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov soar to new heights. Loved.” "Andrew Garfield is terrifyingly precise in ARTIFICIAL. He captures Sam Altman’s chillingly polite, messianic aura in a brilliant balancing act of manic genius and corporate coldness. Absolutely electric!" commented Jairo Jiménez. The Hollywood Reporter's David Canfield noted, "In Guadagnino's bleakly compelling ARTIFICIAL, Andrew Garfield takes some massive & tricky swings in his portrayal of Sam Altman. What he pulls off is mesmerizing, strange and terrifyingly seductive, especially as he finally becomes the film's center. A career-best performance." "ARTIFICIAL is Luca Guadagnino’s telling of the origins of the AI boom and where it may one day lead us. As entertaining as it is terrifying, it’s a brilliantly written human story about power, control, ambition, and greed that might be the most urgently relevant film of our time," shared Next Best Picture's Matt Neglia. "Wanna be clear: Luca Guadagnino’s ARTIFICIAL is a horror comedy. About the destruction of humanity. In real time. You’re laughing at the ridiculous characters & also THESE PEOPLE EXIST, they’re running the world, and the info in the movie is already old. F***ing terrifying," said journalist and author Jada Yuan. "Andrew Garfield walks a fine line between movie monster, buffoonish mogul, and evil genius," Eric Kohn posted. The Playlist's Gregory Ellwood said, "In a year of filmmakers warning us the end is coming Artificial is a sledgehammer. My lord. And not that he needs it, but Andrew Garfield gives Sam Altman the most epic character assassination ever." "Artificial is tremendous, a blistering and furious reworking of The Social Network for a world that’s well past the point of destruction, intimate in character but sweeping in scale, more acutely aware of our expiration date than any other film this year. a major achievement," another wrote. It's fair to say all of these reactions have intrigued many of us, as one person reacted, "People calling Artificial the true Social Network sequel... okay now you got me interested." When is the release date? NEONArtificial is set to be released in US cinemas on Christmas Day and in UK and Ireland on 22 January 2027.Why not read...Andrew Garfield reveals terrifying reason he stopped using ChatGPT after playing Sam Altman in ArtificialWhat are critics saying about 'Verity' starring Anne Hathaway?Sign up to our free indy100 weekly newsletterHave your say in our news democracy. scored.body:
How Funny Can Artificial’s AI Doomerism Be?

By

Jason P. Frank,

a Vulture writer covering comedy, theater, and music

Photo: Neon

Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial premiered at New York Film Festival last night and left many people wondering, Just how funny can a movie about both the terrible capacity of generative AI and the immoral people in charge of it be? The film follows the creation of OpenAI; the man who made the technology, Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov); and how OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield) lied his way into leading the world’s most dangerous technology. It’s also pretty funny. In Q&As following the movie’s first two screenings, Guadagnino and his cast explained how they combined real-life horror and observed comedy.

“There’s a pretty thin line between comedy and horror, and that’s been true for a long time,” the film’s screenwriter, Simon Rich, said after the movie’s first screening. “There’s a reason why there are so many Simpsons episodes that are based on Twilight Zone episodes. Luca’s film does a wonderful job of straddling that line. There are moments where you don’t know whether to laugh or scream, and that’s often my favorite kind of art.”

Following the movie’s second screening, Guadagnino explained that “this is a movie about paradoxes,” which allowed for the combination of tones. “It’s about the dream of the future in this city that dreamt the future for a long time, San Francisco. And yet this future and these dreams are only individual,” he added. “There is no idea of a connection with other people, with us. There is a sort of ridiculousness to this belief.” The oddity of that contradiction then extended to the whole project. “We were working with an incredible cast, which made this paradox almost slapstick,” Guadagnino said. “And at the same time, they registered, with patience, the consequences of their behavior, which are frightening.”

Perhaps the person with the oddest job in the cast is Ike Barinholtz, who plays Elon Musk. His Musk is the funniest character in the movie — both an odd object of admiration during the early years for the main characters and a blustery idiot by the end. “When we were shooting it, at least the scenes I was in, there was a sense of fun and funny,” Barinholtz recalled. “When I watched it, it was a horror movie. I can’t remember the last time I saw a movie where I was laughing throughout and walked away feeling like I have to, like, reevaluate my life.” He also noted how different this time period in Musk’s public image was from the contemporary vision of him. “This is not him at the RNC with the chainsaw,” Barinholtz said. “This is him in 2014 when a lot of people were like, This guy’s gonna save us. He’s amazing. The way we shot those scenes, people looked at Elon like he’s a God, which I think is naturally a funny energy.”

Garfield, meanwhile, did not approach the film looking for humor. “I remember seeing Sam testifying to Congress for the first time, way back when, and I was like, This guy’s great,” Garfield recalled of his first impression of Altman. “He’s clear-eyed, he’s honest, he’s transparent, he’s talking about regulation. He has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in power, and he’s incredibly charismatic. Then, we learn more about a person.” His job, he realized, could not be to represent Altman as he sees himself but to bring forth larger questions. “The deeper responsibility may be to try and do some interrogation on who we are giving all of our autonomy, power, and data to. That felt like the greater service.”
