scored.body:
Anthropic’s March 2026 San Francisco summit gathered 15 Christian leaders to discuss AI ethics, not to bless Claude’s sentienceFlorida Gov. Ron DeSantis recently called Anthropic’s outreach to Christian leaders “a creepy thing,” claiming the company brought clergy to San Francisco to bless the idea that its Claude chatbot is sentient. The available reporting does not support that characterization.What Anthropic actually did was convene roughly 15 Christian leaders, including Catholic and Protestant figures, academics, and business professionals, for a private two-day summit at its San Francisco headquarters in late March 2026.What Actually Happened in San FranciscoAnthropic’s summit focused on ethical and moral guidance, not a religious ceremony for a chatbot.The discussions centered on how Claude should respond to grief, emotional distress, and self-harm. Anthropic described the gathering as a consultation with people from “wisdom traditions” intended to guide the moral formation of its AI systems, according to the SF Standard.The question of whether AI could be considered a “child of God” did come up. Brian Patrick Green, an AI-ethics scholar who attended the summit, told DNYUZ that sentience was not a core subject of the meetings. Anthropic told reporters the effort was about seeking broader societal input into AI development, not a formal religious endorsement of Claude’s consciousness.

What DeSantis Said and Where the Reporting Parts WaysHis “creepy” framing goes further than the available evidence supports.DeSantis argued that treating AI in terms associated with human spirituality was misguided, and that a chatbot simply does not have a soul. That philosophical position is his to hold. His specific claim that Anthropic asked religious leaders to perform a blessing and declare Claude sentient is not substantiated.DeSantis also framed the outreach as part of a broader transhumanist tendency to elevate technology above human beings. That is his political interpretation of the summit’s purpose, not a description verified by participant accounts or the company’s stated rationale.That said, the questions Anthropic raised at this summit are worth scrutinizing on their own terms. A private AI company consulting religious leaders about how its product handles users in crisis, with limited public transparency about the outcomes, is an arrangement that warrants more than a press release.The Policy Debate UnderneathFlorida’s proposed AI consumer protections target practical risks, not metaphysics.DeSantis’ broader AI agenda addresses more concrete ground. His proposed Florida “AI Bill of Rights” covers parental consent for minors interacting with companion chatbots and mandatory disclosure when users are not speaking with a human, according to Route Fifty. It also targets deepfake restrictions and consumer data protections.The Florida Senate passed a version of the legislation containing several of those provisions. It stalled in the Florida House, according to Vox. Whatever its legislative fate, those accountability mechanisms directly affect the people most vulnerable to poorly designed AI systems.The argument worth having is not whether Claude can be baptized. It is whether Anthropic and companies like it will be held responsible when a vulnerable teenager turns to a chatbot during a crisis and that conversation goes wrong. Someone should answer for it when it does.

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield plays Sam Altman in Artificial (Getty Images)

Sam Altman says he once walked out for coffee and found Andrew Garfield wearing an identical outfit and carrying the same backpack as him while Artificial was filming near his home.

Speaking to Vanity Fair, the out gay OpenAI CEO said he has never met Garfield, who plays him in Luca Guadagnino’s film, but the pair did share a brief moment on the street.

Altman said he had seen filming notices beforehand but did not realise what they were for. “And then one morning, I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” he said.

“We waved and went on, but it was really weird,” Altman added. He said it was strange to see someone who had “nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms”.

Artificial dramatises the five-day period in 2023 when Altman was ousted from OpenAI and then rehired.

Garfield previously said he was “really scared” about potential backlash to his portrayal of Altman in the film, and stressed that he had not met him.

‘I don’t think they’re going for accuracy’

Altman said he has watched the trailer and concluded of Garfield’s performance: “He did walk like me.”

Andrew Garfield attends the premiere of Artificial during the 64th New York Film Festival on October 05, 2026 (Getty Images)

He also said he is not expecting the film to be a faithful retelling of events. “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” Altman said. “It will not be good as an accurate depiction. Except for the walk.”

As an example, Altman pointed to a trailer moment showing him rushing into a bunker lined with weapons. “There’s no bunker with firearms on the wall,” he said, adding: “That’s an example of inaccuracy, but I did look kind of cool.”

Andrew Garfield on Sam Altman

Altman’s comments come as Artificial premiered at the New York Film Festival, where Garfield said he was initially charmed by Altman after seeing him testify to Congress.

“I was like, ‘This guy seems f****** great. He’s honest. He’s transparent. He’s talking about regulation, and he has no stake in OpenAI. We need more of these people in control. He’s incredibly charming and charismatic.’ And then you learn more about a person,” he said, as per Variety.

He also said he spent “two to three months” listening to and watching footage of Altman while preparing for the role, and added: “We need to shine the light as bright as possible at the nooks and crannies of people we’re giving all of our autonomy and power to.”

Neon is distributing Artificial after Amazon MGM Studios dropped the film following Amazon’s $50billion investment and partnership with OpenAI.

The film is set for US cinemas on 25 December, with a UK release date of 7 January, 2027.

articles.headline: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
“Aggressive technocapitalism wins, safety dies” is a long name for a movie and a short logline for a film, yet the phrase might accurately be used for both when it comes to Artificial.Luca Guadagnino brought his latest and by far most-topical movie to a world-premiere at the 64th New York Film Festival Monday evening, the first stop of what has already seemed like an unusually long journey. Ditched by Amazon MGM Studios after its parent company’s $50 billion investment in OpenAI, the film, as it turns out, would be non-grata at a large tech firm even if it never signed on for that 5 percent equity stake in Sam Altman‘s company. Persistently bleak under the rays of the California sun, Artificial (now under the aegis of Anora studio Neon) is the movie of the moment — the origin story of our current AI quagmire at the literal, psychological and pretty much every other level.Or as NYFF programming chief Dennis Lim said before the screening:“We are already in a threshold period. We need to understand how we got here, and the film you’re about to see shows us that way.”The movie is notably faithful, at times dutifully chronological and nearly always horror-movie bracing on the subject of the rise of capitalist AI. Ilya Sutskever, an idealistic and socially unpolished Russian immigrant, shows up at the office door of Geoffrey Hinton, a godfather of AI, at the University of Toronto in 2003. There he will learn under the well-intentioned eventual Nobel Prize winner, soon following him to Google and its Bay Area halo. As observers of the space well know, Sutskever ends up meeting Sam Altman at a 2014 conference, where the Y Combinator financier (already well established in Silicon Valley at barely 30) chases down the prodigy to convince him to work at a nascent OpenAI as chief science officer and supercharge its LLM ambitions. Or, more accurately, make them possible in the first place — Sutskever is Wozniak to Altman’s Jobs, but more so.Soon a (last) supper follows with Altman, Elon Musk, Greg Brockman and others — the prelude to a slow realization by Sutskever, and us, that the science Sutskever wants to develop to save the world is the capital Altman wants to use to build a warchest.

We know the rest — OpenAI rushes out ChatGPT in November 2022, shocking the industry and even many of its own employees; Altman displays a growing accelerationism with the abetment of lead investor Microsoft (mixed with blog-y pronouncements of transforming and saving the world, and a weird word-cloud fondness for the word “compute”); and OpenAI transitions from a nonprofit to its opposite. The whole story culminates in Sutskever’s notorious November Coup of 2023 in which Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and assorted OpenAI loyalists back Altman, engineering his return so that he’s stronger than ever — a day clear then and doubly indicative now of capitalism’s ultimate triumph and on which, Yom Kippur-style, our AI fate in many ways was inscribed and sealed.Which brings us to late 2026 — right up to it, as the film collides with the last month of AI safety warnings, which also make the screen with a postscript (one of about five) about AI researcher and whistleblower Jacob Coxon warning of a pox on all their houses (or at least on his former employers Anthropic and OpenAI) for a reckless speedplow over any semblance of safety. On cue, Coxon was taping Jon Stewart a half mile downtown at the exact time the movie was playing, in what one commenter very reasonably called a “most serious and chilling episode” of The Daily Show.A slow-burn account that will not surprise those who have covered the meteoric ascent and Teflon resilience of Altman, Artificial still offers a rich and often entertaining primer on the becoming of OpenAI, how integrity and caution has time and again been sacrificed on the holy altar of finance. (You can read The Hollywood Reporter’s review of the film here.) Not to mention a parable of modern Silicon Valley, the place where advanced science and obscene wealth converge in a manner unprecedented in the history of humanity and can only, if every novel on either subject can be believed, end splendiferously well. Guadagnino took an interest in the subject because “as much as AI belongs to a world of mathematics and computers, it is still generated by people and exists in space of their interaction,” as he noted from the NYFF stage. Screenwriter Simon Rich took an interest in the subject after being told by a childhood friend decades ago about what was possible with AI. That friend ended up going on to work in the industry, prompting Rich, a former Saturday Night Live and Pixar writer as well as a novelist and essayist, to pen this script. “I’m not particularly charismatic or good-looking but as a last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie. I hope to God a couple people pay attention,” he said.Amazon initially backed the movie before, well, “the concept of a conflict of interest is a very important, let’s say, elephant in the room here,” as Guadagnino told THR’s David Canfield. In retrospect it’s almost shocking the company would have even contemplated signing on to a movie so innately critical of a Valley vision in which noble use cases form but a thin camouflaging membrane over the bloody black heart of a human-trampling moneygrab — so much so that the question becomes not why Amazon abandoned the film but which Hollywood agent is responsible for the Houdinian feat of convincing them they should hop aboard in the first place, and why aren’t they the ones ruling the world?

To give you a sense of just how scabrous this film is, and just generally to level you up on how some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful people are getting shown in what will surely be an Oscar mainstay and cultural lodestone this Hollywood season, here’s a quick rundown: Greg Brockman — In real life he’s an AGI evangelist and Altman lock-stepper who’s a jock-like presence that donates millions to a pro-AI Super PAC. In the movie he’s all of those things but nerdier and more simpering. Cooper Hoffman, who plays him, said at NYFF he didn’t read any books about Brockman, but let himself think about a phrase Garfield told him: that the man would leave his wife for Sam Altman.Mira Murati — Long the most enigmatic of OpenAI figures — she tries to stop Altman but also sticks with him; she is at once Cassandra and complicit — the Albanian ex-Tesla engineer gets her due from Monica Barbaro who gives the character just enough warmth to seem like a hero, until undertaking actions that make her seem like the opposite.Sam Altman — Hinton in the film describes Altman as someone so toxically charismatic he would land on an island of cannibals and shortly after become their king. Andrew Garfield portrays him as a completely dishonest personality who will always tell everybody how much he likes them to their face while screwing them behind their back. A flamboyant cipher to a sometimes-cartoonish degree (you can read his articulate descriptions of how he crafted the character here) Garfield’s Altman is going for a different kind of spiritual truth. “Of course it will feel confronting [to Altman],” Garfield said at the screening, “[but I wanted] to a deep interrogation of who are giving our power, our autonomy, our data too.”

The best gift Garfield could give Altman is going so hard on the caricature-y touches, allowing Altman to discredit the whole thing. He’s already tried to do that, without having seen the movie. “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” Altman just said to Vanity Fair, admittedly basing his assessment on the trailer. He and Garfield cannot even agree on whether they waved to each other when the film was shooting near the mogul’s house. Altman says they did; Garfield said at the premiere that “if that happened I must have blacked out because I don’t remember it at all.”

Yann LeCun — The other godfather of AI gets a cameo in which he shows up Sutskever by mockingly asking him from the audience if he’s ever seen 2001. I don’t know that this ever happened, but as an object lesson in Sutskever not being taken seriously by the AI establishment it serves its purpose. It feels like shade that LeCun never appears in the film again, though given the treatment some of the other tech personalities receive, he might want to send Luca a bouquet.

Guy on Bench — Jason Schwarzman plays an anonymous prophet of doom (and ex-techie) who shows up at an San Francisco park to describe to Sutskever all the ways the AI boom can go wrong, providing the movie with its from-the-headlines leitmotif and cinema more broadly its wildest hair since Forrest Gump.Elon Musk — Ike Barinholtz has Musk wandering in from another movie, or dimension, a ramble-y, arrogant but ultimately comically non-threatening figure. This will be noticeable and even triggering to anyone who sees Alex Gibney’s Musk or just followed the man’s DOGE-based eviscerations of important aspects of the federal government. “When you play someone as beloved, as universally admired…” Barinholtz began his intro at the festival, before saying he tried to capture Elon how he was viewed then, long before “the RNC with a chainsaw.” Barenholtz’s portrayal raises what’s actually a key question in fact-based art: are we required to inject a modern understanding we couldn’t know at the time?

Tasha McAuley — Entrepreneur, Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s wife and coup-joiner on the OpenAI board, she is played briefly by Zosia Mamet (though not identified by name).

Geoffrey Hinton — If there’s one good thing about AI going so pop-cultural, it’s that we get a full-blooded character representing one of the great scientific minds of our time, here depicted (accurately) as the conscience of an industry. If there’s a second good thing, it’s that we get Mark Rylance portraying such a conscience. Dario Amodei — He is now known as the man who founded the breakaway Anthropic and, a showdown or two with the Pentagon aside, is running a company that could destroy the job market and the world as we know it (hey, his words). But back during his OpenAI era, he’s part of Altman’s gallery, if a very nerdy and definitely more idealistic member of same. Honestly on the scale of image-rehab to complete evisceration, Amodei is one of the few AI entrepreneurs to end up closer to the former in this film. A far cry, to say the least, from his recent depiction on SNL or portrayal in Stewart’s coverage.

Ilya Sutskever — The story’s unabashed hero, aided in real life by him all but disappearing after the failed coup (though he did raise $1 billion for an AI safety company). Sutskever felt his ideals so betrayed he is said to have not left his home for months after he lost the battle with Altman. Garfield’s is the showier performance but Yura Borisov‘s depiction as a man slowly realizing how he’s been had is Richard-Gere-at-the-end-of-Primal-Fear-level stuff. “I was just trying to put this [lost innocence] in the film so you can feel what I hope you feel,” he said at the screening. The Jacob Coxons and other figures who continue Sutskever’s legacy, not to mention the concerns that only become more urgent by the minute, make him feel less like someone from Ye Olde AI days of 2023 but one whispering in our ear as we scroll the headlines at the breakfast table every morning.

The only downside to such a fiercely of-the-moment take, of course, is that said moment can change in the nearly three months until the film’s Christmas release. Maybe by then Neon will need to include 20 postscripts, and submit to the Oscars’ documentary category.

Photo by Heather Diehl/Getty Images filesThe political, economic and ideological debate over the meaning and future of artificial intelligence keeps moving along with many people chasing the rapidly evolving technology along a twisted road to nobody knows where. Each day brings a new turn as AI haters and alarmists battle AI supporters and proponents.Subscribe now to read the latest news in your city and across Canada.Exclusive articles from Barbara Shecter, Joe O'Connor, Gabriel Friedman, and others.Daily content from Financial Times, the world's leading global business publication.Unlimited online access to read articles from Financial Post, National Post and 15 news sites across Canada with one account.National Post ePaper, an electronic replica of the print edition to view on any device, share and comment on.Daily puzzles, including the New York Times Crossword.Subscribe now to read the latest news in your city and across Canada.Exclusive articles from Barbara Shecter, Joe O'Connor, Gabriel Friedman and others.Daily content from Financial Times, the world's leading global business publication.Unlimited online access to read articles from Financial Post, National Post and 15 news sites across Canada with one account.National Post ePaper, an electronic replica of the print edition to view on any device, share and comment on.Daily puzzles, including the New York Times Crossword.Create an account or sign in to continue with your reading experience.Access articles from across Canada with one account.Share your thoughts and join the conversation in the comments.Enjoy additional articles per month.Get email updates from your favourite authors.Create an account or sign in to continue with your reading experience.Access articles from across Canada with one accountShare your thoughts and join the conversation in the commentsEnjoy additional articles per monthGet email updates from your favourite authorsSign In or Create an AccountorToday we take a look at two of many recent developments that pit unlikely combatants in a seemingly impossible confrontation over the future of AI technology. One is legendary economist John Maynard Keynes, the godfather of Keynesian economics who died in 1946. The other is legendary AI tech billionaire Sam Altman, who was born 40 years after Keynes died and who recently said that as AI advances it will lead to “bad things happening,” but it should not be stopped.Separated by almost a century, the two global celebrities are now portrayed as modern opponents in the political struggle over the regulatory future of AI. We begin with Keynes, who appears live in a New York Times video posted last week. Well, not quite live. It’s a video of a robotic Keynes, in which he states that he is very concerned about the rise of artificial intelligence as a destructive force in the economy. In the Times piece, prepared by Princeton University economist Markus Brunnermeier, Keynes is interviewed as if he were alive today.Get the latest headlines, breaking news and columns.By signing up you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc.A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.The next issue of Top Stories will soon be in your inbox.We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try againKeynes: “Whether AI ends up as a source of broadly shared prosperity and purpose or a machine for manufacturing a new dominant class of wealthy and powerful is not preordained by the technology itself. It will be determined by your government and whether it has the political courage to use its laws and its tax systems to ensure that AI will work to the benefit of all of society’s citizens.”To get Keynes, who’s been deceased for 80 years, to address one of today’s hottest economic topics,  Brunnermeier used an AI robot team to scan 12,000 pages of Keynes’s writings to create what can only be described as a fake video that claims to capture views on circumstances that are far removed from the century-old Keynes era.Brunnermeier cites a 1930 Keynes essay — “The Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren” — as a reason for creating the interview. In the essay, and in his 12,000 pages of work, Keynes generally did not support  government intervention, other than disciplined macro-economic policies to prevent perverse fluctuations. He usually shied away from endorsing the kind of policy moves raised in the robot interview.In the essay, written during the Great Depression, Keynes even approached the deep depression pessimism of 1930 in terms that ring true today. Deep depression pessimism, he wrote, is a “wildly mistaken interpretation“ of what is happening. Britain and the United States are in fact enduring a transition. “The increase of technical efficiency has been taking place faster than we can deal with the problem of labour absorption; the improvement in the standard of life has been a little too quick; the banking and monetary system of the world has been preventing the rate of interest from falling as fast as equilibrium requires,” he wrote.It is admittedly impossible to wade through all of Keynes’s millions of words of economic ideas, but there is no evidence that he endorsed major government intervention to block or delay technological advancements. The fake video of Keynes specifically addressing AI by name is nothing more than an entertaining technical feat, almost a comedy routine, that attempts to shape public opinion.The “Grandchildren” essay is filled with descriptive optimism about the dramatic benefits of centuries of scientific and technical breakthroughs that he believed would, and should, continue. Such change causes “technological unemployment” and other troubles, but they are only temporary because they are part of a process in which “mankind is solving its economic problem.” Over the next 100 years, he said, economic prosperity will continue, despite tech-caused joblessness and widespread pessimism.In other words, the real Keynes would almost certainly reject the fake AI Keynes. Indeed, it is more than odd that the AI search of 12,000 pages of Keynes’s economic writing could not come up with any direct quotes that would flag opposition to modern technological progress and insist on government intervention to prevent disruption. The only option was to fake an interview.Back in 1930, the real Keynes effectively endorsed the idea that the AI transition currently sweeping the world will inevitably lead to “bad things” happening — which is the language used by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman in an interview released Monday by Decoded, a tech podcast created by Politico. In a discussion around OpenAI’s now notorious difficulties with rogue agents, Altman argued that, “The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” which was instantly blasted by AI critics as another indicator of tech oligarch madness.One writer said the words are evidence that Altman “isn’t afraid to throw humanity under the bus to build his dreams of a society powered by AI.” That is not, however, the meaning of the bad-things-happening statement.  Altman is essentially channelling the original Keynesian “Grandchildren” position that economic change, especially technological transformations, inevitably produce negative consequences, ranging from unemployment to unintended accidents and failures, that nevertheless lead to improvements in human existence.Whether AI will live up to the claims of its promoters remains to be seen. But it is nevertheless wrong to claim that Altman and his tech colleagues want the right to throw humanity under a bus to satisfy their egotistical drive for trillionaire status and to overthrow modern society. U.S. democratic Socialist Bernie Saunders asked Altman: “What ‘bad things’ should we accept to advance AI? Losing tens of millions of jobs? A mass surveillance state? A mental health crisis for our kids? A global financial crisis? Mass extinction? Let’s not wait to find out. Pause advanced AI NOW!”In Altman’s view, the AI transition should proceed as quickly as is reasonably possible. He endorsed the U.S. government’s policy, supported by AI corporations, to move cautiously with regulation. The alternative process being advocated by anti-tech activists is based on false economic, political and technological premises. If we halted progress to prevent “bad things from happening,” no progress would occur.Take, for example, the automobile. Since 1900, more than four million Americans have died in auto accidents. Altman is right. Bad things happen. Along with other AI tech firms, he reasonably argues that the corporate and government approach to future AI development should avoid controlling AI to produce an impossible alternative, totally risk-free technology. The real John Maynard Keynes would likely agree with that conclusion. Maybe somebody should run that idea through a bot.Financial Post Join the Conversation This website uses cookies to personalize your content (including ads), and allows us to analyze our traffic. scored.body: Fortune US | October – November 2026 CAN A LOW-KEY ENGINEER WIN THE AI RACE? - - BY SEBASTIAN HERRERA —Indrani Sen BY PHIL WAHBA IN LATE JULY, current and former Apple product developers gathered for a reunion at the company’s Cupertino, Calif., headquarters. As evening fell and guests sipped drinks and ate hors d’oeuvres, John Ternus slipped into the Observatory building, an event space embedded in a landscaped hillside with a large oval window that looks out toward Apple’s main building.Some guests were surprised to see Ternus at the gathering, held to celebrate a design team executive’s 30th anniversary at the company. Ternus, who in April was anointed Apple’s newest CEO, had just finished a long day of reporting the company’s quarterly earnings. But he hung around and worked the crowd, flashing his signature warm smile and reminiscing.Ternus gave no formal speech, but he projected calm confidence, and in individual conversations, he spoke with genuine excitement about Apple’s product road map over the next several years. “It was super reassuring,” one event attendee told Fortune, asking to remain anonymous to discuss a private Apple gathering. “He holds a tremendous amount of optimism and belief that hard things can be worked out.”Ternus will certainly have plenty of hard things to work out at the $4.85 trillion company he now leads. (On Sept. 1 Tim Cook ended his tenure as CEO and became executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors.) While the consumer giant’s reach has never been wider, it’s also confronting some of the biggest trials of its 50-year history.Cook made Apple a cash-flow king and one of the world’s supply-chain titans, but as Ternus inherits the iPhone maker from his legendary predecessor, Apple is grappling with questions about its strategy on artificial intelligence, where it is facing competition from rivals such as OpenAI. Meanwhile, a memory chip shortage threatens to squeeze its margins; its revenue growth is slowing; and even longtime Apple fans admit the maker of aspirational tech has lost some of its product design mojo. articles.headline: Why the internet is rejecting Sam Altman’s high-fashion cover - Firstpost
articles.body: Why the internet is rejecting Sam Altman’s high-fashion cover    Firstpost

scored.body:
Tech billionaires control wealth, but they cannot build genuine cool in a laboratory. Following Sam Altman’s new Vanity Fair spread and Met Gala takeovers, critics argue that legacy media is surrendering its cultural leverage to Silicon Valley When Vanity Fair released Sam Altman’s digital cover shot by Annie Leibovitz, social media quickly filled with frustration. Framed like a brooding, romantic hero, the OpenAI CEO stood at the centre of the magazine’s "New Establishment" issue.The cover arrived right as Artificial—Luca Guadagnino's high-profile movie about the rise of OpenAI and Sam Altman—had its world premiere at the New York Film Festival on October 5, 2026. Rather than offering a critical, independent look at a tech leader dominating the news cycle, the magazine crowns Altman with a glossy, heroic photo spread.Around the same time, Vanity Fair posted a clip from its 'Fair Game' interview series featuring Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci and Tony-nominated playwright Jeremy O. Harris. Sitting directly across from Guiducci, Harris questioned why legacy publications like Vanity Fair and Condé Nast Chief Content Officer Anna Wintour keep granting cultural status to Silicon Valley executives.

The fight over cultural capitalHarris argued that media gatekeepers hold immense power over what is considered stylish, prestigious, and culturally important. Tech founders control billions of dollars and major digital platforms, but they cannot build cultural capital or genuine "cool" in a laboratory. By handing out magazine covers and red-carpet invites, traditional media outlets give up the one piece of leverage they have left over the tech industry.This uncomfortable partnership between high fashion and tech leaders is visible across the industry. At the Met Gala, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez served as honorary co-chairs after donating $10 million, leading to street protests, guerrilla boycott posters, and notable absences from frequent attendees like Zendaya, Bella Hadid, and Meryl Streep. Meanwhile, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg traded his basic gray t-shirts for front-row seats at Prada shows and custom Bode designs.More from LifestyleImage launderingThe effort to gain cultural legitimacy reaches beyond fashion shows. Palantir, a software firm known for military and surveillance analytics, recently sold out a $239 French chore coat. The company adopted the "bleu de travail", a classic blue work jacket popularised by late New York Times photographer Bill Cunningham as a symbol of humble street-style photography.Fashion commentator thisisantwon pointed out that style is now easy to buy off the shelf. A multi-billion-dollar tech company can hire top creative directors, pick a clean typeface, and instantly present itself as an independent, creative lifestyle brand.How "tastewashing" protects big techWriter Kyle Chayka calls this strategy "tastewashing." It describes how companies building automation and surveillance tools use artisanal aesthetics and liberal humanism to soften their public image. When an industry faces heavy criticism over data collection and workplace automation, adopting high-end fashion serves as a protective shield.

What bothers people online is the contradiction at the heart of these profiles. Magazine spreads treat AI executives like misunderstood genius artists or historical figures like Oppenheimer. Yet, for most everyday users, the actual product of AI isn't high art—it's low-quality digital clutter, job insecurity, and corporate disruption. The public sees right through the luxury styling, growing weary of tech leaders using fashion to rebrand products that do more harm than good.

scored.body:
Jacob Birks October 7th, 2026 - 9:15 AM

Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman in 'Artificial'

Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, the true-story drama starring Andrew Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, recently premiered at the New York Film Festival (NYFF). The film was introduced at its premiere screening by NYFF programming chief Dennis Lim, who said the following before the screening:

We are already in a threshold period. We need to understand how we got here, and the film you’re about to see shows us that way.

This quote comes from a recent article by The Hollywood Reporter, which praised the film as the “movie of the moment – the origin story of our current AI quagmire at the literal, psychological, and pretty much every other level.” THR detailed the film’s intricate portrait of its topical subject matter. The article states,

The movie is notably faithful, at times dutifully chronological and nearly always horror-movie bracing on the subject of the rise of capitalist AI.

The article also later describes the film as offering “a rich and often entertaining primer on the becoming of OpenAI, how integrity and caution have time and again been sacrificed on the holy altar of finance.”finance.” As for Andrew Garfield’s much-anticipated performance as Sam Altman, THR’s article also praises his portrayal of the OpenAI CEO, saying the following about Garfield’s portrayal:

Garfield portrays him as a completely dishonest personality who will always tell everybody how much he likes them to their face while screwing them behind their back. A flamboyant cipher to a sometimes-cartoonish degree. Garfield’s Altman is going for a different kind of spiritual truth.

Artificial is notable for being originally scrapped by its original studio, Amazon, which decided to shop the film to other studios, not long after the studio put in a $50 billion investment in OpenAI. Neon is now distributing the film and will release it this Christmas.

articles.body: Artificial Goes After Our Silicon Valley Overlords. Just Not Very Well.    Mother Jones

scored.body:
Open AI CEO Sam Altman before delivering the keynote address at the OpenAI developers conference in San Francisco on September 29, 2026, where he announced new artificial intelligence personal assistant agents named "dots" to rival Meta's Muse.Heather Diehl/Getty

Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily.

The world premiere of Artificial, the new movie centered around the rise of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as he led an unstable company down a dangerous path, was packed. The recent wave of high-profile “rogue AI” security incidents, disputes over tech industry-led safeguards and regulation, and continued multibillion-dollar investments to advance development has clearly piqued public interest.

The movie, directed by Challengers filmmaker Luca Guadagnino, contains scenes derived from real reporting on OpenAI and the industry: discussions on ensuring their products “align” with human values while racing competitors such as Google, and undertaking corporate restructuring to draw investment from the likes of Microsoft. It also hinges on wide public sentiment that major tech companies and their leaders hold too much power and developers should pause development of their most advanced models to mitigate risks to humanity.

The people behind Artificial appear to agree. “The deeper responsibility we all felt is to try to do some interrogation of who we are giving all of our autonomy, power, and data to,” Andrew Garfield, who plays Altman, said on Monday night during the post-screening Q&A at the New York Film Festival, “that felt like the service to the greater thing.” The actor said the filmmakers were adding new scenes while shooting to create a “living document” of how the AI industry was progressing.

The moral center of the film is Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI’s co-founder and former chief scientist played by Yura Borisov, who sees in AI technology potential to solve humanity’s problems, but realizes too late that his idealism doesn’t fit within the constraints of the market. A former AI researcher played by Jason Schwartzman, presented as a prophet who sees the future of the tech with clarity, tells Sutskever that it could lead, if not to total human extinction, at least to life under AI subjugation.

But the filmmakers also portray the tech leaders who don’t recognize this—or simply don’t care—as goofy megalomaniacs. While Garfield portrays Altman as constantly dodging confrontation to get people to be as forgiving toward him as possible, he also plays him with a cartoonish quality—with his frantic shifts in posture played as a joke, and the post-production team changing the actor’s brown eyes to a bright, inhuman blue. Even more so for others like Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, whose facial expressions and demeanor seem to lean far more silly than threatening.

The intermittent comic relief scenes give the movie’s satirical side the energy of Saturday Night Live sketches—the screenwriter, Simon Rich, previously wrote for the comedy show—immediate, but largely short on depth and nuance. The filmmakers could pull their humor, and their wider sense of what’s laughable about these characters, from deeper, and darker, places. (There are vague gestures at a misogynistic Silicon Valley culture, but nothing political or deeply personal.)

With the characters operating more as caricatures, the movie doesn’t meet what Garfield called on Monday “the deeper responsibility” to interrogate the people it depicts or the culture behind them the countless expository conversations on the potential harms of generative AI—between real-life characters who unleashed said harms through global-scale business relationships—don’t feel grounded in any reality. The mentions of existential risks stop at just that: Altman says “Countries will fall. Industries are gonna collapse.” The only specific harm addressed is AI’s contribution to a person’s suicide.

As I wrote on Monday, it’s good that Hollywood might finally be catching up to tech companies’ negative impacts on our world. Many Silicon Valley films before Artificial did not. But only being able to giggle at our tech overlords is not enough.

Disclosure: The Center for Investigative Reporting, the parent company of Mother Jones, has sued OpenAI for copyright violations. OpenAI denies the allegations.

articles.headline: Did Sam Altman Lie About Waving to Andrew Garfield? - The Cut
articles.body: Did Sam Altman Lie About Waving to Andrew Garfield?    The Cut

scored.body:
By

Olivia Craighead,

a news writer for The Cut who covers pop culture and celebrity.

Previously, she wrote about pop culture and entertainment at Gawker.

Photo-Illustration: by The Cut; Photos: Getty Images

Sam Altman has always had what one might call a tenuous relationship with the truth. A New Yorker report from April revealed that OpenAI’s chief scientist once sent a secret memo to the board alleging that Altman had a “consistent pattern” of lying. So it makes sense that Altman may have embellished things when he said that he waved to Andrew Garfield while the actor was filming Artificial outside of his house.

On Monday, Vanity Fair published a lengthy interview with Altman, in which he said he has had only one minor interaction with Garfield, who’s playing Altman in Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial. Altman claims that, while the movie was filming outside of his house, he was walking to get coffee when he saw “a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something.”

“We waved and went on, but it was really weird,” Altman said. He was then asked if he had any follow-up contact with Garfield, but stated that he only “waved at him that one time and that was it.”

Coincidentally, Artificial premiered at the New York Film Festival on Monday night — the perfect time to ask  Garfield about his run-in with Altman. Did he learn anything from this interaction? Did Altman’s wave unlock the key to Garfield’s performance? Was it spooky seeing Altman while in Altman drag outside of Altman’s house? Those would have all been interesting insights, but Garfield said he didn’t see Altman at all.

“If that happened, I must have blacked out,” Garfield told the crowd at NYFF when asked about the alleged wave. He confirmed they did shoot outside Altman’s San Francisco home but said that “we didn’t see him at all that day we were shooting.”

Gosh, who are we to believe here? The guy who was briefly fired from his own company in part because he reportedly couldn’t stop lying? Or the guy who is Andrew Garfield? It’s just too hard to say.

scored.body:
Apple threw a wrench into the digital ad industry, and marketers are bracing for impact

By Lara O'Reilly

You're currently following this author!

Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Author of the CMO Insider newsletter

A new software update from John Ternus' Apple has the adtech world in a fluster.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Apple has its finger on the big red button again.The adtech sector was up in arms this week about a new Apple update within iOS 27 with the potential to wreak havoc on web advertising.Apple's change blocked several major adtech firms from using advertising identifiers across browsers on its devices and, in some cases, also disrupted their ability to serve ads to Apple users on the web.First reported by AdExchanger, the blocking happened through WebKit, the technology that powers Safari and all other browsers that run on iPhones.Apple has long held an anti-tracking stance, doubling down on its principle that privacy is "a fundamental human right."What particularly irked the adtech industry was that Apple didn't just restrict cookies or identifiers this time — it blocked calls to certain adtech domains altogether, in some cases preventing ads from being served at all on the affected browsers unless companies figured out a workaround.Apple on Monday told The Trade Desk it had made changes in a new iOS beta release. Those changes appear to have untangled The Trade Desk's ad-serving domain from being blocked alongside its advertising identifier, Unified ID 2.0.That update is only available in beta for now, said Dustin Cha, co-CEO of the adtech company Ad-Shield. That means The Trade Desk's ad-serving domain will remain blocked in practice until iOS 27.2 ships."Which would likely put it in the second half of Q4 — in time for the holiday season," Cha said.

Apple also hasn't fixed the broader industry gripe: Identifiers are still on the naughty list, and Apple has shown it's prepared to add companies to that list without prior warning.The companies that are feeling the hitThe companies set to feel the most pain from the update are those whose businesses rely heavily on alternative identifiers and other post-cookie technologies. The blocked domains included those operated by The Trade Desk, ID5, LiveRamp, Permutive, and Audigent.The broader impact is on advertisers' ability to identify and reach people across the open web. By blocking the identifiers that many adtech companies use to recognize users across websites, Apple effectively shrinks the pool of people advertisers can target.That's bad news for publishers, too. If advertisers can identify fewer of their visitors, their ad inventory can become less valuable. That potentially pushes more marketing dollars away from the open web and toward platforms with vast stores of first-party user data. (It just so happens that Apple has a growing ad business, too.)For CMOs, that means potentially less reach, higher prices to reach the audiences they can still identify, and poorer campaign performance on the web. It can also make it harder to control how often people see an ad and determine whether those ads actually worked.It's the latest example of how seemingly minor backend changes from Apple can cause tremors across the advertising landscape.Apple's 2017 Intelligent Tracking Prevention feature, limiting adtech firms' ability to track users across the web with cookies, set off a cat-and-mouse game. The industry responded in part by developing alternative identifiers designed to recognize users without cookies. Apple's latest move strikes directly at those workarounds.Apple's privacy crackdown has also extended to apps. In 2022, Meta said Apple's App Tracking Transparency change could hit its ad business, causing $10 billion in lost revenue.Adtech pros say what's particularly concerning about this new move is the uncharacteristic opacity around which companies Apple is blocking, why they've been selected, and how quickly that can change."It's getting more and more aggressive," Mathieu Roche, CEO of ID5, told me.AdExchanger reported on Friday that Apple has created a broader list that can dynamically block potentially hundreds of adtech, martech, and data companies. The way the list is constructed means it can be updated remotely without Apple releasing another version of iOS, the outlet reported. Affected companies may not even know they've been blocked until something stops working.Tony Katsur, CEO of the IAB's Tech Lab, said that it should be up to governments to police the internet, rather than individual corporations."When governments pass laws and regulations in the interest of consumer privacy, it applies them to all, and it's consistent across everyone," Katsur said. "When a corporation like Apple pushes something like this out, it's uneven."

Read next

Lara O'Reilly

Lara O'Reilly is the anchor of the CMO Insider newsletter.She is a chief correspondent who has covered the digital advertising, marketing, and media industries since 2010. scored.body:
POLITICS

New Mexico Democrats accuse Senate Republicans of violating AI campaign law

The Roundhouse in Santa Fe on Feb. 3.

Eddie Moore/Journal

The New Mexico Democratic Party has asked the State Ethics Commission to investigate whether state Senate Republicans’ use of artificial intelligence-generated images in recent social media posts violates a 2024 state law aimed at curbing political misinformation.The Senate Republicans and state Sen. Jay Block, R-Rio Rancho, have published or shared artificially generated images of Democrats in recent weeks as part of a campaign accusing the majority Democrats of being corrupt.Some of the images include a fake jail mugshot of Senate Pro Tem Sen. Mimi Stewart, D-Albuquerque, House Speaker Javier Martinez, D-Albuquerque, wearing a hammer-and-sickle lapel pin and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland embracing an unspecified man in an orange prison jumpsuit.The fake mugshot suggests Stewart was charged with “hit and run,” a reference to an automobile crash between Stewart and a pedestrian in 2024 that has recently surfaced in news reports. Stewart was never issued a citation or booked into jail, and she stayed on scene until police arrived, interim Santa Fe Police Department Chief told the Santa Fe New Mexican. In a complaint to the ethics commission the Democrats provided Friday, DPNM Chair Sara Attleson said the images violate House Bill 182, which imposes strict disclaimer requirements on AI-generated campaign materials. The law requires artificially generated images to carry conspicuous disclaimers with the following text: “This image has been manipulated or generated by artificial intelligence.”In a statement, Attleson called on the Ethics Commission to investigate and impose any penalties as quickly as possible. State law provides for $1,000 fines for each violation. “Voters should not be misled by public officials or their official offices about what is or isn’t real,” Attleson said. “We are asking the Ethics Commission to enforce the law that is meant to protect faith in our elections.”None of the images on social media carried the required disclaimer, though Facebook has since labeled both as AI generated. Block, who originally posted the fake mugshot of Stewart, also noted that his image was AI-generated at the end of a lengthy Facebook post Sept. 22. Block told Source NM on Monday that the SEC complaint is Democrats’ effort to distract from the real corruption the images seek to highlight.  He also defended his post as protected speech under the First Amendment. “I can’t believe they’re crying over that when they refuse to hold themselves accountable,” Block said of Democrats. “It’s called free speech.”

Late Friday, after New Mexico Democrats announced they’d filed the ethics complaint, Senate Republicans republished their post with the contested images along with the required disclaimer. Still, Sen. Minority Leader Bill Sharer, R-Farmington, in a statement, called the matter “funny.”“The Democrat Party, that consistently fails to hold their own members to account when it comes to breaking the law and violating ethical standards, is taking exception to our efforts to expose their failed leadership and lack of accountability,” he said.”

articles.body: Fake ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude Ad Portals Capture Credentials and MFA Codes    The Hacker News

scored.body:
Image Credit: Shutterstock

(Image credit: wk1003mike / Shutterstock)

Fake AI marketing tools impersonate ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and others to steal business accountsAttackers use realistic browser-in-the-browser phishing and live operators to capture credentialsStolen advertising accounts provide access to payment methods, budgets, and linked client accountsCybercriminals are offering fake AI-powered products for advertisers and marketing managers, in an attempt to steal their Google business accounts.Most of today’s biggest AI names, including Chat-GPT, Google Gemini, Claude, Manus, and Muse, are being abused in this campaign, and people are still falling for it.Security researchers Island have published a new report detailing how the campaign works. Apparently, the operators left the source code for earlier versions of their work open on a misconfigured public GitHub repository, giving the researchers unique insight into the operation and its success.What researchers found was an advanced phishing platform that was used to target advertisers and marketing managers. It was used to create websites offering fake marketing-related products powered by Artificial Intelligence.“Every brand gets its own pitch. ChatGPT promises a Monday Google Ads brief. Gemini promises MCC (manager account) and linked-client support. Claude gets its own advertising portal, Perplexity offers campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus offers a private Meta integration,” the researchers explained.All about connectingEach site asked the victim to do the same thing - connect their Google account. After pressing “connect”, the platform launches a typical browser-in-the-browser (BitB) attack - it displays an entire browser, address bar and all, within the actual browser.Therefore, victims not paying attention to the details might see a legitimate domain in their address bar, for example accounts.google.com. However, if they were to lift their gaze just a few inches higher, they would see the actual domain, which has nothing to do with Google, or OpenAI, or any other legitimate business.Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!The phishing kit is advanced, too. The fake browser adapts to whatever the visitor runs, so it won’t happen that a victim running macOS suddenly sees a Windows, well, window. Newer builds also come with nifty little details, like Safari’s URL pill, Chrome’s custom tabs, and even a dark mode.As the victim tries to log in, a “human operator” (the scammer) on the other end follows them through the process. They see each submission, and decide what the victim sees next. They can fake a mistyped password error, or they can choose which MFA screen they see. The device gets fingerprinted, from IP and location, all the way down to screen size and WebGL.The platform supports Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows, it was said.Targeting advertisersAt the end of the day, it’s all about money. Island says the crooks are deliberately going for business accounts because these are connected to credit cards, which they can later abuse.“The lures are written for agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators, because an advertising account is a spending account. It carries a stored payment method and an approved budget, and a manager account can reach several client accounts, each with its own billing profile and linked users.”This is hardly new. Both Google and Facebook have their own advertising networks, displaying ads to billions of people every day. However, getting accounts, payment methods, and ads approved, is a stringent, painstaking process, which is why it’s a lot easier for crooks to simply use someone else’s account, especially if that someone already walked through Google’s fire barefoot.Unfortunately, Island could not disrupt the operation or tear it down. At the moment of writing, the campaign was still ongoing, and the researchers saw “hundreds of victim submissions to the platform”.The researchers are urging organizations to treat fictional AI integrations as account-access requests, inspect the outermost origin, correlate the client pattern, and hunt for the control vocabulary. Finally, they should use phishing-resistant authentication, and review advertising control changes.“Origin-bound passkeys and hardware-backed authentication remove the reusable password and one-time-code material this platform is built to collect,” they said. “After exposure, check every client account the identity could reach for new managers or partners, changed recovery details, and campaigns or spend nobody approved.”Via The Hacker News

Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.

Sead is a seasoned freelance journalist based in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He writes about IT (cloud, IoT, 5G, VPN) and cybersecurity (ransomware, data breaches, laws and regulations). In his career, spanning more than a decade, he’s written for numerous media outlets, including Al Jazeera Balkans. He’s also held several modules on content writing for Represent Communications.

members.title: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 on AWS - Amazon Web Services (AWS)

representative.headline: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 on AWS - Amazon Web Services (AWS)
representative.body: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 on AWS    Amazon Web Services (AWS)

articles.headline: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 on AWS - Amazon Web Services (AWS)
articles.body: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 on AWS    Amazon Web Services (AWS)

scored.body:
Today, we’re excited to announce the availability of Claude Haiku 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. According to Anthropic, Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest and most efficient model in the Claude 5.5 family, built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. It also costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks.

Amazon Bedrock gives you Haiku 5.5 capabilities while keeping your data within AWS infrastructure with Regional data residency. It works with the AWS controls your team already uses, including AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) for access, AWS CloudTrail for audit, Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Usage appears on your AWS bill.

Claude Platform on AWS gives you direct access to Anthropic’s native platform experience and capabilities through the AWS Management Console. Build, test, and deploy with the same APIs, features, and console experience you’d get working with Anthropic directly, unified with AWS billing and authentication.

This post covers Claude Haiku 5.5’s improvements, practical guidance on when to choose Haiku 5.5, and how to get started on Amazon Bedrock.

What makes Claude Haiku 5.5 different

Claude Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic’s most capable Haiku model, across coding, tool use, computer use, and agentic tasks. It’s also the first Haiku model with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task instead of picking one setting for an entire workload.

The improvements stand out on quick and repeatable work at scale. For coding tasks, it acts as a subagent routing requests, reviewing code and classifying long documents. For knowledge work, Haiku 5.5 pulls key information from small-to-medium documents, does initial scans, and answers quick questions over a knowledge base. For interactive applications, it responds fast enough for simple conversations to have quick and helpful answers. It also handles traditional natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as classification, summarization, and text generation at the volume and cost that production features require.

Haiku 5.5 handles agentic coding and multi-step tool use, and supports high-resolution images. Haiku 5.5 can be used as a strong computer use subagent for repetitive browser and desktop tasks, at a cost that holds up at scale. In development workflows, it’s a good fit for iterating quickly on UI and UX changes and for small, specific code base changes across multiple files.

Pairing Claude Haiku 5.5 with Opus 5.5

Haiku 5.5 pairs with the recently announced Claude Opus 5.5. Together, they make a strong team: Opus 5.5 plans and makes the judgment calls, and Haiku 5.5 carries out well-defined tasks quickly and at scale. You get careful reasoning where it counts and lower cost and latency everywhere.

Claude Opus 5.5 plans the work and makes the judgment calls. It breaks down complex problems, decides the approach, and takes on the hardest reasoning, such as release debugging, security review of large pull requests, and long analyses that end in a finished report.

Claude Haiku 5.5 takes on the fast layer of subagents. It handles quick, high-volume tasks, such as routing requests, classifying and summarizing, rewriting long documents, and applying small, specific changes across many files. As a review subagent, it can quickly check the order of operations and high-level direction, so Opus 5.5 can spend its tokens on the hardest reasoning. Because it is fast and cost efficient, you can run many Haiku subagents in parallel.

Getting started with Claude Haiku 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock

To try Haiku 5.5, open the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Test, then Playground, and select Haiku 5.5 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it.

Figure 1: Selecting an Anthropic Claude model in the Amazon Bedrock console Playground

Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime through the Anthropic SDK. You can also use the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK.

Prerequisites

You must have the following prerequisites:

Active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.

AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured.

Python 3.10+.

Boto3 installed: pip install boto3.

Anthropic SDK installed: pip install anthropic.

The Amazon Bedrock Token Generator for Amazon Bedrock authentication installed: pip install aws_bedrock_token_generator.

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.

Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with the InvokeModel API:

import boto3

import json

# Create a Bedrock Runtime client

bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(

service_name="bedrock-runtime",

region_name="us-east-1"

)

# Invoke Claude Haiku 5.5

response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(

modelId="global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5",

contentType="application/json",

accept="application/json",

body=json.dumps({

"anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",

"max_tokens": 4096,

"messages": [

{

"role": "user",

"content": "Can you explain the features of Amazon Bedrock?"

}

]

})

)

result = json.loads(response["body"].read())

# Haiku 5.5 may return a thinking block before the text block,

# so select the text block rather than a fixed index.

print(next(b["text"] for b in result["content"] if b["type"] == "text"))

You can also use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API for a unified multi-model experience:

import boto3

# Create a Bedrock Runtime client

bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(

service_name="bedrock-runtime",

region_name="us-east-1"

)

# Invoke Claude Haiku 5.5

response = bedrock_runtime.converse(

modelId="global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5",

messages=[

{

"role": "user",

"content": [

{

"text": "Can you explain the features of Amazon Bedrock?"

}

]

}

],

inferenceConfig={

"maxTokens": 4096

}

)

if 'output' in response:

blocks = response['output']['message']['content']

print('\n'.join(b.get('text', '') for b in blocks if 'text' in b))

You can also use the Anthropic Messages API through the anthropic SDK package for a streamlined experience:

from anthropic import Anthropic

from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token

token = provide_token(region="us-east-1")

client = Anthropic(

base_url="https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anthropic",

api_key=token,

)

# Invoke Claude Haiku 5.5

response = client.messages.create(

model="global.anthropic.claude-haiku-5-5",

max_tokens=1024,

messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Can you explain the features of Amazon Bedrock?"}],

)

print(response)

You can explore the Getting Started notebook for more examples. You can monitor usage, performance, and costs through Amazon CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer to scale your applications as demand grows.

Availability

Claude Haiku 5.5 is available today on Amazon Bedrock through the US Geo CRIS (us.), EU Geo CRIS (eu.), AU Geo CRIS (au.), JP Geo CRIS (jp.) and Global CRIS (global.) inference profiles on bedrock-runtime. In AWS GovCloud (US), it’s available on both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints.

See the Amazon Bedrock documentation for the full list of supported AWS Regions. For pricing information, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. It’s also available through Claude Platform on AWS in North America

Give Claude Haiku 5.5 a try on the Amazon Bedrock console, in Claude Platform on AWS, or explore the Getting Started notebooks on GitHub.

By

Henry Chandonnet

You're currently following this author!

Claude Code creator Boris Cherny gave three tips for prompting AI.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

The days of the "prompt engineer" seem to be fading away.Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code for Anthropic, said that there's no need for long, formulaic AI prompts anymore. As models have gotten better, the need to perfect your prompt has diminished, he wrote in a Tuesday X post."Talk to Claude the way you would a coworker," Cherny wrote. "There's no secret to prompting. There's no need to be overly scaffolded or prescriptive for most tasks."Not long ago, AI users were passing around their favorite added clauses and sentences to get an AI chatbot to do their bidding. Anthropic's Claude was memed with a common prompting line: "Make no mistakes."Now, Cherny said that users should prompt the model with three basic things:What you want it to doHow much effort you want it to spendHow it should verify that it did the right thingCherny also shared one of his prompts. It was casual, calling a podcast episode "really amazing" and asking Claude to build an artifact based on it. Claude should "use lots of tokens" and make the visuals better than a New Yorker or New York Times data visualization, he wrote.One line of his prompt was controversial: "Maybe add watercolor." An X user responded that Cherny should be definitive; either he wants the watercolor, or he doesn't.Cherny responded that Opus 5.5, Anthropic's latest model, has good taste. "I trust it to cook," he wrote.

He also shared the artifact it created. Indeed, Claude made several watercolor-like graphics in beiges and oranges.

scored.body:
Google is pulling back some Gemini app features for free users.The company announced the change to its AI software suite in a support notice, spotted by 9to5google. Starting on Oct. 9, anyone using the Gemini app without a paid subscription will be limited to just the 3.5 Flash-Lite model, with access to the 3.6 Flash or 3.1 Pro models turned off. Additionally, those who pay $4.99/month for Google AI Plus will lose access to the Pro model, as well, but retain access to Flash-Lite and Flash.

That means if you want to maintain the same experience you've been having with a free account up until now, you'll have to pay at least $19.99/mo for a Google AI Pro subscription. Those who already pay for AI Pro, as a nice little bonus, will get access to the "Deep Think" option that was previously exclusive to even higher tiers of the service.

Mashable Light Speed

You May Also Like

This is not terribly surprising given how subscription-based services usually work on a long enough timeline. Features that were available to all users gradually become available to only some.Google has faced some AI challenges this year. Long-time Google DeepMind leader Demis Hassabis has transitioned into a new role, and it's unclear if the move was a promotion or a demotion. The company has also repeatedly failed to deliver on the promised Gemini 3.5 Pro model, originally set to be launched in June. Bloomberg also reported recently on employee frustrations that Gemini 4 lags far behind rival models from Anthropic and OpenAI, the latest in a series of rumors about behind-the-scenes tensions in Google-land.

scored.body:
If you buy something from a link in this article, we may earn a commission. Learn more

If your pool is still open while leaves are coming down, the cleanup rarely stays in one place. Some debris floats, some collects against the waterline, and some ends up on the floor. Beatbot’s Sora 70 covers all three, and the Navy Blue model is listed at $999 on Amazon, $500 below its displayed $1,499 reference price.

The useful part of this deal is the combination of surface skimming and underwater cleaning in one rechargeable robot. Before spending this much, though, look at the leaves in your pool, the size of its shallow ledges, and how much basket cleaning you’re willing to do.

Deal price: $999Displayed reference price: $1,499Savings: $500Seller and shipper: Beatbot TechWhere to buy: Check out the Sora 70 on Amazon

Beatbot Sora 70 in Navy Blue. Official product image: Beatbot.

Beatbot Sora 70, Navy Blue

Start with the leaves you’re trying to catch

JetPulse uses water jets to direct floating debris toward the intake. That gives the Sora 70 a job a floor-and-wall cleaner leaves for your skimmer net: collecting material before it settles.

There’s useful context in The Gadgeteer’s Sora 70 and iSkim review. Vincent Nguyen found that the Sora 70 drew thick oak leaves inward, while lighter petals and thin synthetic leaves could get pushed aside and sink. Leaves tucked into corners also needed attention after an all-zone run.

For a yard with substantial leaf fall, those observations matter more than a promise of complete coverage. Expect help with the repeated work, and keep a net available for the corners or debris the robot misses. This offer includes one Sora 70; the separate solar-powered iSkim isn’t part of the package.

Measure the shallow shelf before you buy

The Sora 70 also cleans floors, walls, the waterline and suitable shallow platforms. Beatbot specifies an 8-inch minimum water depth for platform cleaning, plus a platform measuring at least 3.3 by 3.3 feet. A broad tanning shelf may qualify; a narrow step shouldn’t be assumed to.

The manufacturer’s maximum pool coverage is 3,229 square feet. Those limits make measuring your pool a useful first step, especially if the shallow end is where debris repeatedly collects. A robot that reaches the main floor can still leave you brushing smaller ledges by hand.

Beatbot illustrates the Sora 70 cleaning a shallow platform. Lavender Purple shown; the linked deal is Navy Blue. Image: Beatbot.

A bigger basket still needs emptying

The standard basket holds 6 liters and uses 150-micron filtration. Beatbot offers a separate 3-micron ultra-fine filter for smaller particles. If your main frustration is fine material rather than leaves, check that accessory instead of assuming the included basket provides the same filtration.

Fall cleanup also means checking what the robot brought back. Beatbot’s retrieval and care guidance recommends emptying the basket, rinsing the robot with fresh water and storing it out of direct sunlight after a run. The company warns that a partly blocked filter reduces suction. Basket capacity buys room for debris; it doesn’t remove the cleanup afterward.

Match the cleaning mode to today’s mess

Beatbot rates the Sora 70 for up to seven hours of surface cleaning, five hours on the floor, or 4.5 hours of full underwater cleaning. Those are separate mode ratings, not hours to add together. A surface-only pass makes sense when floating leaves are the problem; a broader cycle handles debris that’s already spread through the pool.

Surface parking helps bring the cleaner back to the edge, but the robot itself weighs 22.9 pounds. Allow for lifting and carrying it as part of the routine. App steering and one-tap docking work when it’s on the surface, so don’t expect to drive it remotely across the pool floor.

Beatbot Sora 70, Navy BluePrice: $999, saving $500 against the displayed $1,499 referenceWhere to buy: Check out the Sora 70 on Amazon

At $999, the Sora 70 is worth considering for an open pool that regularly needs both surface and underwater cleanup. If you’re closing the pool now, weigh the return window against how long it will sit unused. And this isn’t a new record-low claim: our June review already showed a $999 Sora 70 offer.

New observations from the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea in Hawai‘i reveal the most detailed view yet of Pa 30, a supernova remnant about 7,500 light-years away. Its distinctive streaks of gas look like sparks shooting outward. But zoom in, and those seemingly smooth trails turn out to be chains of knots, resembling pearls on a string. And these are some very big pearls."The planetary region of our solar system could fit in each knot about 10 times with room to spare," astrophysicist Ilaria Caiazzo, an assistant professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria, said in a statement. "The knots are quite strikingly uniform. We are excited to try to model them."The findings, from a team co-led by Caiazzo and astrophysicist Tim Cunningham, are published in The Astrophysical Journal.

You May Also Like

An explosion with a medieval paper trailResearchers consider Pa 30 the likely remains of SN 1181, a supernova recorded by observers in Chinese, Japanese, and Arabic historical sources in 1181. It remained visible in the constellation Cassiopeia for 185 days.But connecting those accounts to something astronomers could study today took centuries. Amateur astronomer Dana Patchick discovered Pa 30 in 2013 while examining data from NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer as part of a citizen science effort. The object turned out to have an especially unusual resident: a surviving stellar remnant at its center, nicknamed a "zombie star."

Mashable Light Speed

Pa 30 is considered the only known remnant of a Type Iax supernova in the Milky Way. These are relatively low-energy, incomplete stellar explosions that can leave a surviving star behind. A standard Type Ia supernova, by comparison, destroys the exploding white dwarf.

The Gemini North telescope’s laser guide star beams up into the atmosphere. The laser guide star is used to measure turbulence in the Earth’s atmosphere so the telescope can correct for it and achieve clear images of the night sky.

Credit: International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab

What the new image revealsThe Gemini observations reveal roughly 10 times as many filamentary features as earlier images showed. They also expose the chains of gas knots that make up those filaments, giving researchers new clues about how the debris took shape.

According to NOIRLab, differences in temperature or density in the material surrounding the star may have helped shape the expanding ejecta. Exactly how those remarkably uniform knots formed remains a question for researchers to investigate.The team also found that the surviving star sits almost exactly at the remnant’s center. An uneven explosion can give a surviving star a "kick," sending it away from the center. Pa 30’s configuration indicates that its star received no large sideways kick, offering another clue about the blast. Researchers hope to use Pa 30’s distinctive features to help find similar remnants in our galaxy and nearby ones. For now, this medieval light show is still giving astronomers something new to look at.

members.title: Will Claude’s new AI “watermark” keep us all honest? - Miami’s Community News

representative.headline: Will Claude’s new AI “watermark” keep us all honest? - Miami’s Community News

articles.headline: Will Claude’s new AI “watermark” keep us all honest? - Miami’s Community News
articles.body: Will Claude’s new AI “watermark” keep us all honest?    Miami’s Community News

scored.body:
It depends. If Claude makes changes to word choice, then it’s possible. But if only light proofreading is needed, it’s unlikely the watermark will make its way into the text.Commercial AI detectors do something completely different. They are trained to detect differences in AI writing and human writing.The watermark is not about a style of writing. Only word choice.I think nobody will. It’s a matter of math.To show you where I’m coming from, I think it’s important to pause here and look at how large language models like Claude work. Then, we can see why the watermark is so hard for people to find.

How large language models write

AI models don’t “think.” They predict.

Here’s an example. If you take out your iPhone, open your messaging app and type this:

Tomorrow I will go to the _______

You’ll notice that before you’ve finished the sentence, your phone suggests three words, such as:

gym      I    store     I     hospital

The app makes predictions based on its training data. Right now, it predicts that one of these three options is highly probable to go next.

AI works the same way. It’s predicting what will likely go next. Yet unlike your messaging app, it has to decide on its own.

To do this, it lays out all words that could reasonably go next based on its training data. Each word has a probability attached to it, based on how well the AI predicts the options will fit. Then, the AI chooses a word at random based on these probabilities.

It’s a little bit like when, in school, you were asked, “If there are 3 red marbles, 4 blue marbles and 5 green marbles in a bag, what’s the probability of pulling a blue marble out without looking?”

Here’s an example of how the word decision happens. Let’s say you asked an AI model for a one-sentence story about fishing, and the model gave you this sentence:

The old man’s rod bent  sharply as the bass fought against the line.

The model ultimately chose “sharply” here as the word. Not because it was the only word that worked here. Instead, it was randomly selected out of a “bag of marbles” — a pool of words that were all highly probable options.

The choices might have looked like this:

How the watermark works

Claude’s watermark works by reducing randomness in word choice. The model takes advantage of its ability to say one idea in 1,000 ways to insert intricate word choice patterns.

To see this in action, let’s pretend we asked Claude to tell us what the greatest food in the world is. It responds:

Pizza is one of the most  satisfying foods there is — crispy crust, gooey cheese, and endless topping combos.

Claude could have easily sewn its watermark into at least one word choice here. Let’s say it was the word “satisfying.”

There are multiple words that could replace “satisfying” here without changing the essence of the sentence. Before the watermark was deployed, Claude would have chosen from these options at random based on each word’s likeliness to fit here, like in our previous example. Here’s what the choice might have looked like:

Words that could go next

Probability the word goes next

Delicious

21%

Fulfilling

19%

Satisfying

17%

Gratifying

14%

Wonderful

12%

Delightful

7%

Comforting

7%

Amazing

3%

But now with the watermark, this word choice decision has changed.

Claude won’t randomly select an option, while respecting each word’s likeliness of going next.

There is no blindly reaching into the “bag of marbles.”

Instead, Claude will be biased. And biased in a way that people will never notice. It’s going to take advantage of its ability to communicate one idea in 1,000 different ways, all without telling us its method.

Essentially, Claude is implementing its watermark by “dyeing” some word choices blue and others red. The blue words will appear more, and the red words will appear less. A high ratio of blue words to red words indicates the watermark.

To see an example of how this might work in action, let’s pretend we can pop open the hood on Anthropic’s watermark and look at how it affects our pizza sentence.

Instead of the old choice, we might see Claude faced with a choice like this:

Words that could go next

Old probability that the word goes next

New probability that the word goes next

Change in how often the word appears

Delicious

21%

8%

-61.9%

Fulfilling

19%

7%

-63.2%

Satisfying

17%

+58.8%

Gratifying

14%

+64.3%

Wonderful

12%

5%

-58.3%

Delightful

7%

13%

+85.7%

Comforting

7%

+71.4%

Amazing
