5%

+66.7%

Now, Claude is biased heavily towards choosing blue words in this context.

A high proportion of blue words to red words in an extended sample makes it clear to Anthropic’s scanner: Claude wrote this text.

Like drawing blackjack 50% of the time at the casino, it’s extremely unlikely for a human to “draw” blue words at such a high rate. There are just too many other card combinations – or in this case, word choices – that a human writer would naturally choose from instead.

Meanwhile, what’s “blue” and what’s “red” stays hidden from us, and won’t be detectable.

The watermark isn’t as simple as Claude pushing a word like “satisfying” all the time. The words that are dyed blue and red are probably changing across contexts, in line with some extremely complicated formula that we need Anthropic’s scanner to decode. For us, it’s untraceable, because all the words look normal; but for the scanner, the watermark looks very visible, because it can see blue and red.

Here’s an example.

Let’s say that you asked Claude to write a novel, and it began writing this:

The sky turned a brilliant shade of amber as the sun sank below the horizon, casting long shadows across the field while a cool breeze swept through the grass.

Here, there are multiple opportunities to weave in the watermark. For example:

The sky turned a brilliant shade of amber as the sun sank below the horizon, casting long shadows across the field while a cool breeze swept through the grass.

Here, 80% of dyed words are blue. Notice that each blue word doesn’t seem out of place; however, they all  have at least one close, common replacement that a human might have used instead.

With so many synonyms available, the chance of a human choosing all these blue words at such a high rate is unlikely.

It’s an early indicator that Claude may have written this. A larger sample would be needed to confirm.

This shows why Claude’s watermark is so hard to remove.

We don’t know which words to look for.

Final takeaway: Do you think watermarking is a good idea?

It’s an excellent idea.

Now, companies will be a bit nervous knowing Claude’s watermark is out there. They’ll have to disclose when they use Claude to make hiring decisions. They can’t just say, “Oh, our HR team made the decision,” and hide the fact that they used the model. If there’s Claude-generated text in the process, they’ll have to disclose that AI was involved. And that’s actually good for applicants, if you think about it.

This is also going to be great for rooting out forged documents and evidence. If the U.S. Department of Justice had this scanner, for example, they could inspect any piece of evidence and say when something is Claude-generated, which would be very helpful to us.

Right now, we don’t know what’s real and what’s not. Now, at least for Claude, we can finally tell.

articles.body: Teenager Rescued After Using Claude AI to Plot Route on B.C.’s ‘Widowmaker Arete’    The Inertia

scored.body:
Senior Editor

Staff

The teen was rescued from the base of Widowmaker Arete after Claude AI sent him off course. Photos: North Shore Rescue

Search and rescue teams in British Columbia rescued a teenager after artificial intelligence sent him on a wayward path.

According to reports, the 16-year-old took a gondola up North Vancouver’s Grouse Mountain at 8 a.m. on October 4. At the top, the teenager asked Claude AI to map him a route to Crown Mountain, another peak just north of Grouse. It’s rugged terrain, marked by soaring cliffs and stunning views, but to those unfamiliar with the area, it can be a dangerous place. Claude AI sent the boy down Crown Pass, up the Crater Slabs zone, and through Crown Couloir before sending him way off course. When he realized he was lost, he wound up calling for help at the base of a relatively famous 10-pitch climbing route called Widowmaker Arete.

“A fall would have resulted in significant injury or potentially death,” Search Manager Paul Markey told CTV News.

Once the teams had the boy’s location, they had to lower two rescuers down to an area above him. The teen was too close to the cliff face’s wall for the helicopter to get close enough, so once the crew members were on the ground above the teen, they began to secure themselves to haul him out.

“When on the ground, the crew established an anchor, and one member was belayed to the subject,” NSR staff wrote in the task debrief. “There, the member established additional protection and was able to move the subject to a suitable extraction point.”

By 6:30 p.m., the teen was safely aboard the helicopter and on his way home. Markey didn’t mince words about a rescue situation involving AI

“Claude has never been in that specific area, has never been on that route, and has never been in the outdoors,” he said. “Do your own research and gain your own knowledge of the area and supplement it with training and navigation.”

While the victim was experienced at climbing in indoor climbing gyms and was apparently well-prepared for the trip, Markey noted that solo trips like this one are not generally a great idea if it’s your first kick at the can.

“Certainly not something you should be doing any time on your own,” Markey said. “He’s a good kid and definitely an adventurous sort. He was very scared and thankful.”

articles.headline: I made 7 Gemini Skills to handle my most repetitive prompts — #4 is my personal favorite - Tom's Guide
articles.body: I made 7 Gemini Skills to handle my most repetitive prompts — #4 is my personal favorite    Tom's Guide

scored.body:
(Image credit: Shutterstock)

I write a lot of prompts. And despite spending most of my working day testing AI, I've realized that I spend way too much time rewriting the same prompt in dozens of different ways. From researching topics and finding sources to simplifying tech jargon and summarizing model notes, I knew I needed a better system. That's why Gemini's Skills caught my attention. Skills let you give Gemini a set of reusable instructions for a particular task.Once you've created one, you can call it from a regular Gemini conversation using a slash command instead of explaining what you want every single time.Now instead of repeatedly explaining how I want Gemini to research something, I can call /research. Instead of reminding it that I want criticism rather than compliments, I can use /critic.Here's what I made.First, what are Gemini Skills?

(Image credit: Shutterstock)If you've used Gemini Gems before, the idea will sound familiar. A Skill is very similar because it's a reusable set of instructions that tells Gemini how you want a particular kind of task handled. The big difference for what I'm doing here is that I can invoke a Skill from a Gemini conversation by typing / followed by its name.Creating a Skill doesn't start with the slash command itself. I first tell Gemini what I want it to create, with a prompt. From there, Gemini then creates and saves the Skill. You can also build one manually from Gemini's Skills settings, where you give it a name, description and instructions. Once it's saved and enabled, that's when the shortcut comes in.Once you do the /command in a regular Gemini conversation, you won't have to repeat those instructions again. Gemini can also recognize when one of my enabled Skills is relevant and use it automatically, so I don't necessarily have to call it by name every time.Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!1. /research

(Image credit: Shutterstock)Research is one of those tasks where I almost never want an AI to simply answer the first version of my question. I don't want the answer watered down because I want to investigate first. I need reliable sources and facts checked.So /research is a great first Skill to make.Skill prompt: You are my research assistant. Investigate the topic I give you before answering. Prioritize primary sources, official documentation and authoritative reporting over summaries or aggregators. Cross-check important claims against multiple reliable sources when possible. Separate confirmed facts from claims, speculation or opinion, and clearly flag anything you can't independently verify. Focus on the most important and useful findings rather than giving me a generic overview. Include links to the sources you used so I can check the information myself.2. /explain

(Image credit: Shutterstock/jud-mackrill)AI is fantastic at explaining complicated things. At the same time, It's also pretty fantastic at replacing one piece of jargon with six new pieces of jargon.My /explain Skill is designed to stop that.Skill prompt: Explain the topic I give you in clear, everyday language. Assume I'm intelligent but unfamiliar with the subject and don't assume I already know the terminology. Avoid jargon when a simpler explanation will work, and define any technical terms you need to use. Start with the simplest explanation of what it is and why it matters, then add more detail if it's helpful. Use a real-world analogy or example when it genuinely makes the concept easier to understand. Don't make the explanation more complicated than the thing I'm trying to learn.3. /compare

Ask an AI to compare two products and there's a decent chance you'll get a giant table containing every difference it can think of. I rarely need that.What I want to know is which differences are actually going to affect my decision.Skill prompt: Compare the two products, services or options I give you based on the differences that will actually matter in everyday use. Don't overwhelm me with every specification or minor distinction you can find. Focus on meaningful differences in things like price, features, performance, ease of use and limitations, depending on what I'm comparing. Explain where each option has an advantage and any important trade-offs. Finish by telling me which option makes the most sense for different types of users or situations rather than declaring one universal winner.4. /critic

(Image credit: Future/Edited with Gemini)I don't want AI to be so nice to me, so this Skill might be my favorite. AI chatbots have an annoying tendency to be agreeable. Give one an idea and ask what it thinks, and you can end up with an enthusiastic explanation of why your mediocre idea is actually brilliant. That's not always useful.Skill prompt: Critique the idea, argument or writing I give you instead of defaulting to praise or agreement. Look specifically for weak assumptions, missing information, contradictions, logical gaps and anything that doesn't hold up under scrutiny. Tell me what isn't working and why, and give me the strongest argument against my position when relevant. Don't invent problems just to be critical, and acknowledge what works when there's a specific reason to do so. Prioritize useful, specific criticism I can actually act on rather than reassurance or generic feedback.5. /rewrite

(Image credit: Pexels / Eren Li)This is another prompt I find myself writing constantly. I'll give an AI a text or email I've written and ask it to make me sound less irritated or to rework anything that isn't as clear as it should be. Then I have to add the important part: don't change more than you need to. This one is a game changer when you're trying to get your point across without sounding too emotional.Skill prompt: Rewrite the text I give you to make it clearer, tighter and more natural while preserving my original meaning, voice and tone. Remove repetition, awkward phrasing and unnecessary words without making the writing sound generic or overly polished. Don't introduce new facts, ideas or claims that aren't in the original. Keep my personality and phrasing wherever they already work, and don't make the writing more formal unless the original is formal. Return the improved version without explaining every change you made.6. /brief

(Image credit: iFLYTEK)Sometimes I don't want research so much as I want to get up to speed. Maybe I'm about to watch a spinoff and barely remember the original show. Maybe I'm going into a meeting about something unfamiliar. Maybe everyone is suddenly talking about a company I've never heard of.Skill prompt: Brief me on the topic I give you as if I need to get up to speed quickly. Assume I have limited prior knowledge and focus on the essential context rather than giving me an exhaustive explainer. Tell me what it is, what's happening now, why it matters and the key people, companies, events or terms I'm likely to hear referenced. Include important recent developments when relevant. Prioritize what I actually need to know and keep the answer concise enough that I can understand the topic in a few minutes.7. /strategy

(Image credit: Getty Images)One of my recurring frustrations with AI is that sometimes I want it to think through something before racing ahead with a solution. That's when I just want a strategy. These instructions tell Gemini to examine my goal, identify information I'm missing, break the task into logical stages, flag potential problems and then give me the plan.Skill prompt: Act as a strategist rather than jumping straight to a solution. Examine the goal I give you and think through the best way to accomplish it before recommending what I should do. Identify any important information I'm missing, break the task into logical stages and flag potential problems, dependencies or trade-offs I should consider. Where there are multiple approaches, explain which makes the most sense and why. Finish with a clear, practical step-by-step plan I can follow.Try making your ownThese seven aren't meant to be the seven Skills everyone should create. They are pertinent to me and my work and solve something I find irritating about using AI every day: repeatedly explaining my preferences.Your list of Skills might look completely different. For example, if you're learning another language, you might make /practice. Or, if you're constantly trying to understand emails full of corporate jargon, /translatework could turn them into normal English.The point is that you'll save time when you don't have to rewrite the same prompt ever time. And you can always adjust the Skill as your workflow or needs change. Give my Skills or try writing some of your own. Let me know what you think in the comments.Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds. Subscribe to Tom's Guide on YouTube and follow us on TikTok.

articles.headline: Cisco brings collaborative agents and Claude into Webex chats - Computerworld
articles.body: Cisco brings collaborative agents and Claude into Webex chats    Computerworld

scored.body:
Cisco is adding AI agents to Webex group chats so colleagues can assign them work and share the results, part of a wider revamp of the Webex app.

Announced at the WebexOne conference Wednesday, users will soon be able to @mention agents in Webex “spaces” to help schedule meetings, take notes, and track tasks.

“You work with AI, but your teammates may never see that work — they can’t build on it, contribute to it, or reuse it,” said Amit Barave, Cisco vice president and general manager for Webex Suite and AI, in a blog post. “With Webex, agents become part of the team, participating where the work is happening.”

“This makes AI a shared capability for the team,” said Snorre Kjesbu, Cisco vice president and general manager for collaboration, in a separate blog post. “It can help people prepare together, carry decisions forward, and coordinate the next steps without losing the context of the conversation.”

As well as Webex spaces, the collaborative agents will be accessible during video and voice calls via the AI Assistant side panel, though these will only be visible to individual users, rather than teams, a Cisco spokesperson said.

Cisco’s announcement reflects the growing push from collaboration software vendors to bring AI agents directly into their applications, said Irwin Lazar, principal analyst at Metrigy. By positioning agents where employees are already collaborating, they are able to perform tasks such as managing meeting agendas, facilitating, and providing contextual information into meetings.

“We’ve seen similar efforts by Slack, with Claude Tag, and with Zoom via ZoomMate,” said Lazar. “Like the others, the strength of the agent is dependent on its access to information, so the key is enabling connectivity to external data sources such as CRM, ERP, project management, etc.”

The changes are part of a wider Webex app refresh app that includes a new personalized landing page to highlight work priorities and upcoming meetings, as well as suggest follow-up actions, such as responding to messages or reviewing meeting recaps.

“The new assistant literally knows what you are doing and your upcoming schedule and knows more than other major providers,” said Jim Lundy, CEO of Aragon Research. “In fact, I’d say that their assistant could be sold unbundled.”

Cisco

In addition, Cisco is extending the range of third-party agents accessible from Webex, too. Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents — cloud-hosted agents that process multi-step tasks in the background — can be added to group conversations as a team member to complete tasks, as well as OpenAI’s recently announced “dot” agents.

Cisco also unveiled more of its own native Webex agents. Personal Agents for Webex Calling can screen calls to help users avoid missing an important call when they’re unavailable to speak. The agents can “converse with callers to understand their needs and determine urgency, prioritize what matters most, and take action on your behalf,” Barava said. Personal Agents for Webex Calling will be available in the first quarter of 2027, alongside the new Webex app, collaborative agents, third-party agents.

A previously announced Translator agent is now in “controlled availability” ahead of a general release in November. This provides real-time translation in the Webex app, as well as Cisco 9800 Series Desk Phones, with support for ten languages: English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, Portuguese, and Spanish.

An AI Coach agent for Vidcast — Cisco’s tool for short form, asynchronous video messaging in Webex — is aimed at helping users improve communication performance. “The AI Coach watches and listens while a presenter delivers, reacts to pacing, tone, and word choice as they happen, and asks the questions a live audience would,” said Barave. The AI Coach agent is available now.

Metrigy’s Lazar said he has witnessed an uptick in business demand for agentic tools in collaboration applications generally. “They offer the potential to bring context into meetings, saving time and increasing focus. Cisco’s aim is to ensure that the Webex App can remain the place where people work, rather than other apps or AI interfaces like Claude Cowork,” he said. “I would say the only weakness in the Cisco portfolio now is ability to capture data from non-Webex meetings. They lack the capability that Zoom now has to capture audio from third-party or external meetings.”

A Cisco spokesperson said that some Webex AI capabilities are available at no extra cost in Webex Suite, which costs $25 per user each month, and Enterprise tiers. More advanced features — such as Polling and Translator agents, the Personal Agents for Calling, and collaborative agent functionality — will require a new “Enhanced AI Offer for AI” add-on. This will be available in the coming weeks, Cisco said, though pricing for the add-on was not provided.

Cisco didn’t specify if any of the AI features will require any additional, usage-based costs on top of fixed subscription fees. The company recently stated that the Translator agent provides 50 minutes of translation per user each month, with additional usage requiring an “add-on.”

scored.body:
Published Oct 7, 2026, 3:30 PM EDT

Abhijith has been writing for the Web since 2011 and has contributed to sites like Beebom and TechWiser. He is curious about making the best of tech accessible to everyone.

He started writing as a hobby after getting a computer at 16. Since then, he has found technical writing a space where he belongs and could make a difference. A curious and self-motivated person, Abhijith's writings focus on productivity, Android, and the Internet.

He holds a Master's degree in English and a PhD in Humanities. Enthusiastic about language, literature, and culture, he works as an Assistant Professor of English.

If not writing or reading, you can find Abhijith playing Chess or CODM.

Until recently, Gemini Gems were the only way to create a repetitive workflow with Google's AI assistant. However, these Gems never worked with the larger workflow within Gemini. Fortunately, Gemini is saying goodbye to Gems and introducing something else in their place: skills. If you've used Claude, you're already familiar with skills that offer efficiency and save time. Gemini's take on skills seems to follow the same approach, and the results are better than Gems ever were.

Skills work in the chat you are already having

Gems made me change rooms to ask one question

The biggest limitation with Gemini Gems is that you need to leave the current chat to access one of them. For instance, I may have a fact-checking Gem that I've built to verify claims. I can't invoke this gem in an existing chat. This is where skills differ, as they work in the chat you're currently having. Let's say that I'm in the middle of a brainstorming session and want to fact-check one of the claims. Now, instead of opening a Gem in a new tab and losing the important context, I can use the /fact-checker command to verify a claim. There's also an option to have Gemini automatically invoke the skill, which saves even more time.

I rebuilt my worst Gem as a skill from scratch

Gemini wrote half of it while I watched

To be completely clear, Gemini hasn't pulled the plug on Gems yet. They will be available until November 16, after which all your Gems will be converted into skills. However, you don't have to wait until next month to use this feature. Instead, you can use the Create Skill link on the Gems page to come up with one yourself. I love that Gemini offers three options to create a skill: Create with Gemini, Create manually, and Upload skill. Depending on your requirements, you can pick the right option. As you can guess, Create with Gemini is the easiest option as the AI assistant asks proactive questions as you build the skill. For instance, you can say something like "Create a fact-checker skill", and Gemini will ask enough follow-up questions to polish it. Once the process is done, that skill will be saved and be accessible across Gemini conversations. However, if you already have skills you use with other AI tools, you can upload SKILL.md files or entire folders.

Gemini also recommends a few skills you can create in a single click.

Stacking two skills did what no Gem could

Using two Gems at once was something you couldn't do with Gemini Gems. It has more to do with how each Gem requires a different tab and how two Gems don't interact. With skills, however, Gemini has gotten rid of that limitation, and you can invoke two or more skills in a single conversation. Depending on your workflow, this feature offers you many opportunities. For instance, let's say you have set up two pre-made skills from Google, /match-my-writing-style and /prep-for-meetings. Now, instead of running these two skills separately, you can use the following prompt and get better results:

/prep-for-meetings /match-my-writing-style Brief me on my next meeting with my editor and write the brief the way I would.

This way, Gemini will consolidate everything into a single workflow and deliver better results. Similarly, you may want to run a decision-advisor skill to get different opinions and have the match-my-writing-style skill create something in your voice. Alternatively, you may have a research assistant skill that works alongside a citation verifier skill.

Let's take another scenario where you want to create a skill to draft customer response emails. You may want to include a tone-checker skill nested within the main skill so that all your email drafts are verified for potentially dismissive phrasing. Alternatively, you can integrate an action-item extractor into a meeting note taker skill so that you get different kinds of output.

What Gems still do better right now

While most things that skills bring to the Gemini experience are great, there are times when I miss Gems. Skills don't currently have access to tools like Create video, Create music, Canvas, Deep Research, and Guided learning. Some other features I regularly use with Gems, such as Google Drive and Gemini Notebook integration, are also still on the way.

On the bright side, when these features are integrated into skills, Gemini should be more useful than it is now, and you can get more done by switching early, before an automated migration.

articles.headline: I put Claude Opus 5.5 against Gemini 3.1 Pro on 3 everyday prompts, and I'm ready to pay for one less subscription now - XDA
articles.body: I put Claude Opus 5.5 against Gemini 3.1 Pro on 3 everyday prompts, and I'm ready to pay for one less subscription now    XDA

scored.body:
Published Oct 7, 2026, 7:30 AM EDT

Abhinav pivoted from a career in banking to pursue his first love in writing. Even while working full-time, he continued contributing as an editor-at-large, a role he has held for more than 7 years. A lifelong tech enthusiast who has built three gaming and productivity powerhouse PCs since 2018, his passion for technology keeps him closely following the semiconductor industry, from NVIDIA and AMD to ARM. His MSc dissertation explored how artificial intelligence will reshape the future of work, reflecting his curiosity about the wider social impact of emerging technologies.

It's hard to imagine productivity without a little bit of AI magic these days. Most developers, designers, advertisers, and content creators swear by at least one model in their workflow, and most of the time, rarely ever see any reason to make a switch. That's because when you're a paying customer, you're subscribed to an entire AI ecosystem, and letting go of one ecosystem in favor of another is a migration hassle that no one wants to go through. But there's a problem with this approach, and it's related to how cloud providers are constantly pushing out new models with better reasoning capabilities and features that can change what an AI assistant is capable of. If you stick with the same service, there's a good chance you're missing out on what's on offer elsewhere. That's why I decided to put two of the best models from Anthropic and Google, each at the highest effort, on three everyday prompts that reflect the sort of things I'd actually ask an AI assistant to do, and there's only one model I'd rather pay for. Here's everything you need to know.

"Create a website in HTML for me"

Gemini kept it minimal, Opus made it pictorial

Creating a website is something most sole proprietors get a cloud-based LLM to do, and most tend to provide thin briefs that don't usually include a color palette, copy direction, or mention what services should sit on the page and where they should belong. Those details come much later during the fine-tuning phase, and by then, they've already made the decision whether to go with the generated site or get it professionally commissioned. To match that, I delivered the following prompt to both the models, verbatim: "Create a landing page for a small local landscaping business called Green & Co in HTML. It should look professional, modern, and trustworthy, and make it easy for potential customers to get in touch and request a quote." As is evident, "trustworthy" was one of the operative words in the brief, and it happens to be one that has an actual framework behind it. Nielsen Norman Group devised four factors in website design in 1999, including design quality, upfront disclosure, comprehensive and correct content, and a visible connection to the rest of the web. These metrics continue to hold up well in modern day, and there was no reason to pick another evaluation criteria. Claude Opus 5.5 took the win here, and it would take you no more than a single cursory glance to see which website you'd find more trustworthy amongst the two. The design is visually appealing with pictorial cues, the messaging is comprehensive, and the framework put forth is consistent with any other website you'd visit in terms of visual hierarchy. What stood out is that it excellently advises anyone on how to structure their content better for clarity and services provided. Gemini went with a flat, minimalistic design that satisfied the prompt literally, but on a zero-shot test like this, that tends to hollow out, and as a result, comprehension suffers. The website showed no iconed services grid, and no service illustration a landscaping business could actually show a client, leaving them with no visual sense of what the work looks like. It also missed the FAQ section, which is rather standard for a trade site and the usual place to pre-empt a buyer's objections.

"Create a presentation for me"

There's a quality chasm between Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro

Turning rough ideas into a slide deck is one of the most common jobs people hand to LLMs, and that's no secret. Given enough context, any cloud model from major providers could conjure an impressive set of slides, but what I wanted to find out was how well Gemini and Claude could independently infer the shape of a story with as little context as possible. Data quality, visual aid, and logical flow were my primary concerns on this test. So I delivered the following prompt: "Create a five-slide presentation explaining why rising memory prices are increasing the cost of components around the world. Make it visually digestible for a general audience." Opus 5.5, again, was the victor, and the margin of victory was the greatest in this test. Every single number mentioned in the deck traced back to a primary source, including the DRAM revenue shares, the quarterly contract-price bars, and price hikes of the products mentioned. All the information was clean and verifiable, and covered a breadth of ground a general audience would appreciate. Given the same prompt, Gemini's deck felt embarrassing. Visually, the deck looked clean, but if you look past that and go into the substance, the questionable sourcing (or the lack thereof) becomes a matter of concern that would alarm anyone using the tool for this purpose. The only citation that I could find in the presentation was for the image that was pulled from an AI image generator called easy peasy AI, and the image sources slide sat at the end in a default serif font on white that broke the deck's own design language.

"Explain this concept like I'm five"

Neither model has ever met a five-year-old

Whether you believe it or not, a surprising number of people go straight to their preferred cloud AI whenever they encounter an abstract concept, and I'm willing to bet the number has only grown since its mainstream adoption. In a 2026 HEPI survey, 95% of students in higher education reported using AI in at least one way, and anecdotally, I'd put the figure outside the classroom at not far behind. The ELI5 prompt is where models get stress-tested on the taking something technical and handing it back in plain language, so it seemed like an important assessment in evaluating the capability of a model in such a use-case. I went with the concept of PCIe bifurcation that I understand well to gauge the models' output, with no limitations on the tools they could use: "Explain PCIe bifurcation like I'm five. Use any tools you want, including interactive visuals or images."

For the first time in the series of tests, Gemini 3.1 Pro cut ahead in one aspect, and that underscored why it was important to factor in the visuals in evaluation criteria. Gemini's interactive toggle was cleaner, and its shared-highway analogy immediately made perfect sense on the first read. The labels underneath, however, were a complete miss with mislabeled slot speeds, with the slot captioned as PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 while every bandwidth figure was a 4.0 number. Those details weren't particularly relevant to an ELI5 explainer either.

Claude went in the same direction, and its road-and-houses analogy was just as digestible. Claude's generated interactive visual was less charming, but it covered a key aspect of a problem that catches most people out when it comes to PCIe bifurcation. The widget showed a cheap four-drive adapter detecting just one SSD until you change the split manually, which is exactly the kind of thing that sends people to support forums after their first purchase. What lost me a little, however, was the prose that went down the rabbit hole of BIOS menus and switch chips that, again, wouldn't make much sense to someone asking explicitly for an ELI5 explanation. While Opus 5.5 managed to illustrate the concept more accurately, the criteria I was evaluating the two models on was largely unmet on both responses, effectively making it a tie. That being said, it would also be reasonable to award Gemini a point on the visuals and Claude on the technical minutiae.

Claude kept my subscription, and it wasn't as close as I expected it to be

Across all the three tests, Claude came out ahead in two and drew third. It's worth noting that Gemini was the faster of the two, and its capabilities are clearly better reflected in visual tasks as seen in the interactive PCIe toggle. It is also worth noting that the Gemini suite exclusively offers image and video generation through Gemini Omni, which is something I wanted to see in the ELI5 explainer test, but unfortunately it doesn't seem to be something Gemini calls on its own mid-chat. If I were to pick one service over another today, it would be Anthropic's, for now.

scored.body: VEO Ophthalmics and VitaPixel are launching an exclusive commercialization partnership for Vita’s stereoscopic digital visualization system.Before we talk details, let's get a look at these companies.First up: VEO. Operating out of Ohio, the medical device developer and distributor specializes in ophthalmic surgical technologies for the treatment of lens disorders.Among these products:CUSTOMFLEX ARTIFICIALIRIS, an FDA-approved device for use as an iris prosthesis to treat iris defects in both pediatric and adult patientsVisionOne, an FDA-cleared portable perimeter device for performing visual field tests via a virtual reality (VR) headset with cloud-based analysisNote: This was the subject of a 2025 strategic partnership with VisionOne VR.And VitaPixel?Based in Pennsylvania, the medical equipment manufacturer was co-founded by a retina surgeon specializing in 3D screen-based visualization.See its full story, executive team, and medical device advisors.To note: VEO’s President and CEO Ron Gilliland is among the latter.As for its manufacturing focus—that would be the focus of our coverage: VitaPixel SVS.Check out more on the impetus for this technology.Before we talk about that system, let’s get some partnership details.There’s really not much to it (or, rather, that has been publicly disclosed).The exclusive commercialization agreement involves VEO heading up VitaPixel’s global commercialization.What this involves: VEO will handle all aspects of the system’s sales and marketing as a commercialization pattern, while VitaPixel will focus on the research and development (R&D) and manufacturing.No other details—including monetary—were shared.Gotcha. Next up: VitaPixel SVS.VitaPixel SVS is a stereoscopic digital visualization and imaging system designed to integrate with existing slit-lamp systems.How: by replacing a slit lamp’s binocular view with a stereoscopic view via organic light-emitting diode (OLED) micro-display glasses—essentially removing the need for a surgeon to position their head at the slit-lamp oculars.Tell me more.The system ensures the left and right channels are separate from the eyepieces to the glasses.And behind each eyepiece: A high-sensitivity image sensor provides a high dynamic range that holds “the brightest beam and the darkest shadow at the same time.”And how does it fit into an existing slit lamp system, exactly?Basically: The SVS’s cameras peer through an (existing) slit lamp’s eye pieces to capture the view through the optics and magnifications a surgeon already uses.The cameras can be easily flipped up to allow a surgeon back at the oculars.The recommendation: “Use the glasses for the exams that suit them and the direct optics for the ones that don’t.”See here for visuals comparing the SVS camera view to a conventional camera view.So what advantages come with this?Four key capabilities are targeted. The first two:Ergonomics: The system’s display glasses bring the exam to a surgeon, enabling a more natural and upright position at the slit lamp.See here for how this works.Digital documentation (at the slit lamp): 3D visualization plus image and video are captured from the live view via the joystick button or tapping a 2D touchscreen attached directly to the slit lamp.Surgeons can review, annotate, and export these visuals.DICOM compliance, PACS integration, local session auto-save, and USB export are also included.And the other two?Patient comfort: The system is designed around flexible positioning and lowered required illumination.What this means: Since the surgeon doesn’t need to be at the oculars, the exam can be built around the patient (and not the slit lamp). See how it works.Teaching and training: Students and residents can follow a surgeon’s live slit lamp view via two options: a second pair of display glasses or on a 3D display for the room.The intent: to support case-based learning, skills assessment, mentoring, and collaborative discussion. More details here.Impressive! So is this cleared for use in the U.S.?The system is reported to be an FDA-listed, Class II medical device.Only question left to ask: When will it be available?VEO is introducing VitaPixel SVS during the American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) annual meeting in New Orleans, Louisiana, this weekend.For surgeons interested in learning more (and receiving a demo!), stop by booth #2300.And if I’m not attending AAO?Click here to inquire about booking a demo.Looking ahead: Units are expected to be available by the end of Q4 2026.

Google launched Playground, a browser-based AI platform that lets adults in the US create their own games using nothing but text input. No coding skills needed. Users can tweak game rules, physics, characters, and environments through a back-and-forth with the AI, then test the results right away. The platform runs on Google's Gemini, Nano Banana, and Lyria models, according to Google spokesperson Nia Carter (via The Verge).

Finished games can be shared via link or published in a public gallery. Some genres will support leaderboards and multiplayer. Playground is free, though Google One subscribers get higher weekly usage limits depending on their plan. Published games go through safety reviews based on Google's community guidelines.

Alongside Playground, Google and Unity announced Unity Spark, an AI tool aimed at professional development with access to the Unity Asset Store. Unity CEO Matt Bromberg says Spark targets gamers and artists who have creative ideas but lacked the technical skills to build them. The closed beta is set to launch sometime in 2026. The announcement follows similar AI game-building tools from Meta and Roblox.

articles.body: Claude Now Runs Inside Salesforce, Slack, and Microsoft 365. Your Security Review Never Saw It Arrive.    LinkedIn

scored.body:
In one week in August 2026, Salesforce launched Slack Code, which lets anyone tag a coding agent into a conversation and ship a pull request, and then announced Claudeforce, which wires Claude directly into live Salesforce data and workflows. It was Anthropic's third native embed of the year, after Slack and Microsoft 365. Each announcement promised the agents would "inherit" the host platform's security model from day one. Not one of them passed through a procurement review, because nothing was procured.

Agents are the first attack surface that grows without an adoption decision.

AI security assumed a moment: a committee, a license, a review, a surface to instrument. The toolkit built for that moment (model scanning, prompt inspection, gateway enforcement) only works when someone in the company chose the thing being secured. Agents skip the moment. The CRM ships an agent platform. The ticketing system ships one. The meeting notetaker, the HR suite, the data warehouse all become launchpads, for vendors and employees alike, in product updates nobody reads. Every governance process an enterprise owns fires at adoption. Agents never trigger it.

Offensive AI went from impossible to $20 in four months.

While the attack surface expands at the pace of vendor release calendars, the attackers' curve is steeper. In February, frontier models could not solve a deliberately hard offensive challenge: reverse-engineer unfamiliar software, find a subtle race condition, weaponize it. By April, the best model solved it occasionally at roughly $2,000 in inference cost. By June, several solved it reliably for about $20. Offensive AI costs are falling roughly tenfold a year. The two curves cross in the third-party application layer, which is exactly where the agents live.

The board is asking three questions the policy document cannot answer.

How many agents do we have?

What can they reach?

Who is accountable if one is compromised?

Workday reports AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, with over 5,500 customers running its agents, so the pressure to adopt is not going away. Security leaders are being asked to say yes faster and to be accountable for the result, in the same meeting. A one-time inventory does not resolve that. What resolves it is a live, continuously updated answer to what is operating, what each agent inherited, what it can reach, and what changed since yesterday.

The bottom line

Agent security is not a feature of AI security. It is a different category for a different kind of problem: third-party, continuous, and growing at machine speed. First-party problems get solved at the decision point. Third-party problems have no decision point.

Nothing for AI security to instrument, because nobody in your company adopted anything. The ecosystem simply grew.

The full series runs six chapters, from why the era changed to a sequenced ninety-day plan, a four-level self-assessment, and the fifteen questions that separate vendors who built for this problem from vendors who renamed a product. None of that is in this article.

Reco is the leader in Agent Security. The Reco Platform secures agents and their operating environments where applications, identities, permissions, and workflows intersect. It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. Security leaders at Fortune 500 enterprises choose Reco to bring order to agent proliferation and the chain reactions that follow. With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat detection together in one place. members.title: I tested Google's new Gemini Windows app; it turns out Mac users got all the best features - Android Police

representative.headline: I tested Google's new Gemini Windows app; it turns out Mac users got all the best features - Android Police
representative.body: I tested Google's new Gemini Windows app; it turns out Mac users got all the best features    Android Police

articles.headline: I tested Google's new Gemini Windows app; it turns out Mac users got all the best features - Android Police
articles.body: I tested Google's new Gemini Windows app; it turns out Mac users got all the best features    Android Police

scored.body:
Published Oct 7, 2026, 9:30 AM EDT

Haroun authors features for Android Police, covering Samsung, Google, and the wider Android ecosystem. He first joined in 2021, cutting his teeth on over 300 news stories before moving on to features and how-tos. A one-time OnePlus die-hard who genuinely couldn't stand Samsung, he's since done a full about-face — he now daily-drives a Galaxy S24 Ultra and keeps an S23+, S22+, and his old S20 within arm's reach, which gives him a lot of hardware to put through its paces.

He's a medical doctor with a decade-plus obsession for consumer tech, and his coverage has also appeared on How-To Geek and Android Authority. When he's not buried in Google's apps or a Samsung settings menu, he's trying to get his chess rating past 1500 or playing table tennis/football.

I use AI a lot to summarize long text, break down complex information, and even build stuff, like this RPG habit tracker. I lean more toward Claude for most things, but Gemini is my go-to when I use Google apps on my phone, since it's built into them. It's the same thing on my laptop, except that I run most Google software through the Chrome browser. So, when I learned that Google released the Gemini app for Windows, I was excited to finally have Google's AI available anywhere on my PC, not only in a browser. Given what Google had done with the Mac app, there was a lot to look forward to. However, the Windows app let me down quickly after I started using it. Let me explain.

The shortcut is the best thing about Gemini on Windows

It's only one command away

The headline feature of the Gemini Windows app is a keyboard shortcut. After you install it, press Alt + Space to open Gemini in a small window over what you're working on. You can type or paste prompts as usual, switch models, and use the same tools your subscription gets you on the web. It works much like Gemini in a browser, just easier to reach. Instead of opening Chrome and finding my Gemini tab, I press Alt + Space, and it's there. That alone is a nice productivity boost. The problem is what it fails to do.

Gemini on Windows has no additional features

It's no different from Gemini in a browser

I quickly realized that, apart from the shortcut, the Gemini app doesn't do anything different from the website. As far as I can tell, it isn't missing anything from the web version, but it doesn't add anything either. That wouldn't have bothered me as much if Google hadn't released a Mac version nearly five months earlier that works like an assistant for your whole computer.

Gemini on Mac has all the best features

Speak to window, screen sharing, Spark

Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police

My personal favorite is window sharing. On a Mac, you can share a window or your whole screen with Gemini, giving it context for whatever you're asking about without copy-pasting text or taking screenshots. If I'm stuck on a confusing settings page or a long PDF, that's exactly when I want an assistant to pop up and understand what I need from a short prompt. Otherwise, I might as well use the web app. Another one is Speak to Windows. On a Mac, you can hold the Fn key to dictate into any app without opening Gemini. It also acts on what you say if you turn on Use reasoning. For example, if you ask it to draft a reply to an email you're reading or summarize the document on your screen, it'll deliver the result inside the respective app. That's different from the Dictate button, which only lets you speak prompts into Gemini's text box, and it's available everywhere, including Windows. There's also Gemini Spark, Google's AI agent, that can access chosen folders on a Mac. It can edit documents, organize files, and email those files if you want. However, Spark on Windows works the same way it does in your browser. It can't access your local files.

I couldn't try it myself, since Spark isn't available in my country, even on my Google AI Pro plan. You'll need to be in a supported country and have a Pro or Ultra subscription to use it.

The missing features will come, but when?

Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police

Google launched the Gemini Windows app on Sept. 10, five months after it arrived on macOS. After all that time, all we got was a direct port of the web app, rather than an actual assistant. Google said those features will eventually come, but we don't know when. It's been over three weeks since launch, and none of the Mac features have arrived. You can still install the app, but you're probably better off sticking to the Google app for desktop. It launches with the same Alt + Space shortcut, searches the web with AI, uses the Fast and Pro Gemini models to answer queries, supports full-screen sharing, and includes a Lens shortcut to share screen snippets or text. And if you spend most of your day in Chrome as I do, use Gemini's Chrome sidebar. It can read your page, which is more than the Gemini Windows app can do.

articles.body: News - Coca Leaves Found in Llama Wool at Peru’s Tambo Viejo    Archaeology Magazine

scored.body:
CALGARY, CANADA—According to a Phys.org report, coca leaves have been found in the fur of sacrificed llamas at the site of Tambo Viejo, a fortified site built in southern Peru’s Acarí Valley by the Inca, who annexed the territory into their empire in the early fifteenth century. “Above all, coca was a sacred plant to the Incas and according to [Spanish] written records was used in almost every single ritual activity,” said Lidio Valdez of the University of Calgary. He explained that although coca leaves and seeds have been previously unearthed in storage areas at Peruvian archaeological sites, this is the first time that they have been discovered in a ritual context. The leaves were found in the wool of three young llamas that had been decorated with tassels and red markings. Their legs had been tied in a folded position. River sand was poured over the bodies of the llamas, and then four guinea pigs were laid on top of the sand. More sand was added, and then a fire was lit before the deposit was sealed under a clay floor. “I would imagine the sacrificial animals (llamas) [being] paraded in a procession in the main plaza and the leaders of the rituals given rousing speeches to those present,” Valdez said. To read about coca plants recovered from the hair of mummified people in southern Peru, go to "Earliest Ayahuasca Trip."

ENGLEWOOD, N.J., Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Dfinitiv today introduced SmartCXP AI™, a platform for loyalty programs to build and manage branded experiences in AI assistants, including ChatGPT and Claude. It is built on SmartCXP™ Cloud, the production-proven commerce experience platform that connects member identity, benefits, partner offers, and approved actions to those assistants.

AI assistants are becoming another channel where members discover, travel, shop, and engage with brands. New assistants such as Meta's Muse keep arriving, each with its own rules. Programs need one way to keep benefits and offers current, govern member actions, and see what members ask.

Forrester sees a choice ahead for brands due to the popularity of answer engines. In "The State Of Agentic Commerce in Mid-2026" (Forrester Research, Inc blogs., May 28, 2026), Principal Analyst Emily Pfeiffer writes, "Brands must decide whether and where to participate, based on their fit for both owned and non-owned conversational commerce experiences."

"SmartCXP AI gives programs one place to act on that decision. Your members are already turning to AI for travel, shopping, dining, and more, and every month brings a new assistant," said Joe Fitzgerald, CEO and co-founder of Dfinitiv. "AI is becoming a channel for loyalty programs, but it is many channels at once. Benefits change. Partners change. Offers change. Delivering accurate answers and useful actions across those channels, while understanding what members ask, requires a platform behind each connected experience."

From Question to Action

Members sign in on the assistant, and the program recognizes them and applies its own rules. Dfinitiv calls these Agentic Loyalty Experiences™. An assistant can surface current benefits and nearby partner offers, route partner questions to the right partner, and start purchases or enrollment with the member's approval. Where an assistant does not support in-chat transactions, the experience hands off to the program's own checkout. All authorized actions are logged. Each AI assistant sets its own rules for which actions are allowed in its environment.

Three Integrated Components

SmartCXP AI Forge lets teams describe what they want, then creates the program's AI app for both owned and non-owned assistants, including the MCP server, tools, interactive responses, and guardrails. Every change is versioned, with rollback.

SmartCXP AI Engine is the governed runtime in the program's private environment, serving every assistant from the same guardrails and knowledge base.

SmartCXP AI Center shows which assistants use the program's tools, the questions and topics members bring, cost per question, and gaps in available answers.

Proven in Production

SmartCXP™ Cloud integrates loyalty programs and their partner ecosystems to engage members across mobile and digital channels, with permissioned, wallet-based purchases, partner enrollment, and affiliate and card-linked offers.

"Dfinitiv has been a good partner to MileagePlus, with its SmartCXP™ Cloud platform powering our MileagePlus X experience across shopping, dining, and gift cards on iOS and Android," said BJ Youngerman, Managing Director, Loyalty Partnerships at United Airlines.

Deployment and Availability

SmartCXP AI™ connects to the loyalty, identity, and partner systems a program already runs. Each deployment runs in a dedicated AWS environment, and Dfinitiv does not use member data to train AI models. Programs can build with Dfinitiv, their own teams, or a systems integrator.

SmartCXP AI is available October 7. Programs can test-drive AI Forge at forge.smartcxp.com, then run a proof of concept on their own benefits and partners. As part of the PhocusWright Innovation program, Dfinitiv will demonstrate SmartCXP AI at The PhocusWright Conference, November 17–19, 2026, in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.

About Dfinitiv

Dfinitiv is the company behind SmartCXP™, the AI-powered Commerce Experience Platform (CXP) for loyalty programs. SmartCXP connects members with their program's partners, offers, benefits and rewards wherever they spend time: inside AI assistants through SmartCXP AI™, which delivers Agentic Loyalty Experiences™, as well as in the program's mobile app, in the browser and on digital screens. Founded in 2022 by the enterprise software team behind Novadigm (acquired by HP), ManageIQ (acquired by Red Hat) and Ansible's growth at Red Hat, Dfinitiv is based in Englewood, N.J. Learn more at dfinitiv.io.

ChatGPT is a trademark of OpenAI. Claude is a trademark of Anthropic, PBC. Muse is a trademark of Meta Platforms, Inc. SmartCXP, SmartCXP AI and Agentic Loyalty Experiences are trademarks of Dfinitiv. All other trademarks are the property of their respective owners.

articles.headline: GPT-6.1 Sol + Claude Opus 5.5: 5 Details That Matter for Builders - BASENOR
articles.body: GPT-6.1 Sol + Claude Opus 5.5: 5 Details That Matter for Builders    BASENOR

scored.body:
A quick demo from Tesla community figure Dirty Tesla this week put a spotlight on something developers are quietly exploring: using OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol as an orchestrator to direct Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 in creative tasks — in this case, building a game from scratch. The pairing works, and the specs behind both models explain why. Here's what's worth knowing.

Source: @DirtyTesLa — October 7, 2026

1. Sol 6.1 Is OpenAI's Agentic Orchestrator, Not an xAI Product

GPT-6.1 Sol was released at OpenAI's DevDay on September 29, 2026 — a week after GPT-6 Sol debuted on September 22. OpenAI positions it as offering "near-Astra intelligence" for agentic coding, computer use, and multi-step professional workflows. The "Sol" tier sits below the flagship Astra line but punches well above its price point: on DeepSWE v1.1 (a complex software engineering benchmark), GPT-6.1 Sol matches GPT-6 Astra at roughly one-fifth of the cost, according to OpenAI.

2. Opus 5.5 Is Anthropic's Answer to Long-Horizon Coding Tasks

Claude Opus 5.5 launched September 22, 2026 as the lead model in Anthropic's Claude 5.5 family. It's built specifically for long-horizon agentic work — the kind of sustained, multi-step reasoning that game development requires. According to Anthropic, early testers completed a 680,000-line code migration in under a day and audited a 200,000-line codebase in under three hours. One tester built a game from a single prompt and reported high marks for graphics and polish — which lines up directly with what @DirtyTesLa demonstrated.

3. The Context Windows Are Enormous — and That's the Point

Both models ship with context windows that would have seemed implausible two years ago. GPT-6.1 Sol supports 1,050,000 tokens of input with up to 128,000 tokens of output. Claude Opus 5.5 matches that output ceiling at 128,000 tokens (expandable to 300,000 via Batch API beta) with a 1,000,000-token context window. For creative projects like games — where you're managing state, assets, logic, and narrative simultaneously — that headroom matters enormously.

4. The Cost Math Is More Reasonable Than You'd Expect

Running frontier models for creative work used to be prohibitively expensive for casual experimentation. The current pricing tells a different story. GPT-6.1 Sol runs at $2.00 per million input tokens and $10.00 per million output tokens, with cached input dropping to $0.10 per million, according to OpenAI. Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at $4.00 per million input tokens and $20.00 per million output tokens, with cache reads at $0.20 per million. Anthropic also notes Opus 5.5 costs 40% less to run than its predecessor, Opus 5, while matching the performance level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks.

5. Orchestrating One Model With Another Is Becoming a Real Workflow

What @DirtyTesLa's demo quietly illustrates isn't just "two good models" — it's a workflow pattern: use one model (Sol 6.1) to plan, coordinate, and delegate, while a second model (Opus 5.5) executes the heavy creative or technical lifting. Both models support adjustable reasoning effort levels (low through max), which means the orchestrating model can dial up deliberation for complex planning steps and dial it back for simpler handoffs. As agentic AI tooling matures, this kind of multi-model pipeline is likely to become a standard approach rather than an enthusiast experiment.

Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has formally documented a joint workflow between their models — that's still a user-driven pattern. But the fact that a casual demo from a Tesla community account generated immediate interest suggests the barrier to entry for this kind of multi-model creative work has dropped significantly. Worth keeping an eye on how this develops as both companies continue iterating on their agentic tiers.

articles.body: CyberXero Combines Claude Code, PentAGI and Cobalt Strike in AI-Augmented Cyberattacks    CyberSecurityNews

scored.body: CyberXero has emerged as an initial access broker that combines familiar hacking tools with artificial intelligence to run large-scale intrusions. The Russian-speaking operator targeted WordPress and e-commerce sites worldwide while separately probing Ukrainian energy and utility organizations. The campaign came to light after an open directory exposed more than 90,000 files, including scripts, AI session records and stolen data. The evidence indicates that the operation remained active during the investigation, raising concern that compromised access could be sold or reused. Analysts at SOCRadar identified the activity and linked it to a financially motivated actor using the CyberXero alias. SOCRadar said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the actor ran both automated and carefully chosen campaigns. The scale is striking. One automated run scanned 4,708 targets, found 429 accessible WordPress administration panels and placed 32 shells in 61 seconds. More than 628,000 Ukrainian people had confirmed data in the actor’s possession, including residents of Kharkiv. CyberXero Combines Claude Code, PentAGI and Cobalt Strike CyberXero used two AI layers rather than treating AI as a simple writing assistant. On a primary workstation, the actor configured up to 51 Claude Code agents for web discovery, password testing, exploitation and data theft, a pattern that mirrors other Claude AI attack automation cases involving commercial AI tools. A second setup connected PentAGI, an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework, to a Cobalt Strike Team Server through an AI provider API. Recovered settings reportedly assigned models and token budgets according to task complexity, reserving greater effort for payload generation while cheaper roles handled searches and installations. CyberXero’s opportunistic and directed pipelines (Source – SOCRadar) Separate Claude Code ransomware intrusions have likewise shown AI handling multiple attack stages. Session logs showed the operator trying to overcome refusals by claiming that targets were owned systems undergoing authorized testing. When a request was rejected, the actor opened a fresh session with the same preloaded story, showing how session resets can weaken the practical value of single-session safeguards. The logs also recorded refusals that held, including requests to install a backdoor, disable a firewall, move across a network and deploy a webshell. This makes secure handling of agent logs essential: organizations should encrypt them, limit access, retain audit trails and treat them like credentials or cryptographic keys. Websites and Ukrainian Infrastructure CyberXero’s broad campaign focused on WordPress and e-commerce targets. Its internal wp2shell package abused the WordPress REST API batch endpoint to inject SQL, create a rogue administrator and install a WSO-family webshell, making prompt patching critical for sites affected by the wp2shell remote execution vulnerability chain on vulnerable installations. The actor also targeted Magento and used Support Board CVE-2026-4815 within 30 days of disclosure. Administrators should verify WordPress updates, inspect for unfamiliar plugins and unexpected administrator accounts, restrict internet-facing Redis, and review authorized SSH keys for unauthorized changes. The more selective pipeline mapped seven Ukrainian energy and utility entities, including the national transmission system operator and the country’s largest private energy holding. Specialized Claude Code agent definitions in the agent directory on the primary workstation (Source – SOCRadar) It enumerated 95 subdomains across two organizations and identified services ranging from email and VPN systems to network dispatch platforms. Four Ukrainian organizations had file-confirmed data theft. A Kharkiv district heating provider lost 564,073 subscriber records and 213,340 access-log entries after the actor used a hardcoded credential in its own script, a reminder that Ukrainian infrastructure attack risks can extend beyond service disruption. The campaign affected more than 40 organizations globally, with activity also observed in Poland, China and Pakistan. While the researchers found no direct proof of an access sale, the mix of broad harvesting and detailed energy-sector reconnaissance suggests a serious risk to organizations whose systems or data are exposed. Investigators first observed the infrastructure in July 2026 and mapped eight connected nodes across European hosting and Tencent Cloud. The exposed working directory contained more than 3,000 subdirectories, allowing researchers to connect workstation activity, provisioning records and attack staging through shared artifacts. This visibility helped distinguish confirmed data theft from reconnaissance that had not produced a verified compromise at the time of the investigation. scored.body: AI coding assistants generate code faster than teams can verify. Legacy frameworks (Selenium, Cypress, Playwright) rely on brittle selectors that break with every UI change, so teams maintain tests instead of shipping. Reliability stalls near 95%, and false failures teach engineers to ignore alerts. Momentic AI lets engineers write tests in plain English. Locator, assertion, visual, and extraction agents call Claude Opus and Sonnet 4.6 plus OpenAI models via Foundry, run on Azure, and report through GitHub Actions and an MCP server for Copilot, Claude Code, and Cursor. Momentic runs 200M+ test steps a month for 2,600+ users at 99.2% reliability, stopping 390,000+ bugs from reaching production monthly. Teams automate about 70% faster than on legacy frameworks. On Microsoft Foundry, onboarding a new model provider dropped from weeks of billing, access, and rate-limit tuning to two or three hours.

Forte Group, the AI-first product development firm, today announced it has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track.

The next phase of enterprise AI won't be won by whoever adopts the fastest; it will be won by those who can prove their AI delivers real value and stays under control.”— Mikael Carlsson, CEO of Forte Group.BOCA RATON, FL, UNITED STATES, October 7, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Forte Group, the AI-first product development firm, today announced it has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track. The designation recognizes the Claude-focused AI consulting practice Forte Group has already built, and the production-grade systems for enterprise clients across financial services, healthcare, SaaS, and private equity that Forte Group has already launched.‍Customer value has already been delivered by Forte Group across industries. At Xceptor, a data automation platform used by financial institutions including Fortune 500 clients, Forte Group moved Xceptor's engineering team from ad hoc AI tool use to a governed, agentic product development pipeline built on Claude, with every AI-generated artifact passing a named human gate before it shipped. Michael Kinloch, Xceptor's SVP of Engineering, co-presented the results publicly at CTO Craft London in March 2026 and CTO Craft Toronto in May 2026. Connector builds that once took two weeks now ship in two days, an 83% cost reduction; rework fell from roughly 30% to under 10%; and story creation runs 3x faster.

"The next phase of enterprise AI won't be won by whoever adopts the fastest," said Mikael Carlsson, CEO of Forte Group. "It will be won by those who can prove their AI delivers real value and stays under control. We've spent the last two years building exactly that, on Claude, in production, for clients in regulated industries. This achievement means we can bring that discipline to far more organizations, done right from day one."

The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers. The Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients, and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through Certified, Select, Preferred, and Global Premier tiers.

"Moving from AI experimentation to AI-native operations needs structure, not just ambition," said Alex Lukashevich, Chief AI Officer at Forte Group. "Our Augment → Automate → Agent methodology gives enterprise clients a stage-gated, risk-managed path with measurable outcomes at every step — every stage owned by a named person, not a model acting alone."

To learn more about Forte Group's Claude practice, visit fortegrp.com

articles.headline: Sen. Cantwell defends AI safety proposal - The Seattle Times
articles.body: Sen. Cantwell defends AI safety proposal    The Seattle Times

scored.body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Sen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate committee overseeing artificial intelligence, on Wednesday unveiled a set of principles for regulating AI, making a fresh push for congressional action as concerns proliferate over the safety of the technology. Cantwell’s framework would put enforceable federal safety standards at the center of U.S. AI policy, including testing and third-party audits of the most advanced systems before they are released. She is betting that a rapidly changing landscape, growing public anxiety and calls from parts of the industry for government intervention could create an opening for bipartisan action.Cantwell’s proposal leaves some fundamental questions unanswered.Tech industry leaders have increasingly called for clear federal standards to govern the development and deployment of advanced AI, arguing that a patchwork of rules or uncertainty could hinder innovation and create conflicting requirements. AI safety experts and advocates say Congress must move quickly to enact specific and rigorous rules that address who should oversee AI, whether development should slow until guardrails are in place, how to ensure independent auditing and how regulators can keep pace with the technology’s rapid evolution.Key details within Cantwell’s proffered principles, including penalties for noncompliance or what a third-party auditing entity would entail, remain unresolved.Asked whether her principles are aggressive or specific enough to meet the moment, Cantwell pointed to the lack of comprehensive alternatives. “Have you seen something else?” she said in an interview with The Seattle Times. “These are very comprehensive, in the way that the system could work. But now we have got to get people to dialogue about that.”

“We have to hear from people about what that looks like,” she added. “We’re not trying to be vague. We’re saying that it is part of the process of figuring out what it actually would look like.”The proposal is the latest attempt by federal lawmakers to suggest how to rein in the fast-growing AI industry amid clarion calls for regulations and growing backlash from voters over data center construction. The scramble for regulations — increasingly framed as a national security imperative — quickened this summer after OpenAI’s unreleased AI agents breached the infrastructure of AI startup Hugging Face.Democratic lawmakers largely agree that AI needs regulation, but not on what the regulator should look like.Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, recently introduced a bill to ban superintelligence and temporarily pause AI development, overseen by a new Cabinet-level federal agency; Rep. Pramila Jayapal last week proposed a framework modeled on bank regulation, requiring every AI firm to hold a federal charter to do business in the U.S.; Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., have not yet released bill text on their own proposal to address catastrophic risks from advanced AI models.Despite the flurry of ideas, Congress has not advanced any comprehensive AI legislation this year, stymied by divisions within and between political parties. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has opposed demands for new regulation, dismissing warnings about AI’s catastrophic risks as a “hoax.”“Now is the opportunity to use the moment of the industry calling for oversight and standards, and their fear of what could happen … to get more people on the same page,” Cantwell said. “When we tried to pass some of these ideas in a bill two years ago, they got blocked, and so I’m hoping that this will now get us back to a more participatory framework with our colleagues from both sides of the aisle.”

“There are members who believe in standards on the Republican side,” she added. “So we have to find those members who want to pursue that avenue.”Cantwell, who is a former tech executive, holds a powerful position to influence what comes next. If Democrats retake the Senate after the November midterm election, she is poised to take the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation gavel in January from Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who has not convened markups on bipartisan AI safety legislation this year.Her principles are a precursor to more comprehensive legislation she says is imminent, and a framework she hopes can give Congress a common starting point.“These principles lay the groundwork for serious and comprehensive legislative action that creates strong guardrails for AI’s risks and earn the public’s trust, while promoting AI’s potential and positioning American AI as the gold standard for the world,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said in a statement backing the proposal.Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith said the senator’s principles “will help the public consider the issues that matter.” “Senator Cantwell’s framework advances the public discussion the nation needs as we consider the future of AI,” Smith said in a statement Wednesday morning.

The blueprintThe newly released principles largely replicate the core ideas from Cantwell and Republican Sen. Todd Young’s Future of AI Innovation Act of 2024, which sought to establish voluntary standards and assessments and create a test bed program at classified national labs. That bill never reached a vote on the Republican-controlled Senate floor.Now, Cantwell is urging the U.S. to adopt enforceable safety standards that are developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in coordination with key federal agencies, such as the Department of Energy and the Department of Defense, as well as researchers and frontier AI companies.Cantwell proposes first building what she calls a national AI ecosystem of frontier AI companies, universities, independent researchers and the federal government. Led by NIST, those entities would establish mandatory safety and security standards for advanced AI systems that pose the most risks, such as cyberattacks and the potential loss of human control. Those standards would be updated as AI evolves. Advanced models would undergo government or third-party testing — or both — followed by a third-party audit to ensure models meets federal standards before release. Companies that fail to comply could face civil and criminal penalties, while government and independent experts would continually scrutinize and stress-test advanced models. The precise testing and oversight regime has yet to be determined.Developers would have to give testers and auditors access to assess risks and promptly report safety incidents, although the principles do not define “promptly.”The approach echoes calls from some of the industry’s most prominent leaders. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for mandatory third-party evaluations and federal authority to block models based on the findings, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has agreed that independent evaluators should have employee-like access.

The principles — which Cantwell’s office said are likely to evolve as discussions continue — also call for greater corporate transparency, public-private partnerships, measures to mitigate social harms and global cooperation. They seek protections for children’s safety online and say AI companies should fund apprenticeships, education and worker training to prevent displacement. Environmental harms are not addressed, though Cantwell said “they should be.”Cantwell also proposes a “secure channel” with China for communication when a significant AI incident could threaten either country or international security. What’s still missingExperts and advocates for AI safety and security — who had not yet seen Cantwell’s principles but discussed with The Times what they want from Congress — broadly called for mandatory federal standards, testing and auditing before advanced models are released. However, among the eight experts The Times spoke with, some calls are left unanswered in Cantwell’s principles. Some called for a new centralized executive agency or subagency to oversee AI regulations. Others argued development should slow down until federal guardrails are in place. Many pointed to environmental harms and growing consumer privacy concerns. Multiple experts preferred government testing over third-party testers, questioning whether private entities could remain independent of corporate interests.Every expert underscored the urgency of the moment.“Unless we act soon, we are actively losing control — and by we, I mean the public and policymakers, everyone who’s not inside of the company,” said Stephen Casper, computer scientist and assistant professor at Harvard Kennedy School.

A closing windowThe House and Senate won’t reconvene until after the midterm election. When Congress returns in mid-November, the chambers will have few remaining days in session together, tanking the likelihood of comprehensive AI legislation this year.But Cantwell signaled confidence that such legislation can advance next year — and suggested Congress could use the remaining weeks to enact short-term guardrails to ward against the biggest risks. She did not elaborate, pointing instead to input from federal players such as NIST and the Department of Energy.“I do think that they can right now come up with the biggest risk scenarios and outline them, and that should be something that we could get done quickly while they’re looking at the larger system,” Cantwell said. “Congress can move fast when it wants to, and it feels like it’s under threat.” Cantwell did not offer a timeline for developing the mandatory federal standards. But she rejected the idea it would take years to establish them.“We don’t know all the answers, but we know the general direction that we need to go, and we know the importance of these various roles that people play,” Cantwell added. “But we have to get even more concrete about it in a short period of time.”Anumita Kaur reported from Washington, D.C., and Destiny Muller reported from Seattle.

Anumita Kaur: akaur@seattletimes.com: Anumita Kaur is the Washington, D.C., correspondent for The Seattle Times, where she covers federal government and national politics with a Pacific Northwest focus.Destiny Muller: 206-652-6373 or dmuller@seattletimes.com: Destiny Muller is an AI reporter and Tarbell Fellow at The Seattle Times who writes about how AI is impacting politics, business, and society across Washington state. She holds degrees in journalism and economics from the University of Missouri and a master's degree in political sociology from the London School of Economics, where she worked in UK AI policy and global governance research.
